rows.credit: NPS Photo / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Polygonal ground and ponds on the tundra in Noatak National Preserve, Alaska, photographed from the air.
rows.caption: Ice-wedge polygons in Alaska's Noatak tundra. Repeated thermal contraction cracking and ice growth organize the permafrost landscape.

rows.credit: Diego Delso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rock formations and the Tara salt flat in northern Chile's Atacama Desert.
rows.caption: Salar de Tara in the high Atacama, northern Chile. Sinking subtropical air, the cold Humboldt Current and the Andes rain shadow together keep this landscape extremely dry.

rows.credit: Jeff Schmaltz / NASA GSFC · Terra MODIS / LANCE-EOSDIS · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Terra MODIS natural-color view of Bangladesh, its delta channels and the Sundarbans beside the Bay of Bengal.
rows.caption: Bangladesh, Terra MODIS, 9 November 2011. River-borne sediment builds the broad delta and coastal plain; folded hills lie to the east.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Long fault-bounded valleys and escarpments in Kenya's East African Rift, viewed from the ISS.
rows.caption: The East African Rift in Kenya, photographed from the ISS. Faults and long rift valleys mark where eastern Africa is slowly being pulled apart.

rows.credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NOAA sea-surface temperature anomaly map with warmer-than-average water across the equatorial Pacific in late 2015.
rows.caption: NOAA, 11 October–7 November 2015: positive sea-surface temperature anomalies extend across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific during El Niño.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Snow-covered Himalayan peaks and valleys photographed from the International Space Station.
rows.caption: The Himalaya photographed from the ISS, looking south from over the Tibetan Plateau. India’s collision with Asia thickened the crust and raised these mountains.

rows.credit: Richard Sutcliffe / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A low grassy coastal terrace below an older cliff near Northbank.
rows.caption: A raised beach near West Kilbride on the Firth of Clyde. This former shoreline now stands above the sea because the land has risen since the ice sheet melted.

rows.credit: Stephen Poole from Malton, England / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A winding road descends Honister Pass through steep slopes in Cumbria.
rows.caption: Honister Pass, Cumbria, where 341.4 mm of rain fell in 24 hours during Storm Desmond in December 2015, a UK record. The photograph shows the fells in calm weather, not the storm.

rows.credit: Mass Communication Specialist 3rd Class Dylan McCord / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of debris, damaged buildings and flooded land at a fishing port in Kesennuma after the 2011 tsunami.
rows.caption: Kesennuma, Japan, after the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami. The photograph shows damage left by the inundation, not the wave itself.

rows.credit: SAC Faye Storer / UK Ministry of Defence · Crown copyright / Open Government Licence v1.0 · cropped and resized
rows.alt: Patchy winter snow over dark exposed rock and heath on a Cairngorm mountainside.
rows.caption: Winter in the Cairngorms. Bright snow reflects far more sunlight than the darker exposed ground, so patchy cover changes the landscape’s albedo.

rows.credit: Steve Redman / US National Park Service · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Snow-covered Mount Adams viewed from the Naches Loop Trail in Washington.
rows.caption: Mount Adams, Washington. This Cascade arc volcano is part of the volcanic chain above the Cascadia subduction zone.

rows.credit: Kyle Hawton / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Glen Canyon Dam holds back Lake Powell above a narrow river gorge.
rows.caption: Glen Canyon Dam and Lake Powell, Arizona. Reservoir storage and controlled releases alter the timing and size of flows downstream.

rows.credit: Rich Keen / DPRA / USFWS · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Denver's skyline and distant mountain slopes seen from Rocky Mountain Arsenal National Wildlife Refuge.
rows.caption: Denver, Colorado. The city stands on high plains beside the Rocky Mountains; elevation reduces air pressure compared with sea level.

rows.credit: Arthur Rothstein / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A car on a Texas Panhandle road beneath a wall of airborne dust during the Dust Bowl.
rows.caption: Texas Panhandle during the Dust Bowl. During severe drought, wind lifted exposed topsoil and filled the air with dust.

rows.credit: Giuseppe Milo / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Waves and wet sand beneath Naples Pier on Florida's Gulf coast at sunset.
rows.caption: Sunset at Naples Pier, on Florida's Gulf coast at almost the same latitude as Miami (about 26° N). Even in December the midday Sun here stands far higher than it does over Minneapolis.

rows.credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
rows.caption: Grand Canyon from Hopi Point, Arizona. Resistant beds form steps and cliffs above valleys cut by running water.

rows.credit: Christine Matthews / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A physical marker of the historic Greenwich Meridian at the Royal Observatory.
rows.caption: The historic Greenwich Meridian makes a reference longitude tangible. Modern WGS84 zero longitude lies about 102 meters east of this line.

rows.credit: Jim D. Griggs, HVO (USGS) staff photographer[1][2] / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An arching orange lava fountain erupts from a vent on Kīlauea amid dark cooling lava.
rows.caption: A lava fountain about 10 meters high at Kīlauea, photographed by USGS on 25 February 1983. Magma reaches the surface here, but the mantle beneath is almost entirely solid.

rows.credit: Christine Johnstone / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A low cliff of soft clay slumping onto a beach, with the sea beyond.
rows.caption: Crumbling till cliffs on the Holderness coast, one of the fastest-eroding coastlines in Europe.

rows.credit: Voice of America (Tang Huiyun) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped and resized
rows.alt: Houses on top of a steep coastal slope at Redhill Peninsula, Hong Kong, with a bare brown landslide scar running down the vegetated slope to the sea.
rows.caption: Redhill Peninsula, Hong Kong, after the record rainstorm of September 2023. The bare brown strip below the houses is the landslide scar, where saturated soil and rock slid down the steep slope toward the sea.

rows.credit: NASA Terra MODIS · Public domain · cropped and resized
rows.alt: Satellite view of Iceland with a long brown ash plume streaming south over the ocean from the south coast.
rows.caption: NASA's Terra satellite on 19 April 2010: ash from Eyjafjallajökull streams south over the Atlantic. Meltwater from the ice cap chilled and shattered the magma, making fine ash that closed much of Europe's airspace.

rows.credit: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio / JPL · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Visualization of the Hawaiian Islands with colored rings marking tsunami signals detected in the upper atmosphere, tide-gauge pins, and a timeline along the bottom.
rows.caption: NASA's GUARDIAN system tracks the 29 July 2025 Kamchatka tsunami approaching Hawaiʻi. GPS signals passing through the upper atmosphere showed the wave's ripples; the Kauaʻi station picked them up 32 minutes before the first tide gauge did, about six hours after the earthquake.

rows.credit: Austin Post, USGS · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A towering gray ash column rising from Mount St. Helens, with dark ash streaks down the snow-covered flanks.
rows.caption: Mount St. Helens, Washington, on 18 May 1980. After the north flank slid away as the largest debris avalanche in recorded history, the volcano blasted sideways and then sent an ash column many kilometers high.

rows.credit: NASA Earth Observatory (Jesse Allen, Robert Simmon) · Public domain · cropped and resized
rows.alt: Satellite view of the brown Mississippi River bending past farmland, with muddy water ponded behind a straight spillway structure on its west side.
rows.caption: The Morganza Spillway, Louisiana, the day after it was partly opened in May 2011. White flecks along the straight structure are whitewater churned through the open gates as Mississippi floodwater passes into the Atchafalaya Basin.

rows.credit: Christian David / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A narrow arm of Lake Mead between dark canyon walls, with a thick white mineral band on the rock above the water line.
rows.caption: Lake Mead in Black Canyon, just upstream of Hoover Dam, April 2026. The pale "bathtub ring" is rock that minerals in the water coated white when the lake stood higher.

rows.credit: NASA Earth Observatory, Landsat · Public domain · two images placed side by side and labeled
rows.alt: Two false-color satellite views of the same Louisiana marsh in 1985 and 2024; green marsh in 1985 has broken up into much more dark open water by 2024.
rows.caption: Bay Dosgris, about 30 miles south of New Orleans, seen by Landsat on 31 August 1985 (left) and 21 October 2024 (right). Vegetation is green and water is dark blue in these false-color images: over 39 years, much of the marsh has turned into open water.

rows.credit: Office of U.S. Senator Lisa Murkowski · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Workers in hard hats beside a new house on a raised gravel pad on the tundra, with the sea in the distance.
rows.caption: Building Mertarvik, the new village for the people of Newtok, Alaska, in September 2019. The house pads were dug through the tundra to bedrock so they will not shift as the ground freezes and thaws.

rows.credit: Lewis Clarke / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: White chalk cliffs, offshore remnants and a wave-cut base near the Pinnacles in Purbeck.
rows.caption: Chalk cliffs near the Pinnacles, Purbeck, Dorset. Waves have cut a cave into the headland, and stacks stand offshore as the cliffs retreat.

rows.credit: NOAA Corps aerial survey: Mark Moran, Phil Eastman and Dave Demers · public domain · 2005 · resized
rows.alt: Flooded streets and houses in New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina in 2005.
rows.caption: New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina, 2005. Floodwater filled low-lying neighborhoods after storm surge and flood-protection failures.

rows.credit: Шелковников Евгений Анатольевич / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of abandoned buildings at the Kola Superdeep Borehole site in Russia in 2020.
rows.caption: Kola Superdeep Borehole site, 2020. The deepest borehole reached 12.262 km within continental crust; it did not enter the mantle.

rows.credit: Stephen Poole from Malton, England / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A winding road descends Honister Pass through steep slopes in Cumbria.
rows.caption: Honister Pass, Cumbria. Glacial erosion has shaped the mountain valleys and passes.

rows.credit: Till Niermann (User:Till.niermann) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Dry, deeply dissected loess slopes near Hunyuan in Shanxi, China.
rows.caption: Loess near Hunyuan, Shanxi. Wind deposited the silt; runoff later cut gullies into the exposed ground.

rows.credit: NPS Photo / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Visitors and a park ranger stand in the broad limestone Broadway passage of Mammoth Cave, Kentucky.
rows.caption: Broadway passage, Mammoth Cave, Kentucky. Groundwater dissolution enlarged fractures in limestone into a large cave system.

rows.credit: David Brossard / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Mississippi River and Natchez–Vidalia Bridge seen from Natchez, Mississippi.
rows.caption: Natchez, Mississippi. A broad river corridor runs below the bluffs along the state's western boundary.

rows.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author or not provided / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of Bodie Island, its lighthouse, wetlands and Atlantic beach in North Carolina.
rows.caption: Bodie Island, North Carolina. A low barrier island separates Atlantic waves from sheltered wetlands.

rows.credit: Robert693 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Phoenix's skyline, transport surfaces and desert mountains seen from Sky Harbor airport.
rows.caption: Phoenix, Arizona. Paving and buildings store heat in this desert city; measuring the urban heat island needs temperature data, not a photograph.

rows.credit: Ikluft / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of the San Andreas Fault as a straight line of ridges and gullies crossing the dry Carrizo Plain.
rows.caption: The San Andreas Fault crossing the Carrizo Plain, California, seen from about 2,600 m. The straight line marks the boundary where the Pacific Plate moves north-west past the North American Plate.

rows.credit: David290 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Huangpu River curves around Lujiazui's towers in Shanghai.
rows.caption: Shanghai. Dense urban development occupies low delta ground beside the tidal Huangpu River.

rows.credit: Petersrockypics / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Snow on Gallt y Wenallt above mist in Nant Gwynant, Eryri / Snowdonia.
rows.caption: Nant Gwynant, Eryri / Snowdonia. A glacial valley lies beneath the steep Snowdon horseshoe.

rows.credit: Luc Viatour / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Nearly full Moon photographed from Hamois, Belgium, with dark maria and bright cratered highlands.
rows.caption: Nearly full Moon photographed from Hamois, Belgium. The phase is nearly the same for observers in Wales and California at the same instant; local rise times and the disc's orientation differ.

rows.credit: Rodw / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Floodwater surrounds Burrowbridge in the Somerset Levels in February 2014.
rows.caption: Burrowbridge, Somerset, February 2014. Low relief slows the drainage of extensive floodwater.

rows.credit: Eirian Evans / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Thames Barrier's silver piers beside the tidal river in London.
rows.caption: Thames Barrier, London. Movable gates reduce tidal-surge flood risk upstream; they do not remove every source of river or surface-water flooding.

rows.credit: USGS National Atlas of the United States · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Map of the United States colored by the Pacific, Mountain, Central and Eastern standard time zones, with clock faces showing 3, 4, 5 and 6 PM.
rows.caption: Standard time zones of the United States (USGS National Atlas). Each zone is roughly 15° of longitude wide, but its boundaries follow state and county lines rather than meridians.

rows.credit: EOSDIS Worldview / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Satellite view of Typhoon Mangkhut with a compact eye and spiraling cloud bands in September 2018.
rows.caption: Typhoon Mangkhut in September 2018, observed by NASA EOSDIS. The western North Pacific storm went on to strike the Philippines and southern China.

rows.credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
rows.alt: Meteosat view of Earth's day–night boundary on the December solstice, with more of the Southern Hemisphere in daylight.
rows.caption: Meteosat-9 SEVIRI, 21 December 2010. The tilted day–night boundary shows the Southern Hemisphere having longer days. Axial tilt, not a change in Earth–Sun distance, causes this seasonal pattern.

rows.credit: Colin Smith / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Sunlit shingle beach and coastal buildings at Southsea, Portsmouth.
rows.caption: Southsea, Portsmouth. In sunshine, land warms faster than the sea, which can set up a sea breeze.

rows.credit: Dietmar Rabich / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Steam and orange microbial mats around Grand Prismatic Spring in Yellowstone National Park.
rows.caption: Grand Prismatic Spring, Yellowstone National Park, Wyoming. Hot groundwater heated by a shallow magma body feeds the spring; heat-tolerant microbes color its edges.

rows.credit: Colin Smith / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: People cross pale limestone blocks separated by deep joints above Malham Cove, England.
rows.caption: Malham Cove limestone pavement. Rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide widens joints into grykes, leaving blocks called clints.

rows.credit: Diliff / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Yosemite Valley's forested floor between steep granite walls, viewed from Tunnel View.
rows.caption: Yosemite Valley, California. Glacial erosion widened and steepened a pre-existing river valley in granite.

rows.credit: Luc Viatour / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Nearly full Moon photographed from Hamois, Belgium, with dark maria and bright cratered highlands.
rows.caption: Nearly full Moon photographed from Hamois, Belgium. The phase is nearly the same for observers in Wales and California at the same instant; local rise times and the disc's orientation differ.

rows.credit: https://www.flickr.com/photos/soilscience/5140644166/ / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A Puerto Rican soil profile has a dark surface above pale carbonate-rich subsoil, with a depth scale.
rows.caption: Calciustoll near Ponce, Puerto Rico: a Mollisol with a roughly 30 cm mollic surface over a calcic horizon. Its parent material includes colluvium and weathered limestone.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rounded potholes cut into dark bedrock beside flowing water in the Presque Isle River, Michigan.
rows.caption: Presque Isle River, Michigan. Swirling, sediment-laden water has drilled potholes into the bedrock of this river in the Upper Peninsula, near Lake Superior.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / Scientific Visualization Studio · public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA CERES map of reflected shortwave radiation averaged over 2000–2015, with a 0–385 W m⁻² color scale.
rows.caption: CERES map of reflected sunlight. The solar energy absorbed by the Earth system is the incoming sunlight minus this reflected part, so the map shows absorption only indirectly.

rows.credit: Aravind Sivaraj / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A hand pump used to draw groundwater at Perambalur, India.
rows.caption: Groundwater hand pump at Perambalur, India. Abstraction removes water from an aquifer, and heavy pumping can lower the water table around a well.

rows.credit: NPS Photo / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Polygonal ground and ponds on the tundra in Noatak National Preserve, Alaska, photographed from the air.
rows.caption: Patterned ground in Alaska's Noatak region. The active layer above the permafrost thaws each summer and refreezes each winter; its depth has to be measured in the field.

rows.credit: Jesse Allen, NASA Earth Observatory, using data obtained from the Goddard Earth Sciences DAAC. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Parallel rows of clouds extend from sea ice across open water in the Bering Sea.
rows.caption: Cloud streets over the Bering Sea, 20 January 2006. Air warmed over the open water rises, expands and cools adiabatically until its water vapor condenses, forming rows of cloud aligned with the wind.

rows.credit: Sidoine MBOGNI / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
rows.caption: Tropical forest at Bodiman, Cameroon, an example of rainforest vegetation. An Af climate is defined by long-term monthly temperature and rainfall, not by vegetation alone.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The Hawaiian volcanic islands stretch across the Pacific beneath scattered white clouds in an ISS photograph.
rows.caption: Hawaiʻi from the ISS. The volcanic chain records Pacific plate motion relative to a long-lived hotspot; the youngest main island is at the southeast end.

rows.credit: National Weather Service Office in Burlington, Vermont / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: US National Weather Service surface weather chart for 6 January 1998 with isobars, high and low centers and fronts.
rows.caption: US National Weather Service surface chart, 6 January 1998. Isobars join places with equal pressure; a strong high over Canada and a low near Lake Erie, with a warm front toward New England, set up a strong pressure gradient during the 1998 ice storm.

rows.credit: SAC Faye Storer / UK Ministry of Defence · Crown copyright / Open Government Licence v1.0 · cropped and resized
rows.alt: Patchy winter snow over dark exposed rock and heath on a Cairngorm mountainside.
rows.caption: Patchy winter snow in the Cairngorms. Fresh snow reflects most incoming sunlight (high albedo), while the dark rock and heath absorb much more (low albedo).

rows.credit: Colin Vosper / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rock layers bent into an arch in a small headland at Coppet Hall beach, Pembrokeshire.
rows.caption: An anticline at Coppet Hall, near Saundersfoot, Pembrokeshire. The rock layers are bent upward into an arch, with the oldest beds in the core.

rows.credit: National Weather Service Office in Burlington, Vermont / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: US National Weather Service surface weather chart for 6 January 1998 with isobars, high and low centers and fronts.
rows.caption: US National Weather Service surface chart, 6 January 1998. Isobars join places with equal pressure; a strong high over Canada and a low near Lake Erie, with a warm front toward New England, set up a strong pressure gradient during the 1998 ice storm.

rows.credit: MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA GSFC / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Satellite image of the parallel folded ridges of the Appalachian Mountains and Chesapeake Bay.
rows.caption: NASA Terra MODIS, 15 September 2023. Appalachian ridges and valleys across Virginia, West Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania preserve the structure of an ancient mountain belt.

rows.credit: USGS Office of Groundwater / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: USGS map showing the distribution of principal aquifers across the United States.
rows.caption: USGS principal aquifers of the United States, 2000. Colors identify aquifer systems; the map does not show water-table depth or whether an aquifer is confined at a particular well.

rows.credit: Peter Pearson / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Gray London Clay exposed below yellow-brown Red Crag in the sea cliffs at Walton-on-the-Naze, Essex.
rows.caption: London Clay forms the lower part of the Naze cliffs. Clay-rich beds let groundwater through only slowly, so they can act as aquitards.

rows.credit: Denali National Park and Preserve / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Glacier ice occupies a steep-sided mountain basin in Denali National Park, Alaska.
rows.caption: Glacial terrain in the Muldrow Glacier area, Denali. Ice erosion enlarges mountain hollows into cirques and sharpens the ridges between them.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Green crystalline mantle peridotite enclosed by darker volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona.
rows.caption: Mantle peridotite in volcanic rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona: a real sample of upper-mantle rock. The mantle is almost entirely solid; magma forms only where small amounts of rock partly melt.

rows.credit: NASA/SDO, AIA / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A sequence of dark Venus silhouettes crosses the Sun in SDO ultraviolet observations.
rows.caption: SDO's time sequence of the 2012 transit of Venus. A transit can happen only when Venus is near a node of its orbit. Timing past transits helped measure the Earth–Sun distance, now defined precisely as the astronomical unit.

rows.credit: Gaisarix / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rounded gray stones and pebbles of different sizes on an English North Sea beach.
rows.caption: Pebbles on the North Sea coast of England. Repeated collisions round and shrink fragments through attrition.

rows.credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
rows.alt: Meteosat view of Earth's day–night boundary on the December solstice, with more of the Southern Hemisphere in daylight.
rows.caption: Meteosat-9 observed this day–night boundary on 21 December 2010. Earth's tilted axis puts the overhead Sun south of the equator, giving southern latitudes longer days. Declination is the Sun's angle north or south of the equator's plane.

rows.credit: The original uploader was Michaila vnuk at Ukrainian Wikipedia. / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A soil profile on the Karelian Isthmus with a dark surface, pale leached layer and browner subsoil.
rows.caption: Podzolic soil on the Karelian Isthmus. The pale E horizon has lost material by eluviation; material may accumulate in the B horizon below.

rows.credit: Luca Galuzzi (Lucag) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: Tall orange sand dunes under a clear sky at Sossusvlei, Namibia.
rows.caption: Sossusvlei dunes, Namib Desert. Wind moves sand grains by saltation (bouncing) and surface creep, building dunes over time.

rows.credit: Jan Nyssen, Sander Tielens, Tesfamichael Gebreyohannes, Tigist Araya, Kassa Teka, Johan Van de Wauw, Karen Degeyndt, Katrien Descheemaeker, Kassa Amare, Mitiku Haile, Amanuel Zenebe, Neil Munro, Kristine Walraevens, Kindeya Gebrehiwot, Jean Poesen, Amaury Frankl, Alemtsehay Tsegay, Jozef Deckers / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: Field photographs of red and black soils at different positions on the Addi Selam hillslope in Ethiopia.
rows.caption: Addi Selam, Ethiopia (published field figure). A: red soil on the upper slope near the town; B: dark, clay-rich soil on the gentler lower ground. Slope position changes drainage and how material moves, so the soils differ along the catena.

rows.credit: NASA Astronaut photograph from ISS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Crescent-shaped dunes around Lagoa dos Barros on Brazil's Atlantic coast, seen from the ISS.
rows.caption: Wind shapes barchan dunes beside Lagoa dos Barros, Brazil. The crescent tips point downwind.

rows.credit: Jacques Descloitres, MODIS Land Rapid Response Team / NASA GSFC · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Hawaiian islands with greener windward slopes, drier leeward slopes and silvery sunglint on the Pacific.
rows.caption: The mountains of the Hawaiian islands interrupt the trade winds. Greener windward slopes and drier leeward slopes show the landscape contrast associated with this mountain barrier.

rows.credit: Jesse Allen / NASA Earth Observatory · Landsat · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Landsat view of the northern Gulf of Mexico coast, with barrier islands off Mississippi and Alabama and the faint Chandeleur arc off Louisiana.
rows.caption: Landsat image of the northern Gulf of Mexico coast (colors enhanced). The bright chain of narrow sandy islands lies off Mississippi and Alabama; the faint curved arc at lower left is Louisiana's Chandeleur Islands. All are barrier islands separated from the mainland by shallow water.

rows.credit: National Oceanic & Atmospheric Adminstration (NOAA) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Rounded pillow lava on a fissured seafloor at the Galápagos Rift, photographed by a NOAA expedition.
rows.caption: NOAA, Galápagos Rift, 21 July 2011. Lava quenched in seawater forms pillows close to a spreading center, where new oceanic crust is built.

rows.credit: Kingsmasher678 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A karst spring in Alabama flows over rocks from a wooded limestone slope.
rows.caption: Groundwater emerges at a karst spring in Alabama. Water stored in connected pores and fractures can return to the surface as spring flow.

rows.credit: Godot13 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view across the dry erosional basin of Makhtesh Ramon in Israel's Negev Desert.
rows.caption: Makhtesh Ramon, Israel, seen from the air: the wide floor of a large basin in the Negev Desert. Erosion of folded sedimentary rock carved it out; it is not an impact crater.

rows.credit: Ustill / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 de · resized
rows.alt: A broad, grassy former river valley near Blumberg, now drained by the much smaller Aitrach.
rows.caption: The Aitrach valley follows the former route of the Feldberg Danube. Capture by the Wutach diverted its upper flow toward the Rhine, leaving the small Aitrach in an oversized valley.

rows.credit: Gordon Hatton / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A lone ash tree growing out of a crack in a limestone pavement above Grassington.
rows.caption: An ash tree growing out of a grike in limestone pavement above Grassington, Yorkshire Dales. Roots in the crack can widen it, and acids from roots and decaying leaves help dissolve the rock.

rows.credit: Bjørn Christian Tørrissen / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Grassland with scattered acacia trees in Serengeti National Park, Tanzania.
rows.caption: Serengeti savanna: seasonal rainfall helps explain the balance between grasses and scattered trees.

rows.credit: Chris Andrews / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Angular rock blocks cover the summit of Foel Fras in Wales.
rows.caption: Blockfield on Foel Fras, Wales. Physical weathering breaks bedrock into angular fragments without changing its minerals.

rows.credit: National Weather Service Office in Burlington, Vermont / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: US National Weather Service surface weather chart for 6 January 1998 with isobars, high and low centers and fronts.
rows.caption: US National Weather Service surface chart, 6 January 1998. Isobars join places with equal pressure; a strong high over Canada and a low near Lake Erie, with a warm front toward New England, set up a strong pressure gradient during the 1998 ice storm.

rows.credit:
Mike Doukas, USGS

derivative work: User:Maps and stuff (cropped to 3:2 ratio; increased brightness in dark areas; color balanced; saved as a high quality JPG) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Deep blue Crater Lake fills a broad volcanic depression, with Wizard Island near its western shore.
rows.caption: USGS aerial photograph of Crater Lake, Oregon. Collapse following the eruption of Mount Mazama formed the caldera; Wizard Island is a younger volcanic cone.

rows.credit: PawełS / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Younger gently dipping red sandstone overlies steep gray beds at Siccar Point, Scotland.
rows.caption: Siccar Point, Scotland: Silurian beds tilted almost vertical during the Caledonian mountain building, then eroded and covered by younger Devonian sandstone. The Caledonides formed as the Iapetus Ocean closed.

rows.credit: Wilson44691 / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Fossilized Ogyopsis klotzi trilobite preserved in dark shale.
rows.caption: Ogyopsis klotzi from the Middle Cambrian Mount Stephen Trilobite Beds, Canada. Fossils help correlate and interpret ancient sedimentary rocks.

rows.credit: Lauren Dauphin / NASA Earth Observatory · Aqua MODIS / EOSDIS · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Green phytoplankton and sediment-rich water off Mauritania's desert coast, observed by Aqua MODIS.
rows.caption: Aqua MODIS, 5 May 2020. Upwelling in the Canary Current system supplies nutrients off Mauritania. The visible green water contains phytoplankton and sediment; it is not a temperature map.

rows.credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
rows.caption: Grand Canyon from Hopi Point, Arizona. Resistant beds form steps and cliffs above valleys cut by running water.

rows.credit: Colin Smith / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: People cross pale limestone blocks separated by deep joints above Malham Cove, England.
rows.caption: Malham Cove limestone pavement. Rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide widens joints into grykes, leaving blocks called clints.

rows.credit: Jan Nyssen, Sander Tielens, Tesfamichael Gebreyohannes, Tigist Araya, Kassa Teka, Johan Van de Wauw, Karen Degeyndt, Katrien Descheemaeker, Kassa Amare, Mitiku Haile, Amanuel Zenebe, Neil Munro, Kristine Walraevens, Kindeya Gebrehiwot, Jean Poesen, Amaury Frankl, Alemtsehay Tsegay, Jozef Deckers / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: Field photographs of red and black soils at different positions on the Addi Selam hillslope in Ethiopia.
rows.caption: Addi Selam, Ethiopia (published field figure). A: red soil on the upper slope near the town; B: dark, clay-rich soil on the gentler lower ground. Slope position changes drainage and how material moves, so the soils differ along the catena.

rows.credit: Manfred Heyde / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Green fields and wooded valleys on Exmoor in North Devon.
rows.caption: Exmoor, North Devon: a landscape within the Cfb oceanic climate region. Köppen classes use long-term monthly temperature and precipitation, not the weather on the day of the photograph.

rows.credit: Colin Smith / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: People cross pale limestone blocks separated by deep joints above Malham Cove, England.
rows.caption: Malham Cove limestone pavement. Rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide widens joints into grykes, leaving blocks called clints.

rows.credit: Denali National Park and Preserve / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Glacier ice occupies a steep-sided mountain basin in Denali National Park, Alaska.
rows.caption: Glacial terrain in the Muldrow Glacier area, Denali. Ice erosion enlarges mountain hollows into cirques and sharpens the ridges between them.

rows.credit: Marie-Lan Taÿ Pamart / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A pale specimen of kaolinite from Ixtassou, France.
rows.caption: Kaolinite, a clay mineral, from Ixtassou, France. In soil texture, 'clay' means particles smaller than 0.002 mm, so mineral type and particle size are different properties.

rows.credit: J.-H. Janßen / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A white Stevenson screen on legs, an instrument mast and a rain gauge on grass at a weather station.
rows.caption: Weather station at Mettingen, Germany, with a Stevenson screen for thermometers, an instrument mast and a rain gauge. Climate is worked out from many years of measurements like these.

rows.credit: Colin Smith / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: People cross pale limestone blocks separated by deep joints above Malham Cove, England.
rows.caption: Malham Cove limestone pavement. Rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide widens joints into grykes, leaving blocks called clints.

rows.credit: bgilliard from St. Catharines, Canada / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A low shelf cloud sweeps over buildings at Brock University in Ontario.
rows.caption: A cold front passes Brock University, St. Catharines, Canada. The cloud edge makes uplift visible; the front itself is a zone of contrasting air.

rows.credit: Géodigital / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A cutting at the foot of a wooded slope exposing unsorted angular stones in brown soil.
rows.caption: Recent colluvium at the foot of a slope near Avanne-Aveney, France: angular, unsorted rock fragments and soil that have moved downslope under gravity and wash.

rows.credit: NASA, MODIS Rapid Response System / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A broad spiral of white clouds over the Pacific northeast of Japan.
rows.caption: MODIS observed this extratropical cyclone northeast of Japan on 22 February 2012. Cloud bands trace the low-pressure circulation. The image joins two satellite passes, so the straight diagonal line is a seam, not a weather feature.

rows.credit: Walter Siegmund / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: Floodwater from the Stillaguamish River surrounds a picnic table and trees.
rows.caption: The Stillaguamish River, Washington, in flood. Its floods follow heavy rain, and faster floodwater can carry larger particles: the river's competence (the largest particle it can move) rises.

rows.credit: NASA Blue Marble / Mdf (projection) · public domain · via Wikimedia Commons · resized
rows.alt: NASA Blue Marble satellite imagery displayed in the curved-outline Robinson projection.
rows.caption: NASA satellite imagery in Robinson projection. This compromise projection balances several distortions; it preserves neither all areas nor all local angles.

rows.credit: Jim D. Griggs, HVO (USGS) staff photographer[1][2] / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An arching orange lava fountain erupts from a vent on Kīlauea amid dark cooling lava.
rows.caption: Lava fountains at Kīlauea show magma reaching the surface through a vent. The conduit below cannot be seen; it is inferred from geophysical measurements and eruption behavior.

rows.credit: Aravind Sivaraj / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A hand pump used to draw groundwater at Perambalur, India.
rows.caption: Groundwater hand pump at Perambalur, India. Abstraction removes water from an aquifer, and heavy pumping can lower the water table around a well.

rows.credit: USGS Office of Groundwater / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: USGS map showing the distribution of principal aquifers across the United States.
rows.caption: USGS map of principal aquifers. Low-permeability layers (aquitards) can confine an aquifer, but showing this needs a geological cross-section and well data, not a surface map.

rows.credit: Jean-Marie Vugnon (2) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Moselle joins the wider Rhine beside the city of Koblenz, Germany.
rows.caption: The Rhine–Moselle confluence at Koblenz, photographed in 1988. A tributary joins the main channel here.

rows.credit: Mdf / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA Blue Marble imagery in Mercator projection, with strongly enlarged high-latitude regions.
rows.caption: NASA Blue Marble imagery reprojected by Mdf into Mercator. Local angles are preserved, area grows toward the poles, and a constant-bearing route plots as a straight line.

rows.credit: Alvesgaspar / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: A breaking wave curls and foams along the coast at Porto Covo, Portugal.
rows.caption: A breaking wave at Porto Covo, Portugal. Whether waves build up or erode a beach depends on the balance of swash and backwash over many waves, which one photograph cannot show.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Snow-covered Himalayan peaks and valleys photographed from the International Space Station.
rows.caption: The Himalaya from the ISS: crust shortened and thickened as India collided with Eurasia.

rows.credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NOAA bathymetry map of the South Atlantic showing continental shelves and the mid-ocean ridge.
rows.caption: NOAA South Atlantic bathymetry. Color represents seafloor depth, revealing continental margins, abyssal basins and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

rows.credit: Richard Mortel / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Open grassland and sparsely vegetated hills near Jargalant, northern Mongolia.
rows.caption: Steppe near Jargalant, Mongolia, far from the moderating influence of the sea. Continental interiors usually have a large annual temperature range.

rows.credit: United States Department of the Interior Geological Survey / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: USGS topographic map of Mount Rainier with contours, glaciers and named summits.
rows.caption: USGS Mount Rainier topographic sheet, published in 1971. Contours connect equal elevations; close spacing marks steep slopes.

rows.credit: USGS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: USGS topographic map extract showing Yosemite Creek, a campground, contours and coordinate markings.
rows.caption: Part of a USGS topographic map near Yosemite Creek, California. Benchmarks (BM) and crosses give spot heights in feet, labeled contours such as 7400 and 7600 show the interval, and contours bend around spurs and valleys.

rows.credit: NASA image courtesy Jeff Schmaltz, LANCE MODIS Rapid Response. Caption by Michon Scott. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Cyclone Evan's spiral cloud bands cross the islands of Fiji in a NASA satellite image.
rows.caption: Aqua MODIS observed Cyclone Evan near Fiji on 16 December 2012. Its cloud bands spiral around the center, roughly following a logarithmic spiral.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Snow-covered Himalayan peaks and valleys photographed from the International Space Station.
rows.caption: The Himalaya from the ISS: crust shortened and thickened as India collided with Eurasia.

rows.credit: Unidentified NOAA photographer / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A Deep SOLO profiling float is lowered from the research vessel Kaʻimikai-O-Kanaloa in 2018.
rows.caption: NOAA Deep SOLO deployment, 2018. Profiling floats measure ocean temperature and salinity at depth, helping scientists study density structure and deep circulation. The ocean conveyor is a simplified description of a complex circulation.

rows.credit: NASA image courtesy Jeff Schmaltz, LANCE MODIS Rapid Response. Caption by Michon Scott. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Cyclone Evan's spiral cloud bands cross the islands of Fiji in a NASA satellite image.
rows.caption: Aqua MODIS observed Cyclone Evan near Fiji on 16 December 2012. Its cloud bands spiral around the center, roughly following a logarithmic spiral.

rows.credit: Photo by Lynn Betts, USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A sloping cornfield in western Iowa cut by rills and a gully where runoff has washed soil away.
rows.caption: Rills cut across a young Iowa cornfield where the crop still left most of the soil bare. Plant cover and residue shield the surface from raindrop impact and slow runoff; without it, soil is detached and carried away.

rows.credit: Jan Nyssen, Sander Tielens, Tesfamichael Gebreyohannes, Tigist Araya, Kassa Teka, Johan Van de Wauw, Karen Degeyndt, Katrien Descheemaeker, Kassa Amare, Mitiku Haile, Amanuel Zenebe, Neil Munro, Kristine Walraevens, Kindeya Gebrehiwot, Jean Poesen, Amaury Frankl, Alemtsehay Tsegay, Jozef Deckers / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: Field photographs of red and black soils at different positions on the Addi Selam hillslope in Ethiopia.
rows.caption: Addi Selam, Ethiopia (published field figure): profile A lies on the upper slope, near the crest, and B on the gentler ground below. Soil changes downslope as drainage and sediment movement vary.

rows.credit: Mark Reid, USGS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An aerial view of the Oso landslide's bare source scar, debris path and deposits across the valley.
rows.caption: Oso, Washington, 2014: an aerial photograph of the landslide source, travel path and deposit. The displaced material crossed the valley floor.

rows.credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
rows.caption: Grand Canyon, Arizona. The canyon cuts about 1.8 km into the continental crust, exposing layered rocks, yet continental crust is roughly 30–70 km thick. Even the deepest borehole, at Kola, reached only 12.262 km.

rows.credit: Chip Clark / Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History · CC0 · resized
rows.alt: Metallic black octahedral magnetite crystals on rock, Smithsonian specimen B10614 from Binnental, Switzerland.
rows.caption: Magnetite in the Smithsonian collection. Pure magnetite loses its magnetism above about 580 °C, its Curie temperature.

rows.credit: NASA/Kjell Lindgren / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The muddy Ucayali River winds through forest in Peru, with abandoned bends beside the active channel.
rows.caption: Ucayali River, Peru, photographed from the ISS. Meander migration leaves cut-offs and abandoned channels across the floodplain.

rows.credit: NASA, MODIS Rapid Response System / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A broad spiral of white clouds over the Pacific northeast of Japan.
rows.caption: MODIS observed this extratropical cyclone northeast of Japan on 22 February 2012. Cloud bands trace the low-pressure circulation. The image joins two satellite passes, so the straight diagonal line is a seam, not a weather feature.

rows.credit: Kyle Hawton / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Glen Canyon Dam holds back Lake Powell above a narrow river gorge.
rows.caption: Glen Canyon Dam and Lake Powell, Arizona. Reservoir storage and controlled releases alter the timing and size of flows downstream.

rows.credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
rows.alt: Meteosat view of Earth's day–night boundary on the December solstice, with more of the Southern Hemisphere in daylight.
rows.caption: Meteosat-9 observed this day–night boundary on 21 December 2010. Earth's tilted axis puts the overhead Sun south of the equator, giving southern latitudes longer days. Declination is the Sun's angle north or south of the equator's plane.

rows.credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
rows.alt: Meteosat view of Earth's day–night boundary on the December solstice, with more of the Southern Hemisphere in daylight.
rows.caption: Meteosat-9 observed this day–night boundary on 21 December 2010. Earth's tilted axis puts the overhead Sun south of the equator, giving southern latitudes longer days. Declination is the Sun's angle north or south of the equator's plane.

rows.credit: PawełS / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Younger gently dipping red sandstone overlies steep gray beds at Siccar Point, Scotland.
rows.caption: The unconformity at Siccar Point represents a gap of many millions of years. Ma means millions of years ago and ka thousands of years ago; geologists date such gaps from evidence such as fossils and radiometric ages.

rows.credit: owamux / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Circular plates of new pancake ice cover the surface of the western Ross Sea in Antarctica.
rows.caption: New pancake ice in the Ross Sea, Antarctica. Freezing leaves much of the salt behind in the water below, making it colder, saltier and denser, so it can sink and form deep water.

rows.credit: Arthur Rothstein / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A car on a Texas Panhandle road beneath a wall of airborne dust during the Dust Bowl.
rows.caption: Texas Panhandle during the 1930s Dust Bowl. Wind lifted fine topsoil from dry, bare fields: deflation removed the soil and carried the dust away in suspension.

rows.credit: none (Landsat) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: False-color Landsat image of the Lena Delta with many branching distributaries and islands.
rows.caption: Landsat's view of the Lena Delta, 2000. Distributaries spread sediment into the Arctic Ocean. The image combines infrared and red bands.

rows.credit: Unidentified NOAA photographer / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A Deep SOLO profiling float is lowered from the research vessel Kaʻimikai-O-Kanaloa in 2018.
rows.caption: A NOAA Deep SOLO float is lowered into the sea. It measures temperature and salinity, which set the water's density and identify deep-water masses such as NADW.

rows.credit: NASA, MODIS Rapid Response System / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A broad spiral of white clouds over the Pacific northeast of Japan.
rows.caption: MODIS observed this extratropical cyclone northeast of Japan on 22 February 2012. Cloud bands trace the low-pressure circulation. The image joins two satellite passes, so the straight diagonal line is a seam, not a weather feature.

rows.credit: Alvesgaspar / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: A breaking wave curls and foams along the coast at Porto Covo, Portugal.
rows.caption: A breaking wave at Porto Covo, Portugal. Whether waves remove sediment from a beach depends on strong backwash over many waves, which one photograph cannot show.

rows.credit: Alan Cressler, USGS · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A small instrument shelter on stilts beside a concrete weir on a forest stream.
rows.caption: A USGS streamgage on Little Back Creek, Virginia. It records stage, the water level, every few minutes; a rating curve turns stage into discharge, the volume of water passing per second.

rows.credit: Mdf / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA Blue Marble imagery in Mercator projection, with strongly enlarged high-latitude regions.
rows.caption: NASA Blue Marble imagery reprojected by Mdf into Mercator. Local angles are preserved, area grows toward the poles, and a constant-bearing route plots as a straight line.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: GOES-East satellite view of the Americas with tropical cloud bands and midlatitude weather systems.
rows.caption: GOES-East cloud data for 22 April 2014, laid over a cloud-free image of land and ocean. Tropical cloud bands and midlatitude storms are evidence of the global circulation. The three-cell model describes a long-term average, so it does not appear as three neat cloud rings in one image.

rows.credit: Olga Ernst / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Steep dark rock walls border the Almannagjá rift at Þingvellir, Iceland.
rows.caption: Almannagjá, Þingvellir: faults accommodate extension within Iceland's broad North American–Eurasian plate boundary zone.

rows.credit: Daredeep33 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Turquoise water fills the steep-sided Bimmah sinkhole in Oman.
rows.caption: Bimmah sinkhole, Oman. Dissolution and collapse in soluble rock can create closed depressions called dolines.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: ASTER satellite image of branching tributary valleys near the Colorado River in Canyonlands, Utah.
rows.caption: ASTER false-color image, 24 September 2005: tributaries cut into sandstone in Canyonlands, Utah. Plants along the valley floors show up red. The branching network carries water toward the Colorado River (top left).

rows.credit: PHG / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 (originally GFDL) · resized
rows.alt: Wide sandy bay with the seabed exposed after the sea drew back, framed by trees and rocks, at Kata Noi Beach, Phuket.
rows.caption: Kata Noi Beach, Phuket, Thailand, 26 December 2004: the sea has drawn back before the third and strongest tsunami wave, exposing the seabed; open water is far out to the right. Many tsunamis arrive without this warning.

rows.credit: Doc Searls from Santa Barbara, USA / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of elongated low hills around Horicon Marsh, Wisconsin.
rows.caption: Drumlin terrain near Horicon Marsh, Wisconsin. The streamlined hills record former glacier flow; they are landforms left after the ice retreated.

rows.credit: The original uploader was Michaila vnuk at Ukrainian Wikipedia. / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A soil profile on the Karelian Isthmus with a dark surface, pale leached layer and browner subsoil.
rows.caption: Podzolic soil on the Karelian Isthmus. Just below the dark surface layer, a thin pale gray band (about 7–10 cm on the tape) is the E horizon, which has lost material by eluviation. The rusty-brown B horizon below it has gained some of that material.

rows.credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NOAA sea-surface temperature anomaly map with warmer-than-average water across the equatorial Pacific in late 2015.
rows.caption: NOAA, 11 October–7 November 2015: positive sea-surface temperature anomalies extend across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific during El Niño.

rows.credit: Lauren Dauphin / NASA Earth Observatory · Aqua MODIS / EOSDIS · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Green phytoplankton and sediment-rich water off Mauritania's desert coast, observed by Aqua MODIS.
rows.caption: Aqua MODIS, 5 May 2020. Upwelling in the Canary Current system supplies nutrients off Mauritania. The visible green water contains phytoplankton and sediment; it is not a temperature map.

rows.credit: U.S. Geological Survey, US Topo 7.5-minute map for Covington, LA (2018) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped
rows.alt: Northwest corner of a USGS US Topo map of Covington, Louisiana, with a 1 km UTM grid labeled 776000 m E and 3377000 m N, and principal digits 77 to 83 along the top edge.
rows.caption: Part of the USGS US Topo map of Covington, Louisiana (2018), with its 1 km UTM grid. Eastings, the numbers along the top and bottom edges (77, 78, 79 …), increase eastward and are read first; northings, along the side edges (73, 74, 75 …), increase northward and are read second.

rows.credit: NASA/SDO, AIA / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A sequence of dark Venus silhouettes crosses the Sun in SDO ultraviolet observations.
rows.caption: SDO's time sequence of the 2012 transit of Venus. A transit can happen only when Venus is near a node of its orbit. Timing past transits helped measure the Earth–Sun distance, now defined precisely as the astronomical unit.

rows.credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NOAA sea-surface temperature anomaly map with warmer-than-average water across the equatorial Pacific in late 2015.
rows.caption: NOAA, 11 October–7 November 2015: positive sea-surface temperature anomalies extend across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific during El Niño.

rows.credit: Karthoo / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Wutach flows through a narrow, wooded gorge below exposed rock walls in the Black Forest.
rows.caption: Wutach Gorge, Germany. Capture diverted drainage from the Danube system toward the Rhine; subsequent incision cut this gorge.

rows.credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio - Marit Jentoft-Nilsen, Global Science and Technology, Inc./Amy Moran, Global Science and Technology, Inc./Heather Hanson / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: CERES global map of outgoing longwave radiation with a color scale in watts per square meter.
rows.caption: NASA CERES, April 2015. Satellite observations map outgoing thermal radiation at the top of the atmosphere in W m⁻²; colder cloud tops generally emit less than warm clear-sky regions.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / Scientific Visualization Studio · public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA CERES map of net radiation averaged over 2000–2015, with a −200 to +200 W m⁻² color scale.
rows.caption: NASA CERES observations, 2000–2015 mean. Net radiation is incoming sunlight minus reflected shortwave and emitted longwave energy at the top of the atmosphere. Positive values indicate a radiative surplus.

rows.credit: USGS · public domain · 14 August 2021 ShakeMap · resized
rows.alt: USGS ShakeMap of the 14 August 2021 Haiti earthquake with colored zones of shaking intensity.
rows.caption: USGS ShakeMap for the 14 August 2021 Haiti earthquake. The star marks the epicenter, the point on the surface above the focus; the colored rings show how shaking intensity fell with distance.

rows.credit: Strebe / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: NASA Blue Marble satellite imagery displayed in a Mollweide projection with a graticule.
rows.caption: NASA satellite imagery reprojected by Strebe into Mollweide. This equal-area projection preserves relative areas but distorts shapes; the ocean has been lightened for legibility.

rows.credit: Reto Stöckli / NASA Earth Observatory · public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA Blue Marble satellite composite of Earth in an equirectangular global map.
rows.caption: NASA Blue Marble monthly composite on an equirectangular latitude–longitude grid. Latitude measures angular distance north or south of the equator, and parallels run east–west. These reference lines are mathematical; they are not marked on the ground.

rows.credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
rows.alt: Meteosat view of Earth's nearly north–south day–night boundary at the March equinox.
rows.caption: Meteosat-9 SEVIRI, 20 March 2011. The terminator passes close to both poles around the equinox; refraction and the Sun's finite disc mean observed daylight is not exactly twelve hours everywhere.

rows.credit: Rosa Cabecinhas and Alcino Cunha / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A sharp dune crest and rippled sand at Erg Chebbi, Morocco.
rows.caption: Erg Chebbi, Morocco: a sand sea where wind-blown sand has built up into large dunes. Most of the Sahara is rock or gravel rather than erg.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rounded potholes cut into dark bedrock beside flowing water in the Presque Isle River, Michigan.
rows.caption: Presque Isle River, Michigan. Swirling, sediment-laden water has drilled potholes into the bedrock of this river in the Upper Peninsula, near Lake Superior.

rows.credit: Operational Land Imager / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Landsat view of the Thames estuary, coastal shallows and offshore wind farms.
rows.caption: NASA Landsat observation of the Thames estuary. The tidal river widens toward the North Sea; pale water reveals suspended material and shallow coastal water.

rows.credit: Giles Laurent / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Aletsch Glacier curves through a steep Alpine valley, with dark medial moraines running along its surface.
rows.caption: The Aletsch Glacier stores water on land. When land ice melts, the water flows to the ocean and raises global (eustatic) sea level.

rows.credit: Bernard Spragg. NZ from Christchurch, New Zealand / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Wisps of low fog rise above a calm lake on a frosty morning, with trees reflected in the water.
rows.caption: Evaporation fog over a lake on a cold morning. Evaporation takes energy from the water surface and cools it; the vapor then condenses into tiny droplets in the colder air above.

rows.credit: Explorer2310 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Microscope photograph of leaf epidermal cells and stomatal pores under drought conditions.
rows.caption: Leaf epidermis viewed through a microscope. Stomata regulate gas exchange and water-vapor loss; transpiration is one part of evapotranspiration.

rows.credit: NASA, MODIS Rapid Response System / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A broad spiral of white clouds over the Pacific northeast of Japan.
rows.caption: MODIS observed this extratropical cyclone northeast of Japan on 22 February 2012. Cloud bands trace the low-pressure circulation. The image joins two satellite passes, so the straight diagonal line is a seam, not a weather feature.

rows.credit: NASA astronaut Ed Lu / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The clear eye and tall spiral cloud walls of Hurricane Isabel, photographed from the ISS.
rows.caption: Astronaut Ed Lu photographed Hurricane Isabel on 13 September 2003. The eye is surrounded by the eyewall's deep convective clouds.

rows.credit: NASA astronaut Ed Lu / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The clear eye and tall spiral cloud walls of Hurricane Isabel, photographed from the ISS.
rows.caption: Astronaut Ed Lu photographed Hurricane Isabel on 13 September 2003. The eye is surrounded by the eyewall's deep convective clouds.

rows.credit: Jerrod Wheeler (submitted to USGS by Kirk Miller, Wyoming) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A streamflow-gauging station beside Huey Creek in Antarctica's rocky McMurdo Dry Valleys.
rows.caption: USGS stream gauge at Huey Creek, Antarctica. Repeated readings from a gauge build a hydrograph with its rising limb, peak and falling limb. Lag time is the time between peak rainfall and peak discharge.

rows.credit: U.S. Geological Survey, US Topo 7.5-minute map for Covington, LA (2018) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped
rows.alt: Northwest corner of a USGS US Topo map of Covington, Louisiana, with a 1 km UTM grid labeled 776000 m E and 3377000 m N, and principal digits 77 to 83 along the top edge.
rows.caption: Part of the USGS US Topo map of Covington, Louisiana (2018), with its 1 km UTM grid. UTM gives each 6° zone’s central meridian a false easting of 500,000 m so eastings stay positive, and Northern Hemisphere northings count from the equator: that is why the corner labels read 776000 m E and 3377000 m N. The British National Grid instead uses one false origin southwest of Great Britain.

rows.credit: Poyt448 Peter Woodard / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Fallen leaves and organic litter beneath white beech trees in New South Wales, Australia.
rows.caption: White beech leaf litter at Carowiry Creek, New South Wales. Organic material on the forest floor stores carbon and provides material for decomposition.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: GOES-East satellite view of the Americas with tropical cloud bands and midlatitude weather systems.
rows.caption: GOES-East cloud data for 22 April 2014, laid over a cloud-free image of land and ocean. Tropical cloud bands and midlatitude storms are evidence of the global circulation. The three-cell model describes a long-term average, so it does not appear as three neat cloud rings in one image.

rows.credit: United States Geological Survey / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A line of lava fountains and gas rises from the Kamoamoa fissure in forest southwest of Puʻu ʻŌʻō, Hawaiʻi.
rows.caption: USGS, 5 March 2011: lava erupts along a newly opened fissure between Puʻu ʻŌʻō and Nāpau, Kīlauea. Several fountains mark the linear opening.

rows.credit: Walter Siegmund / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: Floodwater from the Stillaguamish River surrounds a picnic table and trees.
rows.caption: The South Fork Stillaguamish River in flood. Water spreads beyond the usual channel when discharge exceeds channel capacity.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / Scientific Visualization Studio · public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA CERES map of reflected shortwave radiation averaged over 2000–2015, with a 0–385 W m⁻² color scale.
rows.caption: NASA CERES observations, 2000–2015 mean. Colors show sunlight reflected by the Earth system in W m⁻². This is outgoing shortwave flux, not incoming solar irradiance or albedo itself.

rows.credit: Petr Brož (Czech Academy of Science) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A pen arm resting on a white paper drum covered in fine parallel lines, one section showing a burst of wiggles.
rows.caption: A seismograph drum records ground motion as a line on paper. The arrival times of P-, S- and surface waves at many stations are used to locate an earthquake's focus and epicenter and to estimate its magnitude.

rows.credit: Kevin M. Gill / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A rounded specimen of augen gneiss with pale mineral eyes enclosed in dark, folded bands.
rows.caption: Augen gneiss: deformation and metamorphism organize minerals into bands around larger crystals. Rock-cycle pathways need not follow one fixed loop.

rows.credit: Lysippos / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rock contact exposed along the Moine Thrust at Knockan Crag in northwest Scotland.
rows.caption: The Moine Thrust at Knockan Crag, Scotland: a low-angle reverse fault (a thrust). The hanging wall above the fault plane carries older rocks over the younger footwall rocks below, recording compression.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A rock face with a dark, layered coal seam between paler beds, with dry leaves on the ledges.
rows.caption: A coal seam in Coshocton County, Ohio, about 310 million years old. Coal forms from buried swamp plants; burning it releases carbon stored for millions of years.

rows.credit: U.S. Geological Survey, US Topo 7.5-minute map for Covington, LA (2018) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped
rows.alt: Northwest corner of a USGS US Topo map of Covington, Louisiana, with a 1 km UTM grid labeled 776000 m E and 3377000 m N, and principal digits 77 to 83 along the top edge.
rows.caption: Part of the USGS US Topo map of Covington, Louisiana (2018), with its 1 km UTM grid. A four-figure reference such as 78 75 names the 1 km square whose southwest corner lies at easting 78 and northing 75; a six-figure reference narrows it to a 100 m square.

rows.credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NOAA bathymetry map of the South Atlantic showing continental shelves and the mid-ocean ridge.
rows.caption: NOAA South Atlantic bathymetry. Color represents seafloor depth, revealing continental margins, abyssal basins and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

rows.credit: Geographer / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: An orange windsock extends above a field beside the path to Green Lane Farm.
rows.caption: A windsock shows the wind direction near the ground. Friction with the land surface slows the wind and turns it across the isobars toward low pressure.

rows.credit: Chris Andrews / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Angular rock blocks cover the summit of Foel Fras in Wales.
rows.caption: Blockfield on Foel Fras, Wales. Physical weathering breaks bedrock into angular fragments without changing its minerals.

rows.credit: Surrealplaces / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A band of orange-lit cloud with a clear strip of sky beneath it over a suburban skyline.
rows.caption: A chinook arch over Calgary, Canada. As warm, dry air sinks down the lee of the Rocky Mountains, it leaves a clear strip below a long bank of cloud.

rows.credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Saturn and its broad rings in a natural-color mosaic photographed by the Cassini spacecraft.
rows.caption: Cassini, 6 October 2004: a natural-color mosaic of Saturn and its rings. The rings are a thin disc of orbiting particles.

rows.credit: C.C. Finlay, C. Kloss, N. Gillet / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Swarm-derived maps compare Earth's magnetic field intensity in 2014 and 2025, with a scale in nanotesla.
rows.caption: Maps of magnetic-field strength at Earth's surface in 2014 and 2025, modeled from Swarm satellite measurements (colors show nanotesla). The field is generated mainly by moving liquid iron in the outer core, not by a permanent bar magnet.

rows.credit: National Weather Service Office in Burlington, Vermont / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: US National Weather Service surface weather chart for 6 January 1998 with isobars, high and low centers and fronts.
rows.caption: US National Weather Service surface chart, 6 January 1998. Isobars join places with equal pressure; a strong high over Canada and a low near Lake Erie, with a warm front toward New England, set up a strong pressure gradient during the 1998 ice storm.

rows.credit: Richard Sutcliffe / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A low grassy coastal terrace below an older cliff near Northbank.
rows.caption: A raised beach at Northbank marks a former relative sea level. Relative sea level changes when the land moves (for example, glacial rebound) or when global sea level changes; one photograph cannot separate the two.

rows.credit: Plorpy2 / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
rows.alt: Photographs of clay samples comparing gray reduced material and oxidized reddish material.
rows.caption: The same clay kept airless in a sealed jar (gray gley color) and after oxidizing in open air (orange-brown). In waterlogged soils, iron changes like this give gray colors and rusty mottles.

rows.credit: adam sommerville / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A horizontal bronze sundial with a sharp shadow cast by its gnomon, in a garden at Brodick Castle.
rows.caption: Sundial in the walled garden at Brodick Castle, Isle of Arran. The gnomon's shadow shows the Sun's direction; when the Sun is lower in the sky, shadows are longer.

rows.credit: Hondius, Jodocus; Rossi, Giuseppe Di. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Digitized historical sheets of narrow, tapered terrestrial map strips intended to cover a 19-centimeter globe.
rows.caption: Library of Congress scan of Hondius terrestrial globe gores, reissued by Giuseppe di Rossi in 1615. The tapered paper strips were cut to cover a sphere; the geography is historical, not a modern reference map.

rows.credit: Karthoo / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Wutach flows through a narrow, wooded gorge below exposed rock walls in the Black Forest.
rows.caption: Wutach Gorge, Germany. Capture diverted drainage from the Danube system toward the Rhine; subsequent incision cut this gorge.

rows.credit: Strebe / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: NASA Blue Marble satellite imagery displayed in a Mollweide projection with a graticule.
rows.caption: Satellite imagery in the Mollweide projection with its graticule drawn on: the network of meridians and parallels used to give latitude and longitude.

rows.credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio - Marit Jentoft-Nilsen, Global Science and Technology, Inc./Amy Moran, Global Science and Technology, Inc./Heather Hanson / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: CERES global map of outgoing longwave radiation with a color scale in watts per square meter.
rows.caption: NASA CERES, April 2015. Satellite observations map outgoing thermal radiation at the top of the atmosphere in W m⁻²; colder cloud tops generally emit less than warm clear-sky regions.

rows.credit: U.S. Geological Survey, US Topo 7.5-minute map for Covington, LA (2018) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped
rows.alt: Northwest corner of a USGS US Topo map of Covington, Louisiana, with a 1 km UTM grid labeled 776000 m E and 3377000 m N, and principal digits 77 to 83 along the top edge.
rows.caption: Part of the USGS US Topo map of Covington, Louisiana (2018), with its 1 km UTM grid. Grid lines divide the map into squares 1 km across; a four-figure reference identifies one of them, and more figures identify smaller squares inside it.

rows.credit: Iraphne R. Childs / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A groyne extends across the beach at Tallebudgera Creek on Australia's Gold Coast.
rows.caption: Tallebudgera Creek, Gold Coast, in the 1980s. A groyne interrupts sediment movement along a beach and can change sediment supply farther down-drift.

rows.credit: Colin Smith / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: People cross pale limestone blocks separated by deep joints above Malham Cove, England.
rows.caption: Malham Cove limestone pavement. Rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide widens joints into grykes, leaving blocks called clints.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: False-color MODIS brightness-temperature image showing the Gulf Stream and warm eddies in the North Atlantic.
rows.caption: MODIS, 2 May 2001: thermal contrast traces the Gulf Stream and eddies. Brightness temperature includes the sea surface and overlying moist atmosphere.

rows.credit: Till Niermann (User:Till.niermann) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Dry, deeply dissected loess slopes near Hunyuan in Shanxi, China.
rows.caption: Loess hills near Hunyuan, Shanxi, China. Concentrated runoff has cut deep gullies into the soft wind-deposited silt; they are far too large to be removed by plowing.

rows.credit: NOAA's National Ocean Service / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Multibeam sonar bathymetry reveals a broad undersea mountain in the Arctic Ocean.
rows.caption: NOAA multibeam survey of an Arctic seamount, an undersea mountain. A guyot is a seamount with a flat top; the surveyed shape, not the colors, shows which type this is.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: False-color MODIS brightness-temperature image showing the Gulf Stream and warm eddies in the North Atlantic.
rows.caption: MODIS traces warm Gulf Stream water in the western North Atlantic. The Gulf Stream is one part of the North Atlantic subtropical gyre, which covers the whole ocean basin.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: GOES-East satellite view of the Americas with tropical cloud bands and midlatitude weather systems.
rows.caption: GOES-East cloud data for 22 April 2014, laid over a cloud-free image of land and ocean. Tropical cloud bands and midlatitude storms are evidence of the global circulation. The three-cell model describes a long-term average, so it does not appear as three neat cloud rings in one image.

rows.credit: Diliff / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Yosemite Valley's forested floor between steep granite walls, viewed from Tunnel View.
rows.caption: Bridalveil Fall, Yosemite Valley, California. The fall drops from a hanging valley: its tributary glacier eroded less deeply than the main glacier that deepened Yosemite Valley.

rows.credit: Lysippos / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rock contact exposed along the Moine Thrust at Knockan Crag in northwest Scotland.
rows.caption: The Moine Thrust at Knockan Crag, Scotland: a low-angle reverse fault (a thrust). The hanging wall above the fault plane carries older rocks over the younger footwall rocks below, recording compression.

rows.credit: Karthoo / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Wutach flows through a narrow, wooded gorge below exposed rock walls in the Black Forest.
rows.caption: Wutach Gorge, Germany. Capture diverted drainage from the Danube system toward the Rhine; subsequent incision cut this gorge.

rows.credit: NASA/Kjell Lindgren / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The muddy Ucayali River winds through forest in Peru, with abandoned bends beside the active channel.
rows.caption: Meanders on Peru's Ucayali River, seen from the ISS. Corkscrew-like helicoidal flow around each bend erodes the outer bank and carries sediment to the inner bank.

rows.credit: Donnchadh H / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rounded hills and fields around the Vale of Edale, viewed from Grindslow Knoll.
rows.caption: The Vale of Edale and Lose Hill, Peak District, England. Rounded ridges and valley slopes show the local relief.

rows.credit: USDA Employee / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped
rows.alt: A soil profile with a thin dark topsoil, a pale tan layer below it and thick red subsoil, beside a depth scale in feet.
rows.caption: Layers in this exposed soil profile differ in color and texture. These soil horizons record changes in organic matter, weathering and material movement.

rows.credit: GlacierNPS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The sharp summit and steep ridges of Little Matterhorn in Glacier National Park, Montana.
rows.caption: Little Matterhorn, Glacier National Park, USA. Glacial erosion on several sides can leave a sharp pyramidal peak; this is not the Matterhorn in the Alps.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The Hawaiian volcanic islands stretch across the Pacific beneath scattered white clouds in an ISS photograph.
rows.caption: Hawaiʻi from the ISS. The volcanic chain records Pacific plate motion relative to a long-lived hotspot; the youngest main island is at the southeast end.

rows.credit: Robert Lamb / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Waves crashing into dark, jointed cliffs at Botallack, Cornwall.
rows.caption: Waves striking the cliffs at Botallack, Cornwall. Hydraulic action forces water and air into joints and cracks, loosening the rock; fast river flow does the same to channel banks.

rows.credit: Jerrod Wheeler (submitted to USGS by Kirk Miller, Wyoming) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A streamflow-gauging station beside Huey Creek in Antarctica's rocky McMurdo Dry Valleys.
rows.caption: USGS gauging station at Huey Creek, Antarctica, 12 December 2001. Repeated measurements of stage and discharge produce a river's hydrograph.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: GOES-East satellite view of the Americas with tropical cloud bands and midlatitude weather systems.
rows.caption: GOES-East cloud data for 22 April 2014, laid over a cloud-free image of land and ocean. Tropical cloud bands and midlatitude storms are evidence of the global circulation. The three-cell model describes a long-term average, so it does not appear as three neat cloud rings in one image.

rows.credit: NASA/JPL / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Voyager 2 image of Neptune's blue disc showing cloud bands and the Great Dark Spot.
rows.caption: Voyager 2 image of Neptune, assembled from green and orange filter observations in August 1989. The deep blue here is enhanced; the ice giant's natural color is paler.

rows.credit: NPS Photo / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Polygonal ground and ponds on the tundra in Noatak National Preserve, Alaska, photographed from the air.
rows.caption: Ice-wedge polygons in Alaska's Noatak tundra. Repeated thermal contraction cracking and ice growth organize the permafrost landscape.

rows.credit: National Oceanic & Atmospheric Adminstration (NOAA) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Rounded pillow lava on a fissured seafloor at the Galápagos Rift, photographed by a NOAA expedition.
