rows.caption: A NOAA Deep SOLO float is lowered into the sea. It measures temperature and salinity, which set the water's density and identify deep-water masses such as NADW.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A green auroral band glows below the International Space Station above the southern Indian Ocean.
rows.caption: An ISS photograph of aurora north of Antarctica. Energetic particles excite upper-atmosphere gases; the green light is emitted by the atmosphere, not reflected sunlight.

rows.credit: Dennis G. Jarvis / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A fishing boat rests on exposed mud beside a wharf at low tide in Nova Scotia.
rows.caption: Low water at St Mary's Bay, Nova Scotia. The tidal bulge is an idealized model: real tides arrive as long waves shaped by the coast, and here the falling tide has left the harbor floor dry.

rows.credit: Dennis G. Jarvis / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A fishing boat rests on exposed mud beside a wharf at low tide in Nova Scotia.
rows.caption: Low tide at Waterford on St Mary's Bay, Nova Scotia. The exposed harbor floor makes tidal range visible.

rows.credit: David Medcalf / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: An exposed bank of poorly sorted glacial sediment containing stones of several sizes.
rows.caption: A natural exposure of glacial till. Ice deposits a mixture of grain sizes directly, often without the sorting produced by flowing water.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: South African city lights beneath a curved glowing atmospheric horizon and stars, viewed from the ISS.
rows.caption: South African cities at night from the ISS. Earth's rotation brings day and night; time zones and the International Date Line are agreed conventions, not lines visible on Earth.

rows.credit: Mark Reid, USGS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An aerial view of the Oso landslide's bare source scar, debris path and deposits across the valley.
rows.caption: Oso, Washington, 2014: an aerial photograph of the landslide source, travel path and deposit. The displaced material crossed the valley floor.

rows.credit: Yyuri1989 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial photograph of the Giens peninsula joined to the coast by two narrow sediment barriers.
rows.caption: Giens, near Hyères, France. The double tombolo connects the peninsula to the mainland through two sediment-built barriers.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / Scientific Visualization Studio · public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA CERES map of reflected shortwave radiation averaged over 2000–2015, with a 0–385 W m⁻² color scale.
rows.caption: NASA CERES observations, 2000–2015 mean. Colors show sunlight reflected by the Earth system in W m⁻². This is outgoing shortwave flux, not incoming solar irradiance or albedo itself.

rows.credit: Jacques Descloitres, MODIS Land Rapid Response Team / NASA GSFC · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Hawaiian islands with greener windward slopes, drier leeward slopes and silvery sunglint on the Pacific.
rows.caption: Terra MODIS, 27 May 2003. Northeasterly trade winds favor wetter, greener windward slopes; leeward slopes are drier. The bright ocean is sunglint.

rows.credit: USFS employees / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped and resized
rows.alt: Melting snow patches and a stream near Fourth of July Lake in Idaho's Sawtooth Mountains.
rows.caption: Snowmelt near Fourth of July Lake, Idaho. Seasonal melting transfers stored snow water into streams, soils and groundwater.

rows.credit: Ikluft / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of the San Andreas Fault as a straight line of ridges and gullies crossing the dry Carrizo Plain.
rows.caption: The San Andreas Fault crossing the Carrizo Plain, California, seen from about 2,600 m. The straight line marks the boundary where the Pacific Plate moves north-west past the North American Plate.

rows.credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NOAA seafloor relief map around Puerto Rico identifies the deep Puerto Rico Trench and nearby plate boundary.
rows.caption: NOAA bathymetric visualization of the Puerto Rico region. A trench is an elongated seafloor depression associated here with a complex convergent plate boundary; vertical relief is exaggerated in this perspective.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: ASTER satellite image of branching tributary valleys near the Colorado River in Canyonlands, Utah.
rows.caption: ASTER false-color image, 24 September 2005: tributaries cut into sandstone in Canyonlands, Utah. Plants along the valley floors show up red. The branching network carries water toward the Colorado River (top left).

rows.credit: NASA astronaut Ed Lu / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The clear eye and tall spiral cloud walls of Hurricane Isabel, photographed from the ISS.
rows.caption: Astronaut Ed Lu photographed Hurricane Isabel on 13 September 2003. The eye is surrounded by the eyewall's deep convective clouds.

rows.credit: Reto Stöckli / NASA Earth Observatory · public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA Blue Marble satellite composite of Earth in an equirectangular global map.
rows.caption: NASA Blue Marble monthly composite on an equirectangular latitude–longitude grid. Latitude measures angular distance north or south of the equator, and parallels run east–west. These reference lines are mathematical; they are not marked on the ground.

rows.credit: NASA / Expedition 66 crew · ISS066-E-86970 · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Orange and blue atmospheric layers above Earth's curved horizon, with a crescent Moon in the black sky.
rows.caption: Earth's thin atmosphere seen edge-on from the ISS on 6 December 2021. Scattered sunlight lights the lower layers; the colored bands do not mark exact layer boundaries.

rows.credit: NASA / Expedition 66 crew · ISS066-E-86970 · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Orange and blue atmospheric layers above Earth's curved horizon, with a crescent Moon in the black sky.
rows.caption: Earth's thin atmosphere seen edge-on from the ISS on 6 December 2021. Scattered sunlight lights the lower layers; the colored bands do not mark exact layer boundaries.

rows.credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Saturn and its broad rings in a natural-color mosaic photographed by the Cassini spacecraft.
rows.caption: Cassini photographed Saturn and its rings together. A true-scale model shrinks every length by the same factor; this perspective view also foreshortens the rings.

rows.credit: Mass Communication Specialist 3rd Class Dylan McCord / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of debris, damaged buildings and flooded land at a fishing port in Kesennuma after the 2011 tsunami.
rows.caption: Coastal damage at Kesennuma, Japan, after the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami. Run-up is the greatest height above sea level that the water reaches on land; field surveys are needed to measure it.

rows.credit: Diliff / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Yosemite Valley's forested floor between steep granite walls, viewed from Tunnel View.
rows.caption: Yosemite Valley from Tunnel View, California: a broad, flat floor between steep granite walls. Glaciers enlarged a river valley into this U-shaped trough.

rows.credit: USDA NRCS Montana / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Two cupped hands holding a handful of dark, crumbly topsoil.
rows.caption: Soil scientists judge texture by feel in the field. The proportions of sand, silt and clay can then be plotted on a ternary texture triangle.

rows.credit: NASA Armstrong Flight Research Center / NASA/Carla Thomas / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The dark lunar disc surrounded by the Sun's pale corona during the 2017 total solar eclipse.
rows.caption: The 21 August 2017 total solar eclipse, photographed from inside the Moon's umbra. Where the full shadow falls, the bright photosphere is completely hidden and only the faint corona shows.

rows.credit: Lauren Dauphin / NASA Earth Observatory · Aqua MODIS / EOSDIS · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Green phytoplankton and sediment-rich water off Mauritania's desert coast, observed by Aqua MODIS.
rows.caption: Aqua MODIS, 5 May 2020. Upwelling in the Canary Current system supplies nutrients off Mauritania. The visible green water contains phytoplankton and sediment; it is not a temperature map.

rows.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech · ECOSTRESS, PIA25423 · underlying map attribution retained in image · resized
rows.alt: ECOSTRESS thermal map shows warm urban surfaces in London late at night on 15 July 2022.
rows.caption: ECOSTRESS measured London's land-surface temperatures near midnight on 15 July 2022. Built surfaces remained warmer than many vegetated areas. These are surface temperatures, not standard air-temperature readings.

rows.credit: Malik Ahamed from Colombo, Sri Lanka / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A broad bend of the New River in a steep forested gorge in West Virginia.
rows.caption: New River Gorge, West Virginia. Steep forested slopes fall straight to the river, giving a V-shaped cross-section formed by river downcutting and slope processes.

rows.credit: Donnchadh H / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rounded hills and fields around the Vale of Edale, viewed from Grindslow Knoll.
rows.caption: The Vale of Edale and Lose Hill, Peak District, England. Rounded ridges and valley slopes show the local relief.

rows.credit: NOAA NCEI / CIRES · EMAG2 v3 · public domain · resized
rows.alt: EMAG2 global magnetic-anomaly map with alternating anomalies across the ocean floor.
rows.caption: NOAA EMAG2 v3 map of magnetic anomalies. Stripes on the ocean floor record crust formed as Earth's magnetic field reversed. Matching them to dated reversals supports seafloor spreading and gives a rate (distance ÷ age); the colors themselves are not ages.

rows.credit: Jim D. Griggs, HVO (USGS) staff photographer[1][2] / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An arching orange lava fountain erupts from a vent on Kīlauea amid dark cooling lava.
rows.caption: A lava fountain about 10 meters high at Kīlauea, photographed by USGS on 25 February 1983. Magma reaches the surface here, but the mantle beneath is almost entirely solid.

rows.credit: Christine Matthews / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A physical marker of the historic Greenwich Meridian at the Royal Observatory.
rows.caption: The historic Greenwich Meridian makes a reference longitude tangible. Modern WGS84 zero longitude lies about 102 meters east of this line.

rows.credit: NASA Earth Observatory image by Lauren Dauphin, using modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2025) processed by the European Space Agency and further processed by Josh Willis, and Kevin Marlis/NASA/JPL-Caltech. Story by Emily Cassidy. / Wikimedia Commons · Attribution · resized
rows.alt: Sentinel-6 sea-surface height anomaly map shows lower-than-average levels across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific.
rows.caption: Sentinel-6 map of sea-surface height during La Niña, January 2025. La Niña strengthens the Walker circulation, which can affect weather far away through teleconnections.

rows.credit: National Weather Service Office in Burlington, Vermont / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: US National Weather Service surface weather chart for 6 January 1998 with isobars, high and low centers and fronts.
rows.caption: US National Weather Service surface chart, 6 January 1998. Isobars join places with equal pressure; a strong high over Canada and a low near Lake Erie, with a warm front toward New England, set up a strong pressure gradient during the 1998 ice storm.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped and resized
rows.alt: World map of sea-surface temperature, with red in the western Pacific and Indian Ocean and blue near the poles.
rows.caption: NASA map of sea-surface temperature from two weeks of satellite infrared data. Red marks the warmest water; the western Pacific warm pool is the large red area near Indonesia and northern Australia (left edge).

rows.credit: National Weather Service Office in Burlington, Vermont / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: US National Weather Service surface weather chart for 6 January 1998 with isobars, high and low centers and fronts.
rows.caption: US National Weather Service surface chart, 6 January 1998. Isobars join places with equal pressure; a strong high over Canada and a low near Lake Erie, with a warm front toward New England, set up a strong pressure gradient during the 1998 ice storm.

rows.credit: Michael Rivera / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A USGS groundwater observation station in Stephen C. Foster State Park, Georgia.
rows.caption: USGS observation well in Stephen C. Foster State Park, Georgia. Instruments record groundwater levels; the water table itself lies beneath the surface.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: ASTER satellite image of branching tributary valleys near the Colorado River in Canyonlands, Utah.
rows.caption: ASTER false-color image, 24 September 2005: tributaries cut into sandstone in Canyonlands, Utah. Plants along the valley floors show up red. The branching network carries water toward the Colorado River (top left).

rows.credit: Alvesgaspar / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: A breaking wave curls and foams along the coast at Porto Covo, Portugal.
rows.caption: A breaking wave at Porto Covo, Portugal. In shallow water a wave slows and steepens; its crest eventually breaks.

rows.credit: Dexter Perkins / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
rows.alt: Rounded remnants of granite emerge from loose weathered material in an exposed rock profile.
rows.caption: Weathered granite. As its minerals break down, solid rock gradually turns into loose weathered material.

rows.credit: Dexter Perkins / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
rows.alt: Rounded remnants of granite emerge from loose weathered material in an exposed rock profile.
rows.caption: Weathered granite. As its minerals break down, solid rock gradually turns into loose weathered material.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: GOES-East satellite view of the Americas with tropical cloud bands and midlatitude weather systems.
rows.caption: GOES-East cloud data for 22 April 2014, laid over a cloud-free image of land and ocean. Tropical cloud bands and midlatitude storms are evidence of the global circulation. The three-cell model describes a long-term average, so it does not appear as three neat cloud rings in one image.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: False-color MODIS brightness-temperature image showing the Gulf Stream and warm eddies in the North Atlantic.
rows.caption: MODIS, 2 May 2001: thermal contrast traces the Gulf Stream and eddies. Brightness temperature includes the sea surface and overlying moist atmosphere.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Long fault-bounded valleys and escarpments in Kenya's East African Rift, viewed from the ISS.
rows.caption: The East African Rift in Kenya: continental extension is an opening stage of a possible ocean-basin cycle. A rift does not inevitably become an ocean.

rows.credit: DanHobley / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: View up a dry valley in Ladakh toward a notch in the mountain ridge on the skyline, with a village in the foreground.
rows.caption: A wind gap above the Karu valley, Ladakh. Glacial erosion on the far side of the ridge beheaded this valley, leaving the outline of its U-shaped head as a dry notch on the skyline, with no river flowing through it.

rows.credit: NOAA Photo Library / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An aerial view of damaged buildings and washed-over land on the Bolivar Peninsula after Hurricane Ike.
rows.caption: Bolivar Peninsula, Texas, September 2008. NOAA documented coastal damage from Hurricane Ike's storm surge.

rows.credit: Jacques Descloitres, MODIS Land Rapid Response Team / NASA GSFC · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Hawaiian islands with greener windward slopes, drier leeward slopes and silvery sunglint on the Pacific.
rows.caption: Terra MODIS, 27 May 2003. Northeasterly trade winds favor wetter, greener windward slopes; leeward slopes are drier. The bright ocean is sunglint.

rows.credit: lwtt93 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Long, wind-eroded rock ridges rise above the desert at Dunhuang, China.
rows.caption: Yardangs at Dunhuang, China. Persistent wind erosion shapes elongated ridges in relatively soft rock or sediment.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Green crystalline mantle peridotite enclosed by darker volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona.
rows.caption: The lava that carried this Peridot Mesa xenolith erupted about 580 ka (580,000 years ago). That dates the eruption, not the much older mantle rock inside it.

rows.credit: NASA Astronaut photograph from ISS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Crescent-shaped dunes around Lagoa dos Barros on Brazil's Atlantic coast, seen from the ISS.
rows.caption: Wind shapes barchan dunes beside Lagoa dos Barros, Brazil. The crescent tips point downwind.

rows.credit: NASA / Expedition 66 crew · ISS066-E-86970 · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Orange and blue atmospheric layers above Earth's curved horizon, with a crescent Moon in the black sky.
rows.caption: Earth's atmosphere seen edge-on from the ISS on 6 December 2021. Its colored bands reveal a thin envelope above the surface.

rows.credit: Sidoine MBOGNI / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
rows.caption: Tropical forest at Bodiman, Cameroon: living vegetation is a carbon store, exchanging carbon with the air and soil.

rows.credit: Bjørn Christian Tørrissen / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Grassland with scattered acacia trees in Serengeti National Park, Tanzania.
rows.caption: Serengeti savanna: seasonal rainfall helps explain the balance between grasses and scattered trees.

rows.credit: Abhinaba Basu / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Sea stacks and rocky headlands along a curving beach with waves rolling in, below forested hills.
rows.caption: The Oregon coast south from Ecola State Park toward Cannon Beach. Waves cut back the headlands and leave sea stacks such as Haystack Rock offshore.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Snow-covered Himalayan peaks and valleys photographed from the International Space Station.
rows.caption: The Himalaya from the ISS: crust shortened and thickened as India collided with Eurasia.

rows.credit: United States Department of the Interior Geological Survey / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: USGS topographic map of Mount Rainier with contours, glaciers and named summits.
rows.caption: USGS Mount Rainier topographic sheet, published in 1971. Contours connect equal elevations; close spacing marks steep slopes.

rows.credit: NASA, MODIS Rapid Response System / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A broad spiral of white clouds over the Pacific northeast of Japan.
rows.caption: MODIS observed this extratropical cyclone northeast of Japan on 22 February 2012. Cloud bands trace the low-pressure circulation. The image joins two satellite passes, so the straight diagonal line is a seam, not a weather feature.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: ASTER satellite image of branching tributary valleys near the Colorado River in Canyonlands, Utah.
rows.caption: ASTER false-color image, 24 September 2005: tributaries cut into sandstone in Canyonlands, Utah. Plants along the valley floors show up red. The branching network carries water toward the Colorado River (top left).

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Green crystalline mantle peridotite enclosed by darker volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona.
rows.caption: A mantle xenolith brought to the surface by magma: direct evidence of solid rock within Earth's mantle.

rows.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Wanmei Liang, using data provided by the ARIA team at NASA/JPL-Caltech. The displacement map is based on Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey and ALOS-2 data from the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Story by Adam Voiland. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA ARIA map showing measured ground displacement along the Kamchatka Peninsula after the 2025 earthquake.
rows.caption: NASA ARIA displacement mapping after the 2025 Kamchatka earthquake. Colors encode surface movement, rather than the color of the ground.

rows.credit: NASA Armstrong Flight Research Center / NASA/Carla Thomas / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The dark lunar disc surrounded by the Sun's pale corona during the 2017 total solar eclipse.
rows.caption: NASA's airborne view of the 21 August 2017 total solar eclipse. The Moon blocks the bright photosphere, revealing the corona.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / Scientific Visualization Studio · public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA CERES map of net radiation averaged over 2000–2015, with a −200 to +200 W m⁻² color scale.
rows.caption: NASA CERES observations, 2000–2015 mean. Net radiation is incoming sunlight minus reflected shortwave and emitted longwave energy at the top of the atmosphere. Positive values indicate a radiative surplus.

rows.credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NOAA sea-surface temperature anomaly map with warmer-than-average water across the equatorial Pacific in late 2015.
rows.caption: NOAA, 11 October–7 November 2015: positive sea-surface temperature anomalies extend across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific during El Niño.

rows.credit: Gordon Hatton / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Tilted and folded sedimentary beds exposed at The Settlands coast.
rows.caption: Folded strata at The Settlands, Wales. Trace a bed through the exposure to see deformation recorded in solid rock.

rows.credit: bgilliard from St. Catharines, Canada / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A low shelf cloud sweeps over buildings at Brock University in Ontario.
rows.caption: A cold front passes Brock University, St. Catharines, Canada. The cloud edge makes uplift visible; the front itself is a zone of contrasting air.

rows.credit: PawełS / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Younger gently dipping red sandstone overlies steep gray beds at Siccar Point, Scotland.
rows.caption: Siccar Point: Devonian sandstone overlies much older, tilted Silurian beds. The unconformity records deformation, erosion and missing time.

rows.credit: Giles Laurent / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Aletsch Glacier curves through a steep Alpine valley, with dark medial moraines running along its surface.
rows.caption: Aletsch Glacier, Switzerland. Flowing ice carries debris; its dark medial moraines record where tributary glaciers join.

rows.credit: Reto Stöckli / NASA Earth Observatory · public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA Blue Marble satellite composite of Earth in an equirectangular global map.
rows.caption: NASA Blue Marble Next Generation, July 2004. A cloud-free satellite composite in a latitude–longitude grid: the map stretches high latitudes and is not equal-area.

rows.credit: U.S. Geological Survey, US Topo 7.5-minute map for Covington, LA (2018) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped
rows.alt: Northwest corner of a USGS US Topo map of Covington, Louisiana, with a 1 km UTM grid labeled 776000 m E and 3377000 m N, and principal digits 77 to 83 along the top edge.
rows.caption: Part of the USGS US Topo map of Covington, Louisiana (2018), with its 1 km UTM grid. Give eastings (along the corridor) before northings (up the stairs).

rows.credit: Michael Rivera / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The clear, shallow Ichetucknee River flowing between grassy, wooded banks in Florida.
rows.caption: The Ichetucknee River in Florida is fed by springs: groundwater from the limestone aquifer flows out at the surface and keeps the water clear.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The Hawaiian volcanic islands stretch across the Pacific beneath scattered white clouds in an ISS photograph.
rows.caption: Hawaiʻi from the ISS. The volcanic chain records Pacific plate motion relative to a long-lived hotspot; the youngest main island is at the southeast end.

rows.credit: Alan Cressler, USGS · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A small instrument shelter on stilts beside a concrete weir on a forest stream.
rows.caption: A USGS streamgage on Little Back Creek, Bath County, Virginia. The shelter records the water level (stage) every few minutes; a rating curve converts stage to discharge, the numbers plotted on a storm hydrograph.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Space Shuttle view of snow-covered land around Hannah Bay with many curved, parallel lines of old shorelines.
rows.caption: Hannah Bay, at the south end of James Bay, Canada, in winter. Snow picks out dozens of old shorelines left behind as the land rose after the ice sheet melted.

rows.credit: NASA/Chris Hadfield / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Astronaut photograph of central Florida dotted with round, dark lakes among farm fields.
rows.caption: Central Florida from the International Space Station, near Lake Wales. Many of the round lakes fill sinkholes formed where the limestone below dissolved.

rows.credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
rows.caption: Grand Canyon from Hopi Point, Arizona. Resistant beds form steps and cliffs above valleys cut by running water.

rows.credit: Reto Stöckli / NASA Earth Observatory · public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA Blue Marble satellite composite of Earth in an equirectangular global map.
rows.caption: NASA Blue Marble Next Generation, July 2004. A cloud-free satellite composite in a latitude–longitude grid: the map stretches high latitudes and is not equal-area.

rows.credit: David Martin / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Uneven displaced ground and scarps above the coast at Redcliff Point, Dorset.
rows.caption: Slumping above Redcliff Point, Dorset. Rotational movement displaces blocks along a curved shear surface; the surface scars and tilted ground provide evidence.

rows.credit: NASA Johnson Space Center / NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A thin sunlit lunar crescent with crater shadows along the terminator against black space.
rows.caption: The Artemis II crew photographed this lunar crescent on 7 April 2026. Phase is the visible fraction of the sunlit hemisphere, not Earth's shadow.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: False-color MODIS brightness-temperature image showing the Gulf Stream and warm eddies in the North Atlantic.
rows.caption: MODIS, 2 May 2001: thermal contrast traces the Gulf Stream and eddies. Brightness temperature includes the sea surface and overlying moist atmosphere.

rows.credit: NPS Photo / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Polygonal ground and ponds on the tundra in Noatak National Preserve, Alaska, photographed from the air.
rows.caption: Ice-wedge polygons in Alaska's Noatak tundra. Repeated thermal contraction cracking and ice growth organize the permafrost landscape.

rows.credit: Olga Ernst / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Steep dark rock walls border the Almannagjá rift at Þingvellir, Iceland.
rows.caption: Almannagjá, Þingvellir: faults accommodate extension within Iceland's broad North American–Eurasian plate boundary zone.

rows.credit: Jacques Descloitres, MODIS Land Rapid Response Team / NASA GSFC · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Hawaiian islands with greener windward slopes, drier leeward slopes and silvery sunglint on the Pacific.
rows.caption: Terra MODIS, 27 May 2003. Northeasterly trade winds favor wetter, greener windward slopes; leeward slopes are drier. The bright ocean is sunglint.

rows.credit: H. Zell / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A shallow river flowing through a steep, wooded gorge in the Black Forest, Germany.
rows.caption: The Wutach Gorge, Black Forest, Germany. After the Wutach was captured by a steeper Rhine tributary, it cut this deep gorge.

rows.credit: none (Landsat) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: False-color Landsat image of the Lena Delta with many branching distributaries and islands.
rows.caption: Landsat's view of the Lena Delta, 2000. Distributaries spread sediment into the Arctic Ocean. The image combines infrared and red bands.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rounded potholes cut into dark bedrock beside flowing water in the Presque Isle River, Michigan.
rows.caption: Presque Isle River, Michigan. Swirling, sediment-laden water has drilled potholes into the bedrock of this river in the Upper Peninsula, near Lake Superior.

rows.credit: Walter Siegmund / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: Floodwater from the Stillaguamish River surrounds a picnic table and trees.
rows.caption: The South Fork Stillaguamish River in flood. Water spreads beyond the usual channel when discharge exceeds channel capacity.

rows.credit: NASA/Kjell Lindgren / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The muddy Ucayali River winds through forest in Peru, with abandoned bends beside the active channel.
rows.caption: Ucayali River, Peru, photographed from the ISS. Meander migration leaves cut-offs and abandoned channels across the floodplain.

rows.credit: Kevin M. Gill / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A rounded specimen of augen gneiss with pale mineral eyes enclosed in dark, folded bands.
rows.caption: Augen gneiss: deformation and metamorphism organize minerals into bands around larger crystals. Rock-cycle pathways need not follow one fixed loop.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: South African city lights beneath a curved glowing atmospheric horizon and stars, viewed from the ISS.
rows.caption: South Africa at night, seen from the ISS. Earth's rotation carries every place through daylight and darkness each day.

rows.credit: National Oceanic & Atmospheric Adminstration (NOAA) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Rounded pillow lava on a fissured seafloor at the Galápagos Rift, photographed by a NOAA expedition.
rows.caption: NOAA, Galápagos Rift, 21 July 2011. Lava quenched in seawater forms pillows close to a spreading center, where new oceanic crust is built.

rows.credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
rows.alt: Meteosat view of Earth's day–night boundary on the December solstice, with more of the Southern Hemisphere in daylight.
rows.caption: Meteosat-9 SEVIRI, 21 December 2010. The tilted day–night boundary shows the Southern Hemisphere having longer days. Axial tilt, not a change in Earth–Sun distance, causes this seasonal pattern.

rows.credit: Photo by Tim McCabe, USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Rolling wheat fields on smooth loess hills in the Palouse region of eastern Washington.
rows.caption: The Palouse, eastern Washington. Soil on these wind-deposited loess hills changes from hilltop to footslope as water and sediment move downslope.

rows.credit: Photo by Lynn Betts, USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A sloping cornfield in western Iowa cut by rills and a gully where runoff has washed soil away.
rows.caption: Rill and gully erosion in a western Iowa cornfield. Runoff has carried away young corn plants, topsoil and nutrients from the loess soil.

rows.credit: USDA Employee / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped
rows.alt: A soil profile with a thin dark topsoil, a pale tan layer below it and thick red subsoil, beside a depth scale in feet.
rows.caption: Bama, Alabama's state soil, an Ultisol: a thin dark A horizon, a pale leached E horizon, then thick red Bt subsoil where washed-down clay and iron oxides collect (scale in feet). Unlike the model's temperate brown soil, it has an E horizon and a clay-enriched Bt instead of a Bw.

rows.credit: USDA NRCS Montana / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Two cupped hands holding a handful of dark, crumbly topsoil.
rows.caption: A handful of topsoil. Soil scientists judge texture by feel: sand is gritty, silt is smooth like flour, and clay is sticky and can be pressed into a ribbon.

rows.credit: adam sommerville / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A horizontal bronze sundial with a sharp shadow cast by its gnomon, in a garden at Brodick Castle.
rows.caption: Sundial in the walled garden at Brodick Castle, Isle of Arran. The gnomon's shadow shows the Sun's direction; when the Sun is lower in the sky, shadows are longer.

rows.credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Saturn and its broad rings in a natural-color mosaic photographed by the Cassini spacecraft.
rows.caption: Cassini, 6 October 2004: a natural-color mosaic of Saturn and its rings. The rings are a thin disc of orbiting particles.

rows.credit: NOAA Photo Library / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An aerial view of damaged buildings and washed-over land on the Bolivar Peninsula after Hurricane Ike.
rows.caption: Bolivar Peninsula, Texas, September 2008. NOAA documented coastal damage from Hurricane Ike's storm surge.

rows.credit: Timmonswilliams / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
rows.alt: A figure-eight curve painted on a house wall in Woodland, California, with a scale from 23.5° N (Tropic of Cancer) at the top to 23.5° S (Tropic of Capricorn) at the bottom.
rows.caption: Woodland, California: a small mirror reflected the noon Sun onto this wall, and its position was marked every day for two years. The figure eight runs from 23.5° N in June to 23.5° S in December: the Sun's declination, which sets how steeply sunlight strikes the ground.

rows.credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · Aqua MODIS / EOSDIS · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Afternoon cumulus clouds over Sri Lanka, observed by Aqua MODIS on 9 April 2013.
rows.caption: Aqua MODIS, 9 April 2013. Cumulus clouds form over Sri Lanka while the surrounding sea stays clear. Daytime heating of the land drives a sea breeze inland, where the air rises.

rows.credit: owamux / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Circular plates of new pancake ice cover the surface of the western Ross Sea in Antarctica.
rows.caption: New sea ice forming in the Ross Sea. Freezing rejects much of the salt into the surrounding water, increasing its density and helping drive polar overturning.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: GOES-East satellite view of the Americas with tropical cloud bands and midlatitude weather systems.
rows.caption: GOES-East cloud data for 22 April 2014, laid over a cloud-free satellite image of land and ocean, so the whole disc is shown lit. Cloud belts reveal aspects of the global circulation; a single image does not outline every atmospheric cell.

rows.credit: Dennis G. Jarvis / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A fishing boat rests on exposed mud beside a wharf at low tide in Nova Scotia.
rows.caption: Low tide at Waterford on St Mary's Bay, Nova Scotia. The exposed harbor floor makes tidal range visible.

rows.credit: NASA astronaut Ed Lu / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The clear eye and tall spiral cloud walls of Hurricane Isabel, photographed from the ISS.
rows.caption: Astronaut Ed Lu photographed Hurricane Isabel on 13 September 2003. The eye is surrounded by the eyewall's deep convective clouds.

rows.credit: U.S. Air Force photo / Staff Sgt. Samuel Morse · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of Sendai Airport, Japan, with seawater and debris covering the runways and the flat farmland around them.
rows.caption: Sendai Airport, Japan, two days after the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami. The water spread across the flat coastal plain and still covered the runways on 13 March.

rows.credit: Astrobond / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Andromeda Galaxy, a large spiral of stars with two small companion galaxies, against a field of foreground stars.
rows.caption: The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) with its two small companion galaxies. Its light has traveled about 2.5 million years to reach us; the scattered points are much nearer stars in our own galaxy.

rows.credit: Jim D. Griggs, HVO (USGS) staff photographer[1][2] / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An arching orange lava fountain erupts from a vent on Kīlauea amid dark cooling lava.
rows.caption: A lava fountain about 10 meters high at Kīlauea, photographed by USGS on 25 February 1983. Magma reaches the surface here, but the mantle beneath is almost entirely solid.

rows.credit: Jfred1962 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A towering thunderhead cloud backlit by the Sun, with rays of light spreading across a blue sky.
rows.caption: A thunderhead over Rainy Lake, Minnesota. Water evaporated from lakes and land rises, cools and condenses into cloud before falling again as rain.

rows.credit: PatríciaR / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: Rounded, stacked granite boulders under a cloudy sky in Joshua Tree National Park.
rows.caption: Granite boulders in Joshua Tree National Park, California. Weathering along cracks in the granite rounds the blocks into piles of boulders.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Long fault-bounded valleys and escarpments in Kenya's East African Rift, viewed from the ISS.
rows.caption: The East African Rift in Kenya: continental extension is an opening stage of a possible ocean-basin cycle. A rift does not inevitably become an ocean.

rows.credit: Geographer / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: An orange windsock extends above a field beside the path to Green Lane Farm.
rows.caption: A windsock responds to moving air. Its open mouth faces into the wind; meteorological wind direction names where the air comes from.

rows.credit: NASA / Expedition 66 crew · ISS066-E-86970 · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Orange and blue atmospheric layers above Earth's curved horizon, with a crescent Moon in the black sky.
rows.caption: Earth's atmosphere seen edge-on from the ISS on 6 December 2021. Its colored bands reveal a thin envelope above the surface.

rows.credit: EOSDIS Worldview / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Satellite view of Typhoon Mangkhut with a compact eye and spiraling cloud bands in September 2018.
rows.caption: Typhoon Mangkhut in September 2018, observed by NASA EOSDIS. The western North Pacific storm went on to strike the Philippines and southern China.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Green crystalline mantle peridotite enclosed by darker volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona.
rows.caption: A mantle xenolith brought to the surface by magma: direct evidence of solid rock within Earth's mantle.

rows.credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
rows.caption: Grand Canyon from Hopi Point, Arizona. Resistant beds form steps and cliffs above valleys cut by running water.

rows.credit: NASA/Apollo 17 crew; taken by either Harrison Schmitt or Ron Evans / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The fully sunlit Earth showing Africa, Arabia, Antarctica and swirling clouds in the Apollo 17 photograph.
rows.caption: Apollo 17's Blue Marble, 7 December 1972. Earth's axial tilt changes the angle and duration of sunlight over the year.

rows.credit: U.S. Geological Survey, US Topo 7.5-minute map for Covington, LA (2018) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped
rows.alt: Northwest corner of a USGS US Topo map of Covington, Louisiana, with a 1 km UTM grid labeled 776000 m E and 3377000 m N, and principal digits 77 to 83 along the top edge.
rows.caption: Part of the USGS US Topo map of Covington, Louisiana (2018). Thin lines mark the 1 km UTM grid used by the US National Grid; the corner labels give full coordinates (776000 m E, 3377000 m N), and the large two-digit numbers are the principal digits read in a grid reference.

rows.caption: Landsat's view of the Lena Delta, 2000. Distributaries spread sediment into the Arctic Ocean. The image combines infrared and red bands.

rows.credit: NASA Astronaut photograph from ISS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Crescent-shaped dunes around Lagoa dos Barros on Brazil's Atlantic coast, seen from the ISS.
rows.caption: Wind shapes barchan dunes beside Lagoa dos Barros, Brazil. The crescent tips point downwind.

rows.credit: NASA / Expedition 66 crew · ISS066-E-86970 · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Orange and blue atmospheric layers above Earth's curved horizon, with a crescent Moon in the black sky.
rows.caption: Earth's atmosphere seen edge-on from the ISS on 6 December 2021. Its colored bands reveal a thin envelope above the surface.

rows.credit: Sidoine MBOGNI / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
rows.caption: Tropical forest at Bodiman, Cameroon: living vegetation is a carbon store, exchanging carbon with the air and soil.

rows.credit: Bjørn Christian Tørrissen / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Grassland with scattered acacia trees in Serengeti National Park, Tanzania.
rows.caption: Serengeti savanna: seasonal rainfall helps explain the balance between grasses and scattered trees.

rows.credit: Abhinaba Basu / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Sea stacks and rocky headlands along a curving beach with waves rolling in, below forested hills.
rows.caption: The Oregon coast south from Ecola State Park toward Cannon Beach. Waves cut back the headlands and leave sea stacks such as Haystack Rock offshore.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Snow-covered Himalayan peaks and valleys photographed from the International Space Station.
rows.caption: The Himalaya from the ISS: crust shortened and thickened as India collided with Eurasia.

rows.credit: United States Department of the Interior Geological Survey / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: USGS topographic map of Mount Rainier with contours, glaciers and named summits.
rows.caption: USGS Mount Rainier topographic sheet, published in 1971. Contours connect equal elevations; close spacing marks steep slopes.

rows.credit: NASA, MODIS Rapid Response System / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A broad spiral of white clouds over the Pacific northeast of Japan.
rows.caption: MODIS observed this extratropical cyclone northeast of Japan on 22 February 2012. Cloud bands trace the low-pressure circulation. The image joins two satellite passes, so the straight diagonal line is a seam, not a weather feature.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: ASTER satellite image of branching tributary valleys near the Colorado River in Canyonlands, Utah.
rows.caption: ASTER false-color image, 24 September 2005: tributaries cut into sandstone in Canyonlands, Utah. Plants along the valley floors show up red. The branching network carries water toward the Colorado River (top left).

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Green crystalline mantle peridotite enclosed by darker volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona.
rows.caption: A mantle xenolith brought to the surface by magma: direct evidence of solid rock within Earth's mantle.

rows.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Wanmei Liang, using data provided by the ARIA team at NASA/JPL-Caltech. The displacement map is based on Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey and ALOS-2 data from the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Story by Adam Voiland. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA ARIA map showing measured ground displacement along the Kamchatka Peninsula after the 2025 earthquake.
rows.caption: NASA ARIA displacement mapping after the 2025 Kamchatka earthquake. Colors encode surface movement, rather than the color of the ground.

rows.credit: NASA Armstrong Flight Research Center / NASA/Carla Thomas / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The dark lunar disc surrounded by the Sun's pale corona during the 2017 total solar eclipse.
rows.caption: NASA's airborne view of the 21 August 2017 total solar eclipse. The Moon blocks the bright photosphere, revealing the corona.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / Scientific Visualization Studio · public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA CERES map of net radiation averaged over 2000–2015, with a −200 to +200 W m⁻² color scale.
rows.caption: NASA CERES observations, 2000–2015 mean. Net radiation is incoming sunlight minus reflected shortwave and emitted longwave energy at the top of the atmosphere. Positive values indicate a radiative surplus.

rows.credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NOAA sea-surface temperature anomaly map with warmer-than-average water across the equatorial Pacific in late 2015.
rows.caption: NOAA, 11 October–7 November 2015: positive sea-surface temperature anomalies extend across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific during El Niño.

rows.credit: Gordon Hatton / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Tilted and folded sedimentary beds exposed at The Settlands coast.
rows.caption: Folded strata at The Settlands, Wales. Trace a bed through the exposure to see deformation recorded in solid rock.

rows.credit: bgilliard from St. Catharines, Canada / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A low shelf cloud sweeps over buildings at Brock University in Ontario.
rows.caption: A cold front passes Brock University, St. Catharines, Canada. The cloud edge makes uplift visible; the front itself is a zone of contrasting air.

rows.credit: PawełS / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Younger gently dipping red sandstone overlies steep gray beds at Siccar Point, Scotland.
rows.caption: Siccar Point: Devonian sandstone overlies much older, tilted Silurian beds. The unconformity records deformation, erosion and missing time.

rows.credit: Giles Laurent / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Aletsch Glacier curves through a steep Alpine valley, with dark medial moraines running along its surface.
rows.caption: Aletsch Glacier, Switzerland. Flowing ice carries debris; its dark medial moraines record where tributary glaciers join.

rows.credit: Reto Stöckli / NASA Earth Observatory · public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA Blue Marble satellite composite of Earth in an equirectangular global map.
rows.caption: NASA Blue Marble Next Generation, July 2004. A cloud-free satellite composite in a latitude–longitude grid: the map stretches high latitudes and is not equal-area.

rows.credit: U.S. Geological Survey, US Topo 7.5-minute map for Covington, LA (2018) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped
rows.alt: Northwest corner of a USGS US Topo map of Covington, Louisiana, with a 1 km UTM grid labeled 776000 m E and 3377000 m N, and principal digits 77 to 83 along the top edge.
rows.caption: Part of the USGS US Topo map of Covington, Louisiana (2018), with its 1 km UTM grid. Give eastings (along the corridor) before northings (up the stairs).

rows.credit: Michael Rivera / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The clear, shallow Ichetucknee River flowing between grassy, wooded banks in Florida.
rows.caption: The Ichetucknee River in Florida is fed by springs: groundwater from the limestone aquifer flows out at the surface and keeps the water clear.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The Hawaiian volcanic islands stretch across the Pacific beneath scattered white clouds in an ISS photograph.
rows.caption: Hawaiʻi from the ISS. The volcanic chain records Pacific plate motion relative to a long-lived hotspot; the youngest main island is at the southeast end.

rows.credit: Alan Cressler, USGS · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A small instrument shelter on stilts beside a concrete weir on a forest stream.
rows.caption: A USGS streamgage on Little Back Creek, Bath County, Virginia. The shelter records the water level (stage) every few minutes; a rating curve converts stage to discharge, the numbers plotted on a storm hydrograph.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Space Shuttle view of snow-covered land around Hannah Bay with many curved, parallel lines of old shorelines.
rows.caption: Hannah Bay, at the south end of James Bay, Canada, in winter. Snow picks out dozens of old shorelines left behind as the land rose after the ice sheet melted.

rows.credit: NASA/Chris Hadfield / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Astronaut photograph of central Florida dotted with round, dark lakes among farm fields.
rows.caption: Central Florida from the International Space Station, near Lake Wales. Many of the round lakes fill sinkholes formed where the limestone below dissolved.

rows.credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
rows.caption: Grand Canyon from Hopi Point, Arizona. Resistant beds form steps and cliffs above valleys cut by running water.

rows.credit: Reto Stöckli / NASA Earth Observatory · public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA Blue Marble satellite composite of Earth in an equirectangular global map.
rows.caption: NASA Blue Marble Next Generation, July 2004. A cloud-free satellite composite in a latitude–longitude grid: the map stretches high latitudes and is not equal-area.

rows.credit: Mark Reid, USGS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An aerial view of the Oso landslide's bare source scar, debris path and deposits across the valley.
rows.caption: Oso, Washington, 2014: an aerial photograph of the landslide source, travel path and deposit. The displaced material crossed the valley floor.

rows.credit: NASA Johnson Space Center / NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A thin sunlit lunar crescent with crater shadows along the terminator against black space.
rows.caption: The Artemis II crew photographed this lunar crescent on 7 April 2026. Phase is the visible fraction of the sunlit hemisphere, not Earth's shadow.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: False-color MODIS brightness-temperature image showing the Gulf Stream and warm eddies in the North Atlantic.
rows.caption: MODIS, 2 May 2001: thermal contrast traces the Gulf Stream and eddies. Brightness temperature includes the sea surface and overlying moist atmosphere.

rows.credit: NPS Photo / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Polygonal ground and ponds on the tundra in Noatak National Preserve, Alaska, photographed from the air.
rows.caption: Ice-wedge polygons in Alaska's Noatak tundra. Repeated thermal contraction cracking and ice growth organize the permafrost landscape.

rows.credit: Olga Ernst / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Steep dark rock walls border the Almannagjá rift at Þingvellir, Iceland.
rows.caption: Almannagjá, Þingvellir: faults accommodate extension within Iceland's broad North American–Eurasian plate boundary zone.

rows.credit: Jacques Descloitres, MODIS Land Rapid Response Team / NASA GSFC · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Hawaiian islands with greener windward slopes, drier leeward slopes and silvery sunglint on the Pacific.
rows.caption: Terra MODIS, 27 May 2003. Northeasterly trade winds favor wetter, greener windward slopes; leeward slopes are drier. The bright ocean is sunglint.

rows.caption: The Wutach Gorge, Black Forest, Germany. After the Wutach was captured by a steeper Rhine tributary, it cut this deep gorge.

rows.alt: Afternoon cumulus clouds over Sri Lanka, observed by Aqua MODIS on 9 April 2013.
rows.caption: Aqua MODIS, 9 April 2013. Cumulus clouds form over Sri Lanka while the surrounding sea stays clear. Daytime heating of the land drives a sea breeze inland, where the air rises.

rows.credit: owamux / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Circular plates of new pancake ice cover the surface of the western Ross Sea in Antarctica.
rows.caption: New sea ice forming in the Ross Sea. Freezing rejects much of the salt into the surrounding water, increasing its density and helping drive polar overturning.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: GOES-East satellite view of the Americas with tropical cloud bands and midlatitude weather systems.
rows.caption: GOES-East cloud data for 22 April 2014, laid over a cloud-free satellite image of land and ocean, so the whole disc is shown lit. Cloud belts reveal aspects of the global circulation; a single image does not outline every atmospheric cell.

rows.credit: Dennis G. Jarvis / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A fishing boat rests on exposed mud beside a wharf at low tide in Nova Scotia.
rows.caption: Low tide at Waterford on St Mary's Bay, Nova Scotia. The exposed harbor floor makes tidal range visible.

rows.credit: NASA astronaut Ed Lu / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The clear eye and tall spiral cloud walls of Hurricane Isabel, photographed from the ISS.
rows.caption: Astronaut Ed Lu photographed Hurricane Isabel on 13 September 2003. The eye is surrounded by the eyewall's deep convective clouds.

rows.credit: U.S. Air Force photo / Staff Sgt. Samuel Morse · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of Sendai Airport, Japan, with seawater and debris covering the runways and the flat farmland around them.
rows.caption: Sendai Airport, Japan, two days after the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami. The water spread across the flat coastal plain and still covered the runways on 13 March.

rows.credit: Astrobond / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Andromeda Galaxy, a large spiral of stars with two small companion galaxies, against a field of foreground stars.
rows.caption: The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) with its two small companion galaxies. Its light has traveled about 2.5 million years to reach us; the scattered points are much nearer stars in our own galaxy.

rows.credit: Jim D. Griggs, HVO (USGS) staff photographer[1][2] / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An arching orange lava fountain erupts from a vent on Kīlauea amid dark cooling lava.
rows.caption: A lava fountain about 10 meters high at Kīlauea, photographed by USGS on 25 February 1983. Magma reaches the surface here, but the mantle beneath is almost entirely solid.

rows.credit: Jfred1962 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A towering thunderhead cloud backlit by the Sun, with rays of light spreading across a blue sky.
rows.caption: A thunderhead over Rainy Lake, Minnesota. Water evaporated from lakes and land rises, cools and condenses into cloud before falling again as rain.

rows.credit: PatríciaR / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: Rounded, stacked granite boulders under a cloudy sky in Joshua Tree National Park.
rows.caption: Granite boulders in Joshua Tree National Park, California. Weathering along cracks in the granite rounds the blocks into piles of boulders.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Long fault-bounded valleys and escarpments in Kenya's East African Rift, viewed from the ISS.
rows.caption: The East African Rift in Kenya: continental extension is an opening stage of a possible ocean-basin cycle. A rift does not inevitably become an ocean.

rows.credit: Geographer / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: An orange windsock extends above a field beside the path to Green Lane Farm.
rows.caption: A windsock responds to moving air. Its open mouth faces into the wind; meteorological wind direction names where the air comes from.

rows.credit: NASA Astronaut photograph from ISS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Crescent-shaped dunes around Lagoa dos Barros on Brazil's Atlantic coast, seen from the ISS.
rows.caption: Wind shapes barchan dunes beside Lagoa dos Barros, Brazil. The crescent tips point downwind.

rows.credit: Arthur Rothstein / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A car on a Texas Panhandle road beneath a wall of airborne dust during the Dust Bowl.
rows.caption: Texas Panhandle during the 1930s Dust Bowl. Wind lifted fine topsoil from dry, bare fields: deflation removed the soil and carried the dust away in suspension.

rows.credit: Rosa Cabecinhas and Alcino Cunha / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A sharp dune crest and rippled sand at Erg Chebbi, Morocco.
rows.caption: Erg Chebbi, Morocco: a sand sea where wind-blown sand has built up into large dunes. Most of the Sahara is rock or gravel rather than erg.

rows.credit: Chris M Morris / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A mesquite shrub grows on a mound of trapped sand in the Mojave Desert.
rows.caption: Mesquite in Mojave National Preserve, California. Vegetation traps wind-blown sand and can build a small dune called a nabkha.

rows.credit: matteo caprari / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Wind-blown sand and ripples in Libya's desert.
rows.caption: Wind-blown sand streams across rippled dunes in Libya. Most moving grains travel in short hops just above the surface; this hopping is saltation.

rows.credit: Arthur Rothstein / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A car on a Texas Panhandle road beneath a wall of airborne dust during the Dust Bowl.
rows.caption: A Dust Bowl dust storm in the Texas Panhandle. Turbulent wind keeps the finest particles aloft in suspension, so they can travel far beyond their source fields.

rows.credit: lwtt93 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Long, wind-eroded rock ridges rise above the desert at Dunhuang, China.
rows.caption: Yardangs at Dunhuang, China. Persistent wind erosion shapes elongated ridges in relatively soft rock or sediment.

rows.credit: Storm Prediction Center / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A skew-T chart from a weather-balloon sounding, with red temperature and green dew-point lines rising through the atmosphere.
rows.caption: Weather-balloon sounding from Lake Charles, Louisiana, 16 December 2019. The radiosonde measured temperature (red) and dew point (green) with height; the slope of the red line shows the lapse rate.

rows.credit: NASA / Expedition 66 crew · ISS066-E-86970 · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Orange and blue atmospheric layers above Earth's curved horizon, with a crescent Moon in the black sky.
rows.caption: Earth's thin atmosphere seen edge-on from the ISS on 6 December 2021. Scattered sunlight lights the lower layers; the colored bands do not mark exact layer boundaries.

rows.credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio - Amy Moran, Lauren Dauphin, Paul Newman, Katie Jepson, Aaron E. Lepsch / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA map of low ozone concentrations over Antarctica in September 2023.
rows.caption: NASA Ozone Watch and GEOS-5, 21 September 2023. The ozone hole is a region of depleted stratospheric ozone; the colors show ozone amounts, not a visible gap.

rows.credit: Storm Prediction Center / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A skew-T chart from a weather-balloon sounding, with red temperature and green dew-point lines rising through the atmosphere.
rows.caption: Weather-balloon sounding from Lake Charles, Louisiana, 16 December 2019. The radiosonde measured temperature (red) and dew point (green) with height; the slope of the red line shows the lapse rate.

rows.credit: NASA / Expedition 66 crew · ISS066-E-86970 · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Orange and blue atmospheric layers above Earth's curved horizon, with a crescent Moon in the black sky.
rows.caption: Earth's thin atmosphere seen edge-on from the ISS on 6 December 2021. Scattered sunlight lights the lower layers; the colored bands do not mark exact layer boundaries.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A green auroral band glows below the International Space Station above the southern Indian Ocean.
rows.caption: An ISS photograph of aurora north of Antarctica. Energetic particles excite upper-atmosphere gases; the green light is emitted by the atmosphere, not reflected sunlight.

rows.credit: NASA / Expedition 66 crew · ISS066-E-86970 · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Orange and blue atmospheric layers above Earth's curved horizon, with a crescent Moon in the black sky.
rows.caption: Earth's thin atmosphere seen edge-on from the ISS on 6 December 2021. Scattered sunlight lights the lower layers; the colored bands do not mark exact layer boundaries.

rows.credit: NASA / Expedition 66 crew · ISS066-E-86970 · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Orange and blue atmospheric layers above Earth's curved horizon, with a crescent Moon in the black sky.
rows.caption: Earth's thin atmosphere seen edge-on from the ISS on 6 December 2021. Scattered sunlight lights the lower layers; the colored bands do not mark exact layer boundaries.

rows.credit: Poyt448 Peter Woodard / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Fallen leaves and organic litter beneath white beech trees in New South Wales, Australia.
rows.caption: White beech leaf litter at Carowiry Creek, New South Wales. Organic material on the forest floor stores carbon and provides material for decomposition.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / Scientific Visualization Studio · public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA CERES map of reflected shortwave radiation averaged over 2000–2015, with a 0–385 W m⁻² color scale.
rows.caption: NASA CERES observations, 2000–2015 mean. Colors show sunlight reflected by the Earth system in W m⁻². This is outgoing shortwave flux, not incoming solar irradiance or albedo itself.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A rock face with a dark, layered coal seam between paler beds, with dry leaves on the ledges.
rows.caption: A coal seam in Coshocton County, Ohio, about 310 million years old. Coal forms from buried swamp plants; burning it releases carbon stored for millions of years.

rows.credit: Sidoine MBOGNI / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
rows.caption: Forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon. Leaves intercept falling rain and absorb sunlight for photosynthesis, storing carbon in living plants.

rows.credit: Poyt448 Peter Woodard / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Fallen leaves and organic litter beneath white beech trees in New South Wales, Australia.
rows.caption: White beech leaf litter at Carowiry Creek, New South Wales. Organic material on the forest floor stores carbon and provides material for decomposition.

rows.credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
rows.caption: Layered rocks in the Grand Canyon record deep time and the slow carbon cycle. Lithification turns sediment into rock, and the inner gorge exposes much older Precambrian basement.

rows.credit: Sidoine MBOGNI / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
rows.caption: Tropical forest at Bodiman, Cameroon: living vegetation is a carbon store, exchanging carbon with the air and soil.

rows.credit: Dexter Perkins / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
rows.alt: Rounded remnants of granite emerge from loose weathered material in an exposed rock profile.
rows.caption: Weathered granite. As its minerals break down, solid rock gradually turns into loose weathered material.

rows.credit: Sidoine MBOGNI / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
rows.caption: Tropical forest at Bodiman, Cameroon, an example of rainforest vegetation. An Af climate is defined by long-term monthly temperature and rainfall, not by vegetation alone.

rows.credit: Bjørn Christian Tørrissen / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Grassland with scattered acacia trees in Serengeti National Park, Tanzania.
rows.caption: Serengeti savanna: seasonal rainfall helps explain the balance between grasses and scattered trees.

rows.credit: Luca Galuzzi (Lucag) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: Tall orange sand dunes under a clear sky at Sossusvlei, Namibia.
rows.caption: Sossusvlei dunes, Namib Desert. Wind moves sand grains by saltation (bouncing) and surface creep, building dunes over time.

rows.credit: Manfred Heyde / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Green fields and wooded valleys on Exmoor in North Devon.
rows.caption: Exmoor, North Devon: a landscape within the Cfb oceanic climate region. Köppen classes use long-term monthly temperature and precipitation, not the weather on the day of the photograph.

rows.credit: J.-H. Janßen / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A white Stevenson screen on legs, an instrument mast and a rain gauge on grass at a weather station.
rows.caption: Weather station at Mettingen, Germany, with a Stevenson screen for thermometers, an instrument mast and a rain gauge. Climate is worked out from many years of measurements like these.

rows.credit: Richard Mortel / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Open grassland and sparsely vegetated hills near Jargalant, northern Mongolia.
rows.caption: Steppe near Jargalant, Mongolia, far from the moderating influence of the sea. Continental interiors usually have a large annual temperature range.

rows.credit: Manfred Heyde / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Green fields and wooded valleys on Exmoor in North Devon.
rows.caption: Exmoor, North Devon: a landscape within the Cfb oceanic climate region. Köppen classes use long-term monthly temperature and precipitation, not the weather on the day of the photograph.

rows.credit: Alvesgaspar / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: A breaking wave curls and foams along the coast at Porto Covo, Portugal.
rows.caption: A breaking wave at Porto Covo, Portugal. Whether waves build up or erode a beach depends on the balance of swash and backwash over many waves, which one photograph cannot show.

rows.credit: Alvesgaspar / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: A breaking wave curls and foams along the coast at Porto Covo, Portugal.
rows.caption: A breaking wave at Porto Covo, Portugal. In shallow water a wave slows and steepens; its crest eventually breaks.

rows.credit: Iraphne R. Childs / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A groyne extends across the beach at Tallebudgera Creek on Australia's Gold Coast.
rows.caption: Tallebudgera Creek, Gold Coast, in the 1980s. A groyne interrupts sediment movement along a beach and can change sediment supply farther down-drift.

rows.credit: Chris / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial photograph of Spurn Point curving across the Humber estuary entrance.
rows.caption: Spurn Point, England, photographed in 2024. Longshore drift feeds this spit across the mouth of the Humber estuary.

rows.credit: Chris / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial photograph of Spurn Point curving across the Humber estuary entrance.
rows.caption: Spurn Point, England, photographed in 2024. Longshore drift feeds this spit across the mouth of the Humber estuary.

rows.credit: Chris / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial photograph of Spurn Point curving across the Humber estuary entrance.
rows.caption: Spurn Point, England, photographed in 2024. Longshore drift feeds this spit across the mouth of the Humber estuary.

rows.credit: Jakub Hałun / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The isolated rock stack Hvítserkur rises from shallow coastal water in northwestern Iceland.
rows.caption: Hvítserkur, Iceland: a sea stack with openings eroded through its base.

rows.credit: Simaron / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of chalk cliffs at Handfast Point with stacks, an arch and low stumps standing in the sea.
rows.caption: Old Harry Rocks, Handfast Point, Dorset. Waves erode the chalk headland into caves, arches and stacks; low remnants just above the water are stumps.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Snow-covered Himalayan peaks and valleys photographed from the International Space Station.
rows.caption: The Himalaya from the ISS: crust shortened and thickened as India collided with Eurasia.

rows.credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NOAA bathymetry map of the South Atlantic showing continental shelves and the mid-ocean ridge.
rows.caption: NOAA South Atlantic bathymetry. Color represents seafloor depth, revealing continental margins, abyssal basins and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Green crystalline mantle peridotite enclosed by darker volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona.
rows.caption: Mantle peridotite carried to the surface as a xenolith in volcanic rock: a sample of solid upper mantle, not crust. The lithosphere includes the crust and the rigid uppermost mantle.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A dark Glossopteris fossil leaf from Permian rocks in Antarctica, with a branching vein network.
rows.caption: Permian Glossopteris leaf from Antarctica. Related fossils on separated southern continents are evidence that these lands were once joined within Gondwana, which formed part of Pangaea.

rows.credit: National Oceanic & Atmospheric Adminstration (NOAA) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Rounded pillow lava on a fissured seafloor at the Galápagos Rift, photographed by a NOAA expedition.
rows.caption: NOAA, Galápagos Rift, 21 July 2011. Lava quenched in seawater forms pillows close to a spreading center, where new oceanic crust is built.

rows.credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NOAA bathymetry map of the South Atlantic showing continental shelves and the mid-ocean ridge.
rows.caption: NOAA South Atlantic bathymetry. Color represents seafloor depth, revealing continental margins, abyssal basins and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

rows.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Wanmei Liang, using data provided by the ARIA team at NASA/JPL-Caltech. The displacement map is based on Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey and ALOS-2 data from the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Story by Adam Voiland. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA ARIA map showing measured ground displacement along the Kamchatka Peninsula after the 2025 earthquake.
rows.caption: NASA ARIA map of ground displacement after the 2025 Kamchatka megathrust earthquake. The colors show measured surface movement; the fault itself lies buried offshore.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized

rows.caption: Permian Glossopteris leaf from Antarctica. Related fossils on separated southern continents are evidence that these lands were once joined within Gondwana, which formed part of Pangaea.

rows.alt: USGS topographic map of Mount Rainier with contours, glaciers and named summits.
rows.caption: USGS Mount Rainier topographic sheet, published in 1971. Contours connect equal elevations; close spacing marks steep slopes.

rows.credit: USGS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: USGS topographic map extract showing Yosemite Creek, a campground, contours and coordinate markings.
rows.caption: Part of a USGS topographic map near Yosemite Creek, California. Benchmarks (BM) and crosses give spot heights in feet, labeled contours such as 7400 and 7600 show the interval, and contours bend around spurs and valleys.

rows.credit: Medenmaun / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Thorpe Cloud, a steep isolated grassy limestone hill, rising above fields with sheep in Derbyshire.
rows.caption: Thorpe Cloud, Derbyshire (267 m): a small, steep, isolated limestone hill, or knoll, standing above the surrounding fields. It formed from a reef in a warm Carboniferous sea.

rows.credit: USGS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: USGS topographic map extract showing Yosemite Creek, a campground, contours and coordinate markings.
rows.caption: Part of a USGS topographic map near Yosemite Creek, California. Benchmarks (BM) and crosses give spot heights in feet, labeled contours such as 7400 and 7600 show the interval, and contours bend around spurs and valleys.

rows.credit: USGS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: USGS topographic map extract showing Yosemite Creek, a campground, contours and coordinate markings.
rows.caption: Part of a USGS topographic map near Yosemite Creek, California. Benchmarks (BM) and crosses give spot heights in feet, labeled contours such as 7400 and 7600 show the interval, and contours bend around spurs and valleys.

rows.credit: Donnchadh H / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rounded hills and fields around the Vale of Edale, viewed from Grindslow Knoll.
rows.caption: The Vale of Edale and Lose Hill, Peak District, England. Rounded ridges and valley slopes show the local relief.

rows.credit: National Weather Service Office in Burlington, Vermont / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: US National Weather Service surface weather chart for 6 January 1998 with isobars, high and low centers and fronts.
rows.caption: US National Weather Service surface chart, 6 January 1998. Isobars join places with equal pressure; a strong high over Canada and a low near Lake Erie, with a warm front toward New England, set up a strong pressure gradient during the 1998 ice storm.

rows.alt: A broad spiral of white clouds over the Pacific northeast of Japan.
rows.caption: MODIS observed this extratropical cyclone northeast of Japan on 22 February 2012. Cloud bands trace the low-pressure circulation. The image joins two satellite passes, so the straight diagonal line is a seam, not a weather feature.

rows.caption: Aqua MODIS observed Cyclone Evan near Fiji on 16 December 2012. Its cloud bands spiral around the center, roughly following a logarithmic spiral.

rows.alt: The Moselle joins the wider Rhine beside the city of Koblenz, Germany.
rows.caption: The Rhine–Moselle confluence at Koblenz, photographed in 1988. A tributary joins the main channel here.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: ASTER satellite image of branching tributary valleys near the Colorado River in Canyonlands, Utah.
rows.caption: ASTER false-color image, 24 September 2005: tributaries cut into sandstone in Canyonlands, Utah. Plants along the valley floors show up red. The branching network carries water toward the Colorado River (top left).

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: ASTER satellite image of branching tributary valleys near the Colorado River in Canyonlands, Utah.
rows.caption: ASTER false-color image, 24 September 2005: tributaries cut into sandstone in Canyonlands, Utah. Plants along the valley floors show up red. The branching network carries water toward the Colorado River (top left).

rows.credit: none (Landsat) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: False-color Landsat image of the Lena Delta with many branching distributaries and islands.
rows.caption: Landsat's view of the Lena Delta, 2000. Distributaries spread sediment into the Arctic Ocean. The image combines infrared and red bands.

rows.credit: USFS employees / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped and resized
rows.alt: Melting snow patches and a stream near Fourth of July Lake in Idaho's Sawtooth Mountains.
rows.caption: Snowmelt near Fourth of July Lake, Idaho. Seasonal melting transfers stored snow water into streams, soils and groundwater.

rows.caption: ASTER false-color image, 24 September 2005: tributaries cut into sandstone in Canyonlands, Utah. Plants along the valley floors show up red. The branching network carries water toward the Colorado River (top left).
