rows.caption: ASTER false-color image, 24 September 2005: tributaries cut into sandstone in Canyonlands, Utah. Plants along the valley floors show up red. The branching network carries water toward the Colorado River (top left).

rows.credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
rows.caption: Grand Canyon, Arizona. The canyon cuts about 1.8 km into the continental crust, exposing layered rocks, yet continental crust is roughly 30–70 km thick. Even the deepest borehole, at Kola, reached only 12.262 km.

rows.credit: C.C. Finlay, C. Kloss, N. Gillet / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Swarm-derived maps compare Earth's magnetic field intensity in 2014 and 2025, with a scale in nanotesla.
rows.caption: Maps of magnetic-field strength at Earth's surface in 2014 and 2025, modeled from Swarm satellite measurements (colors show nanotesla). The field is generated mainly by moving liquid iron in the outer core, not by a permanent bar magnet.

rows.credit: Karla Panchuk, Steven Earle / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Diagram of S-wave and P-wave paths through Earth, showing the solid inner core, liquid outer core and shadow zones.
rows.caption: Diagram of seismic wave paths through Earth (not to scale). S-waves cannot cross the liquid outer core, leaving a large S-wave shadow zone; P-waves bend at the core boundary, leaving P-wave shadow zones between about 103° and 150° from the earthquake.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Green crystalline mantle peridotite enclosed by darker volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona.
rows.caption: Mantle peridotite carried to the surface as a xenolith in volcanic rock: a sample of solid upper mantle, not crust. The lithosphere includes the crust and the rigid uppermost mantle.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Green crystalline mantle peridotite enclosed by darker volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona.
rows.caption: Mantle peridotite in volcanic rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona: a real sample of upper-mantle rock. The mantle is almost entirely solid; magma forms only where small amounts of rock partly melt.

rows.credit: Karla Panchuk, Steven Earle / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Diagram of S-wave and P-wave paths through Earth, showing the solid inner core, liquid outer core and shadow zones.
rows.caption: Diagram of seismic wave paths through Earth (not to scale). S-waves cannot cross the liquid outer core, leaving a large S-wave shadow zone; P-waves bend at the core boundary, leaving P-wave shadow zones between about 103° and 150° from the earthquake.

rows.credit: Petr Brož (Czech Academy of Science) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A pen arm resting on a white paper drum covered in fine parallel lines, one section showing a burst of wiggles.
rows.caption: A seismograph drum records ground motion as a line on paper. The arrival times of P-, S- and surface waves at many stations are used to locate an earthquake's focus and epicenter and to estimate its magnitude.

rows.alt: A sequence of dark Venus silhouettes crosses the Sun in SDO ultraviolet observations.
rows.caption: SDO's time sequence of the 2012 transit of Venus. A transit can happen only when Venus is near a node of its orbit. Timing past transits helped measure the Earth–Sun distance, now defined precisely as the astronomical unit.

rows.alt: The Moon appears copper-red during a lunar eclipse viewed from Merritt Island, Florida.
rows.caption: NASA Kennedy Space Center photograph of a total lunar eclipse. Earth's shadow falls on the Moon; sunlight filtered through Earth's atmosphere gives the eclipsed surface a reddish color.

rows.credit: H. Raab (User:Vesta) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Three photographs of the full Moon side by side; the middle one is faintly darker along its lower edge.
rows.caption: Penumbral lunar eclipse, 10 January 2020: three photographs an hour apart, combined. In the middle image about 90% of the Moon is inside Earth's penumbra, which dims it only slightly; there is no dark umbral bite.

rows.credit: NASA Armstrong Flight Research Center / NASA/Carla Thomas / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The dark lunar disc surrounded by the Sun's pale corona during the 2017 total solar eclipse.
rows.caption: NASA's airborne view of the 21 August 2017 total solar eclipse. The Moon blocks the bright photosphere, revealing the corona.

rows.credit: NASA Johnson Space Center / NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A thin sunlit lunar crescent with crater shadows along the terminator against black space.
rows.caption: The Moon's sunlit crescent photographed from Artemis II. A synodic month, about 29.5 days, is the time between one new Moon and the next.

rows.credit: NASA Armstrong Flight Research Center / NASA/Carla Thomas / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The dark lunar disc surrounded by the Sun's pale corona during the 2017 total solar eclipse.
rows.caption: The 21 August 2017 total solar eclipse, photographed from inside the Moon's umbra. Where the full shadow falls, the bright photosphere is completely hidden and only the faint corona shows.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / Scientific Visualization Studio · public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA CERES map of reflected shortwave radiation averaged over 2000–2015, with a 0–385 W m⁻² color scale.
rows.caption: CERES map of reflected sunlight. The solar energy absorbed by the Earth system is the incoming sunlight minus this reflected part, so the map shows absorption only indirectly.

rows.credit: SAC Faye Storer / UK Ministry of Defence · Crown copyright / Open Government Licence v1.0 · cropped and resized
rows.alt: Patchy winter snow over dark exposed rock and heath on a Cairngorm mountainside.
rows.caption: Patchy winter snow in the Cairngorms. Fresh snow reflects most incoming sunlight (high albedo), while the dark rock and heath absorb much more (low albedo).

rows.credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio - Marit Jentoft-Nilsen, Global Science and Technology, Inc./Amy Moran, Global Science and Technology, Inc./Heather Hanson / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: CERES global map of outgoing longwave radiation with a color scale in watts per square meter.
rows.caption: NASA CERES, April 2015. Satellite observations map outgoing thermal radiation at the top of the atmosphere in W m⁻²; colder cloud tops generally emit less than warm clear-sky regions.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / Scientific Visualization Studio · public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA CERES map of net radiation averaged over 2000–2015, with a −200 to +200 W m⁻² color scale.
rows.caption: NASA CERES observations, 2000–2015 mean. Net radiation is incoming sunlight minus reflected shortwave and emitted longwave energy at the top of the atmosphere. Positive values indicate a radiative surplus.

rows.credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio - Marit Jentoft-Nilsen, Global Science and Technology, Inc./Amy Moran, Global Science and Technology, Inc./Heather Hanson / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: CERES global map of outgoing longwave radiation with a color scale in watts per square meter.
rows.caption: NASA CERES, April 2015. Satellite observations map outgoing thermal radiation at the top of the atmosphere in W m⁻²; colder cloud tops generally emit less than warm clear-sky regions.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An SDO observation of the solar photosphere showing a large dark sunspot group.
rows.caption: NASA SDO view of the Sun's visible surface and sunspots. Insolation is the incoming solar radiation Earth receives. The solar constant, about 1,361 W m⁻², is the solar power per square meter on a surface facing the Sun at Earth's average distance.

rows.credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio - Marit Jentoft-Nilsen, Global Science and Technology, Inc./Amy Moran, Global Science and Technology, Inc./Heather Hanson / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized

rows.alt: NASA CERES map of reflected shortwave radiation averaged over 2000–2015, with a 0–385 W m⁻² color scale.
rows.caption: NASA CERES observations, 2000–2015 mean. Colors show sunlight reflected by the Earth system in W m⁻². This is outgoing shortwave flux, not incoming solar irradiance or albedo itself.

rows.caption: Sentinel-6 map of sea-surface height during La Niña, January 2025. La Niña strengthens the Walker circulation, which can affect weather far away through teleconnections.

rows.alt: Green phytoplankton and sediment-rich water off Mauritania's desert coast, observed by Aqua MODIS.
rows.caption: Aqua MODIS, 5 May 2020. Upwelling in the Canary Current system supplies nutrients off Mauritania. The visible green water contains phytoplankton and sediment; it is not a temperature map.

rows.alt: World map of sea-surface temperature, with red in the western Pacific and Indian Ocean and blue near the poles.
rows.caption: NASA map of sea-surface temperature from two weeks of satellite infrared data. Red marks the warmest water; the western Pacific warm pool is the large red area near Indonesia and northern Australia (left edge).

rows.credit: Colin Vosper / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rock layers bent into an arch in a small headland at Coppet Hall beach, Pembrokeshire.
rows.caption: An anticline at Coppet Hall, near Saundersfoot, Pembrokeshire. The rock layers are bent upward into an arch, with the oldest beds in the core.

rows.credit: Lysippos / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rock contact exposed along the Moine Thrust at Knockan Crag in northwest Scotland.
rows.caption: The Moine Thrust at Knockan Crag, Scotland: a low-angle reverse fault (a thrust). The hanging wall above the fault plane carries older rocks over the younger footwall rocks below, recording compression.

rows.alt: White chalk cliffs, offshore remnants and a wave-cut base near the Pinnacles in Purbeck.
rows.caption: Chalk cliffs on the Purbeck coast, where the Wessex Basin first subsided and was later squeezed and uplifted (basin inversion). Reconstructing that history needs regional geological evidence, not one view.

rows.caption: Almannagjá, Þingvellir: faults accommodate extension within Iceland's broad North American–Eurasian plate boundary zone.

rows.alt: Aerial view of Wallace Creek, whose channel bends sharply where it crosses the San Andreas Fault.
rows.caption: Wallace Creek, Carrizo Plain, California. Where the stream crosses the San Andreas Fault its channel is offset about 130 m sideways: horizontal (strike-slip) movement over thousands of years.

rows.credit: Gordon Hatton / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Tilted and folded sedimentary beds exposed at The Settlands coast.
rows.caption: Folded strata at The Settlands, Wales. Trace a bed through the exposure to see deformation recorded in solid rock.

rows.caption: US National Weather Service surface chart, 6 January 1998. Isobars join places with equal pressure; a strong high over Canada and a low near Lake Erie, with a warm front toward New England, set up a strong pressure gradient during the 1998 ice storm.

rows.caption: A cold front passes Brock University, St. Catharines, Canada. The cloud edge makes uplift visible; the front itself is a zone of contrasting air.

rows.caption: Cloud along a cold front at Brock University, Ontario. A surface front is where the sloping boundary between two air masses meets the ground; the cloud edge shows roughly, not exactly, where that is.

rows.credit: Wilson44691 / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Fossilized Ogyopsis klotzi trilobite preserved in dark shale.
rows.caption: Ogyopsis klotzi from the Middle Cambrian Mount Stephen Trilobite Beds, Canada. Fossils help correlate and interpret ancient sedimentary rocks.

rows.credit: PawełS / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Younger gently dipping red sandstone overlies steep gray beds at Siccar Point, Scotland.
rows.caption: The unconformity at Siccar Point represents a gap of many millions of years. Ma means millions of years ago and ka thousands of years ago; geologists date such gaps from evidence such as fossils and radiometric ages.

rows.credit: Nationalparks / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: A rock outcrop with a dashed line drawn along a thin pale layer between darker beds below and sandstone above.
rows.caption: The K–Pg boundary at Trinidad Lake State Park, Colorado. The dashed line marks the thin clay layer laid down about 66 million years ago, when the non-bird dinosaurs died out.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Green crystalline mantle peridotite enclosed by darker volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona.
rows.caption: The lava that carried this Peridot Mesa xenolith erupted about 580 ka (580,000 years ago). That dates the eruption, not the much older mantle rock inside it.

rows.credit: PawełS / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Younger gently dipping red sandstone overlies steep gray beds at Siccar Point, Scotland.
rows.caption: The unconformity at Siccar Point represents a gap of many millions of years. Ma means millions of years ago and ka thousands of years ago; geologists date such gaps from evidence such as fossils and radiometric ages.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A dark Glossopteris fossil leaf from Permian rocks in Antarctica, with a branching vein network.
rows.caption: Permian Glossopteris leaf from Antarctica. Related fossils on separated southern continents are evidence that these lands were once joined within Gondwana, which formed part of Pangaea.

rows.credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
rows.caption: Layered rocks in the Grand Canyon record deep time and the slow carbon cycle. Lithification turns sediment into rock, and the inner gorge exposes much older Precambrian basement.

rows.credit: Denali National Park and Preserve / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Glacier ice occupies a steep-sided mountain basin in Denali National Park, Alaska.
rows.caption: Glacial terrain in the Muldrow Glacier area, Denali. Ice erosion enlarges mountain hollows into cirques and sharpens the ridges between them.

rows.credit: Denali National Park and Preserve / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Glacier ice occupies a steep-sided mountain basin in Denali National Park, Alaska.
rows.caption: Glacial terrain in the Muldrow Glacier area, Denali. Ice erosion enlarges mountain hollows into cirques and sharpens the ridges between them.

rows.credit: Doc Searls from Santa Barbara, USA / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of elongated low hills around Horicon Marsh, Wisconsin.
rows.caption: Drumlin terrain near Horicon Marsh, Wisconsin. The streamlined hills record former glacier flow; they are landforms left after the ice retreated.

rows.credit: Diliff / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Yosemite Valley's forested floor between steep granite walls, viewed from Tunnel View.
rows.caption: Bridalveil Fall, Yosemite Valley, California. The fall drops from a hanging valley: its tributary glacier eroded less deeply than the main glacier that deepened Yosemite Valley.

rows.credit: GlacierNPS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The sharp summit and steep ridges of Little Matterhorn in Glacier National Park, Montana.
rows.caption: Little Matterhorn, Glacier National Park, USA. Glacial erosion on several sides can leave a sharp pyramidal peak; this is not the Matterhorn in the Alps.

rows.credit: Giles Laurent / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Aletsch Glacier curves through a steep Alpine valley, with dark medial moraines running along its surface.
rows.caption: Aletsch Glacier, Switzerland. Flowing ice carries debris; its dark medial moraines record where tributary glaciers join.

rows.credit: David Medcalf / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: An exposed bank of poorly sorted glacial sediment containing stones of several sizes.
rows.caption: A natural exposure of glacial till. Ice deposits a mixture of grain sizes directly, often without the sorting produced by flowing water.

rows.credit: Diliff / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Yosemite Valley's forested floor between steep granite walls, viewed from Tunnel View.
rows.caption: Yosemite Valley from Tunnel View, California: a broad, flat floor between steep granite walls. Glaciers enlarged a river valley into this U-shaped trough.

rows.alt: NASA Blue Marble satellite composite of Earth in an equirectangular global map.
rows.caption: NASA Blue Marble monthly composite on an equirectangular latitude–longitude grid. Latitude measures angular distance north or south of the equator, and parallels run east–west. These reference lines are mathematical; they are not marked on the ground.

rows.caption: Satellite imagery in the Mollweide projection with its graticule drawn on: the network of meridians and parallels used to give latitude and longitude.

rows.alt: Big and Little Diomede islands in the Bering Strait, between snow-covered Russia and Alaska, seen by Landsat 8.
rows.caption: Landsat 8, 6 June 2017: Big Diomede (the larger island, left) belongs to Russia and Little Diomede (right) to the US. The International Date Line passes through the water between them; it is a convention, not a visible physical feature.

rows.caption: Part of the USGS US Topo map of Covington, Louisiana (2018), with its 1 km UTM grid. Eastings, the numbers along the top and bottom edges (77, 78, 79 …), increase eastward and are read first; northings, along the side edges (73, 74, 75 …), increase northward and are read second.

rows.credit: U.S. Geological Survey, US Topo 7.5-minute map for Covington, LA (2018) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped
rows.alt: Northwest corner of a USGS US Topo map of Covington, Louisiana, with a 1 km UTM grid labeled 776000 m E and 3377000 m N, and principal digits 77 to 83 along the top edge.
rows.caption: Part of the USGS US Topo map of Covington, Louisiana (2018), with its 1 km UTM grid. UTM gives each 6° zone’s central meridian a false easting of 500,000 m so eastings stay positive, and Northern Hemisphere northings count from the equator: that is why the corner labels read 776000 m E and 3377000 m N. The British National Grid instead uses one false origin southwest of Great Britain.

rows.caption: USGS principal aquifers of the United States, 2000. Colors identify aquifer systems; the map does not show water-table depth or whether an aquifer is confined at a particular well.

rows.alt: Gray London Clay exposed below yellow-brown Red Crag in the sea cliffs at Walton-on-the-Naze, Essex.
rows.caption: London Clay forms the lower part of the Naze cliffs. Clay-rich beds let groundwater through only slowly, so they can act as aquitards.

rows.alt: A hand pump used to draw groundwater at Perambalur, India.
rows.caption: Groundwater hand pump at Perambalur, India. Abstraction removes water from an aquifer, and heavy pumping can lower the water table around a well.

rows.credit: USGS Office of Groundwater / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: USGS map showing the distribution of principal aquifers across the United States.
rows.caption: USGS map of principal aquifers. Low-permeability layers (aquitards) can confine an aquifer, but showing this needs a geological cross-section and well data, not a surface map.

rows.credit: Colin Smith / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: People cross pale limestone blocks separated by deep joints above Malham Cove, England.
rows.caption: Limestone pavement at Malham, North Yorkshire. Rain falling here drains down the widened joints (grykes) into the rock, recharging the groundwater below.

rows.credit: Peter Cox / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Fulking village at the foot of the steep, grassy South Downs scarp, with fields stretching away below.
rows.caption: Fulking, West Sussex, at the foot of the South Downs. Water soaks into the permeable chalk and comes out as springs where it meets less permeable rock at the base of the scarp, so villages grew up along this spring line.

rows.credit: Michael Rivera / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A USGS groundwater observation station in Stephen C. Foster State Park, Georgia.
rows.caption: USGS observation well in Stephen C. Foster State Park, Georgia. Instruments record groundwater levels; the water table itself lies beneath the surface.

rows.caption: The South Fork Stillaguamish River in flood. Water spreads beyond the usual channel when discharge exceeds channel capacity.

rows.caption: A USGS streamgage on Little Back Creek, Virginia. It records stage, the water level, every few minutes; a rating curve turns stage into discharge, the volume of water passing per second.

rows.caption: Seasonal snowmelt feeds a stream near Fourth of July Lake, Idaho. A nival river regime is dominated by snow building up in winter and melting in spring.

rows.caption: The Stillaguamish River, Washington, in flood. Its floods follow heavy rain, and faster floodwater can carry larger particles: the river's competence (the largest particle it can move) rises.

rows.caption: USGS gauging station at Huey Creek, Antarctica, 12 December 2001. Repeated measurements of stage and discharge produce a river's hydrograph.

rows.caption: Snowmelt near Fourth of July Lake, Idaho. Seasonal melting transfers stored snow water into streams, soils and groundwater.

rows.alt: Field photographs of red and black soils at different positions on the Addi Selam hillslope in Ethiopia.
rows.caption: Addi Selam, Ethiopia: thin red soils on the upper slope (A) and thick, dark, clay-rich soils at the foot of the slope (B). At the toe of a hillslope, water and fine sediment from upslope collect, so soils are often deeper and wetter.

rows.credit: https://www.flickr.com/photos/soilscience/5140644166/ / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A Puerto Rican soil profile has a dark surface above pale carbonate-rich subsoil, with a depth scale.
rows.caption: Calciustoll near Ponce, Puerto Rico: a Mollisol with a roughly 30 cm mollic surface over a calcic horizon. Its parent material includes colluvium and weathered limestone.

rows.credit: Photo by Lynn Betts, USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A sloping cornfield in western Iowa cut by rills and a gully where runoff has washed soil away.
rows.caption: Rills cut across a young Iowa cornfield where the crop still left most of the soil bare. Plant cover and residue shield the surface from raindrop impact and slow runoff; without it, soil is detached and carried away.

rows.credit: Arthur Rothstein / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A car on a Texas Panhandle road beneath a wall of airborne dust during the Dust Bowl.
rows.caption: Texas Panhandle during the 1930s Dust Bowl. Wind lifted fine topsoil from dry, bare fields: deflation removed the soil and carried the dust away in suspension.

rows.credit: Till Niermann (User:Till.niermann) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Dry, deeply dissected loess slopes near Hunyuan in Shanxi, China.
rows.caption: Loess hills near Hunyuan, Shanxi, China. Concentrated runoff has cut deep gullies into the soft wind-deposited silt; they are far too large to be removed by plowing.

rows.credit: US Navy / USDA NRCS Photo Gallery, NRCSIA99138 · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Close-up photograph of a raindrop splashing on soil and throwing droplets and particles outward.
rows.caption: USDA NRCS archive photograph of raindrop impact. Splash detaches and redistributes soil particles before surface runoff carries them farther.

rows.credit: Willem van Aken, CSIRO / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Bare eroded soil with small gullies on a hillslope near Charters Towers, Queensland.
rows.caption: Hillslope gully and sheet erosion near Charters Towers, Queensland, documented by CSIRO. Loss of cover exposes soil to runoff.

rows.credit: matteo caprari / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Wind-blown sand and ripples in Libya's desert.
rows.caption: Wind-blown sand streams across rippled dunes in Libya. Most moving grains travel in short hops just above the surface; this hopping is saltation.

rows.alt: A soil profile on the Karelian Isthmus with a dark surface, pale leached layer and browner subsoil.
rows.caption: Podzolic soil on the Karelian Isthmus. The pale E horizon has lost material by eluviation; material may accumulate in the B horizon below.

rows.credit: The original uploader was Michaila vnuk at Ukrainian Wikipedia. / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A soil profile on the Karelian Isthmus with a dark surface, pale leached layer and browner subsoil.
rows.caption: Podzolic soil on the Karelian Isthmus. Just below the dark surface layer, a thin pale gray band (about 7–10 cm on the tape) is the E horizon, which has lost material by eluviation. The rusty-brown B horizon below it has gained some of that material.

rows.credit: USDA Employee / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped
rows.alt: A soil profile with a thin dark topsoil, a pale tan layer below it and thick red subsoil, beside a depth scale in feet.
rows.caption: Layers in this exposed soil profile differ in color and texture. These soil horizons record changes in organic matter, weathering and material movement.

rows.credit: Poyt448 Peter Woodard / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Fallen leaves and organic litter beneath white beech trees in New South Wales, Australia.
rows.caption: White beech leaf litter at Carowiry Creek, New South Wales. Organic material on the forest floor stores carbon and provides material for decomposition.

rows.credit: Samuel Rios / USDA NRCS · public domain · via Wikimedia Commons · resized
rows.alt: A deep reddish Nipe-series soil profile with a measuring tape in Puerto Rico.
rows.caption: USDA NRCS Nipe-series profile at Cerro Las Mesas, Puerto Rico, January 2002. Classified as Typic Acrudox, this Oxisol formed through deep weathering of iron-rich parent material.

rows.credit: Marie-Lan Taÿ Pamart / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A pale specimen of kaolinite from Ixtassou, France.
rows.caption: Kaolinite, a clay mineral, from Ixtassou, France. In soil texture, 'clay' means particles smaller than 0.002 mm, so mineral type and particle size are different properties.

rows.credit: USDA NRCS Montana / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Two cupped hands holding a handful of dark, crumbly topsoil.
rows.caption: A handful of topsoil. Soil scientists judge texture by feel: sand is gritty, silt is smooth like flour, and clay is sticky and can be pressed into a ribbon.

rows.credit: Luca Galuzzi (Lucag) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: Tall orange sand dunes under a clear sky at Sossusvlei, Namibia.
rows.caption: Sossusvlei dunes, Namib Desert. Wind moves sand grains by saltation (bouncing) and surface creep, building dunes over time.

rows.credit: Bill Whittaker / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Steep, grassy Loess Hills rising behind a cornfield east of Mondamin, Iowa.
rows.caption: Loess Hills, western Iowa. These hills are made of loess, wind-deposited sediment dominated by silt-sized grains (0.002–0.05 mm).

rows.caption: Soil scientists judge texture by feel in the field. The proportions of sand, silt and clay can then be plotted on a ternary texture triangle.

rows.caption: Sundial in the walled garden at Brodick Castle, Isle of Arran. The gnomon's shadow shows the Sun's direction; when the Sun is lower in the sky, shadows are longer.

rows.alt: Three time-lapse sunrises blended into one panorama, with the Sun rising further north in summer and further south in winter.
rows.caption: Composite of three time-lapse sunrises photographed from the same spot: at the summer solstice (left, furthest north), the spring equinox (center) and the winter solstice (right, furthest south). The sunrise point and the Sun's path shift through the year.

rows.alt: A sequence of dark Venus silhouettes crosses the Sun in SDO ultraviolet observations.
rows.caption: SDO's time sequence of the 2012 transit of Venus. A transit can happen only when Venus is near a node of its orbit. Timing past transits helped measure the Earth–Sun distance, now defined precisely as the astronomical unit.

rows.alt: Saturn and its broad rings in a natural-color mosaic photographed by the Cassini spacecraft.
rows.caption: Cassini, 6 October 2004: a natural-color mosaic of Saturn and its rings. The rings are a thin disc of orbiting particles.

rows.credit: NASA/JPL / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Voyager 2 image of Neptune's blue disc showing cloud bands and the Great Dark Spot.
rows.caption: Voyager 2 image of Neptune, assembled from green and orange filter observations in August 1989. The deep blue here is enhanced; the ice giant's natural color is paler.

rows.credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Saturn and its broad rings in a natural-color mosaic photographed by the Cassini spacecraft.
rows.caption: Cassini's natural-color mosaic of Saturn and its rings. Ring particles closer to Saturn orbit faster than those farther out: orbital period depends on orbital size and the central mass.

rows.alt: The fully sunlit Earth showing Africa, Arabia, Antarctica and swirling clouds in the Apollo 17 photograph.
rows.caption: Apollo 17's Blue Marble, 7 December 1972. Earth's axial tilt changes the angle and duration of sunlight over the year.

rows.credit: Jesse Allen / NASA Earth Observatory · Landsat · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Landsat view of the northern Gulf of Mexico coast, with barrier islands off Mississippi and Alabama and the faint Chandeleur arc off Louisiana.
rows.caption: Landsat image of the northern Gulf of Mexico coast (colors enhanced). The bright chain of narrow sandy islands lies off Mississippi and Alabama; the faint curved arc at lower left is Louisiana's Chandeleur Islands. All are barrier islands separated from the mainland by shallow water.

rows.credit: NOAA Photo Library / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An aerial view of damaged buildings and washed-over land on the Bolivar Peninsula after Hurricane Ike.
rows.caption: Hurricane Ike damage on Texas's Bolivar Peninsula, photographed by NOAA. Low air pressure lets the sea surface rise slightly (the inverse barometer effect), but wind pushing water onshore causes most of a surge.

rows.credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NOAA bathymetry map of the South Atlantic showing continental shelves and the mid-ocean ridge.
rows.caption: NOAA South Atlantic bathymetry. Color represents seafloor depth, revealing continental margins, abyssal basins and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

rows.credit: NOAA Corps aerial survey: Mark Moran, Phil Eastman and Dave Demers · public domain · 2005 · resized
rows.alt: Flooded streets and houses in New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina in 2005.
rows.caption: New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina, 2005. Floodwater stands level across neighborhoods; still-water flood level is the water height once waves are averaged out.

rows.credit: NOAA Photo Library / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An aerial view of damaged buildings and washed-over land on the Bolivar Peninsula after Hurricane Ike.
rows.caption: Bolivar Peninsula, Texas, September 2008. NOAA documented coastal damage from Hurricane Ike's storm surge.

rows.credit: Mass Communication Specialist 3rd Class Dylan McCord / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of debris, damaged buildings and flooded land at a fishing port in Kesennuma after the 2011 tsunami.
rows.caption: Coastal damage at Kesennuma, Japan, after the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami. Run-up is the greatest height above sea level that the water reaches on land; field surveys are needed to measure it.

rows.credit: NOAA Photo Library / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An aerial view of damaged buildings and washed-over land on the Bolivar Peninsula after Hurricane Ike.
rows.caption: Bolivar Peninsula, Texas, September 2008. NOAA documented coastal damage from Hurricane Ike's storm surge.

rows.caption: Meteosat-9, 21 December 2010. Near the day–night boundary, sunlight strikes the surface at a large incidence angle and is spread over more ground, so the surface appears dimmer than where the Sun is high.

rows.caption: NASA SDO view of the Sun's visible surface and sunspots. Insolation is the incoming solar radiation Earth receives. The solar constant, about 1,361 W m⁻², is the solar power per square meter on a surface facing the Sun at Earth's average distance.

rows.caption: NASA SDO observation of active region AR 12192 in 2014. Sunspots are cooler areas of the photosphere; the orange display color is image processing.

rows.caption: NASA CERES observations, 2000–2015 mean. Colors show sunlight reflected by the Earth system in W m⁻². This is outgoing shortwave flux, not incoming solar irradiance or albedo itself.

rows.credit: Bernard Spragg. NZ from Christchurch, New Zealand / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Wisps of low fog rise above a calm lake on a frosty morning, with trees reflected in the water.
rows.caption: Evaporation fog over a lake. Water evaporating from the warmer lake condenses into tiny droplets in the cold air above; the fog is droplets, not invisible water vapor.

rows.credit: NOAA GOES-19 / CIMSS, University of Wisconsin–Madison · public domain · 30 October 2025 · resized
rows.alt: GOES-19 satellite view of a cloud-free band beside western Lake Michigan as a land breeze pushes offshore.
rows.caption: GOES-19, 30 October 2025 at 13:20 UTC. A land breeze keeps clouds away from part of Lake Michigan’s western shore. The product combines visible and infrared observations across the night-to-day transition; station measurements confirm the offshore flow.

rows.credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · Aqua MODIS / EOSDIS · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Afternoon cumulus clouds over Sri Lanka, observed by Aqua MODIS on 9 April 2013.
rows.caption: Aqua MODIS, 9 April 2013. Sea-breeze air moves inland and helps cumulus clouds develop over the warmer island. The silvery water is sunglint.

rows.credit: National Weather Service Office in Burlington, Vermont / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: US National Weather Service surface weather chart for 6 January 1998 with isobars, high and low centers and fronts.
rows.caption: US National Weather Service surface chart, 6 January 1998. Isobars join places with equal pressure; a strong high over Canada and a low near Lake Erie, with a warm front toward New England, set up a strong pressure gradient during the 1998 ice storm.

rows.credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · Aqua MODIS / EOSDIS · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Afternoon cumulus clouds over Sri Lanka, observed by Aqua MODIS on 9 April 2013.
rows.caption: Aqua MODIS, 9 April 2013. Sea-breeze air moves inland and helps cumulus clouds develop over the warmer island. The silvery water is sunglint.

rows.credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · Aqua MODIS / EOSDIS · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Afternoon cumulus clouds over Sri Lanka, observed by Aqua MODIS on 9 April 2013.
rows.caption: Aqua MODIS, 9 April 2013. By day Sri Lanka heats faster than the sea; air rises over the island, building cumulus clouds, while cooler sea air flows in below: a sea-breeze circulation.

rows.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech · ECOSTRESS, PIA25423 · underlying map attribution retained in image · resized
rows.alt: ECOSTRESS thermal map shows warm urban surfaces in London late at night on 15 July 2022.
rows.caption: ECOSTRESS measured London's land-surface temperatures near midnight on 15 July 2022. Built surfaces remained warmer than many vegetated areas. These are surface temperatures, not standard air-temperature readings.

rows.alt: A Deep SOLO profiling float is lowered from the research vessel Kaʻimikai-O-Kanaloa in 2018.
rows.caption: NOAA Deep SOLO deployment, 2018. Profiling floats measure ocean temperature and salinity at depth, helping scientists study density structure and deep circulation. The ocean conveyor is a simplified description of a complex circulation.

rows.credit: owamux / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Circular plates of new pancake ice cover the surface of the western Ross Sea in Antarctica.
rows.caption: New pancake ice in the Ross Sea, Antarctica. Freezing leaves much of the salt behind in the water below, making it colder, saltier and denser, so it can sink and form deep water.

rows.alt: A Deep SOLO profiling float is lowered from the research vessel Kaʻimikai-O-Kanaloa in 2018.
rows.caption: A NOAA Deep SOLO float is lowered into the sea. It measures temperature and salinity, which set the water's density and identify deep-water masses such as NADW.

rows.caption: At first quarter the Moon is at right angles to the Sun, so their tidal pulls partly cancel, giving neap tides. The smallest local tidal range can come a little later, depending on the coast.

rows.alt: A fishing boat rests on exposed mud beside a wharf at low tide in Nova Scotia.
rows.caption: Low tide at Waterford on St Mary's Bay, Nova Scotia. The exposed harbor floor makes tidal range visible.

rows.credit: Dennis G. Jarvis / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A fishing boat rests on exposed mud beside a wharf at low tide in Nova Scotia.
rows.caption: Low water at St Mary's Bay, Nova Scotia. Tidal range changes through the spring–neap cycle as the Moon's and Sun's tidal pulls combine or partly cancel; one photograph cannot show which tide this was.

rows.credit: NASA Armstrong Flight Research Center / NASA/Carla Thomas / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The dark lunar disc surrounded by the Sun's pale corona during the 2017 total solar eclipse.
rows.caption: NASA's airborne view of the 21 August 2017 total solar eclipse. The Moon blocks the bright photosphere, revealing the corona.

rows.credit: Dennis G. Jarvis / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A fishing boat rests on exposed mud beside a wharf at low tide in Nova Scotia.
rows.caption: Low water at St Mary's Bay, Nova Scotia. The tidal bulge is an idealized model: real tides arrive as long waves shaped by the coast, and here the falling tide has left the harbor floor dry.

rows.credit: Dennis G. Jarvis / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A fishing boat rests on exposed mud beside a wharf at low tide in Nova Scotia.
rows.caption: Low tide at Waterford on St Mary's Bay, Nova Scotia. The exposed harbor floor makes tidal range visible.

rows.credit: NASA astronaut Ed Lu / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The clear eye and tall spiral cloud walls of Hurricane Isabel, photographed from the ISS.
rows.caption: Astronaut Ed Lu photographed Hurricane Isabel on 13 September 2003. The eye is surrounded by the eyewall's deep convective clouds.

rows.credit: NASA astronaut Ed Lu / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The clear eye and tall spiral cloud walls of Hurricane Isabel, photographed from the ISS.
rows.caption: Astronaut Ed Lu photographed Hurricane Isabel on 13 September 2003. The eye is surrounded by the eyewall's deep convective clouds.

rows.credit: NASA, MODIS Rapid Response System / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A broad spiral of white clouds over the Pacific northeast of Japan.
rows.caption: MODIS observed this extratropical cyclone northeast of Japan on 22 February 2012. Cloud bands trace the low-pressure circulation. The image joins two satellite passes, so the straight diagonal line is a seam, not a weather feature.

rows.credit: EOSDIS Worldview / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Satellite view of Typhoon Mangkhut with a compact eye and spiraling cloud bands in September 2018.
rows.caption: Typhoon Mangkhut, September 2018. Curved bands of cloud spiral into the storm well outside the compact eye; these rainbands bring heavy showers far from the center.

rows.credit: NASA astronaut Ed Lu / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The clear eye and tall spiral cloud walls of Hurricane Isabel, photographed from the ISS.
rows.caption: Astronaut Ed Lu photographed Hurricane Isabel on 13 September 2003. The eye is surrounded by the eyewall's deep convective clouds.

rows.credit: NOAA Photo Library / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An aerial view of damaged buildings and washed-over land on the Bolivar Peninsula after Hurricane Ike.
rows.caption: Bolivar Peninsula, Texas, September 2008. NOAA documented coastal damage from Hurricane Ike's storm surge.

rows.credit: NASA astronaut Ed Lu / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The clear eye and tall spiral cloud walls of Hurricane Isabel, photographed from the ISS.
rows.caption: Astronaut Ed Lu photographed Hurricane Isabel on 13 September 2003. The eye is surrounded by the eyewall's deep convective clouds.

The displacement map is based on Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey and ALOS-2 data from the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Story by Adam Voiland. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA ARIA map showing measured ground displacement along the Kamchatka Peninsula after the 2025 earthquake.
rows.caption: NASA ARIA map of ground displacement after the 2025 Kamchatka megathrust earthquake. The colors show measured surface movement; the fault itself lies buried offshore.

rows.credit: Mass Communication Specialist 3rd Class Dylan McCord / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of debris, damaged buildings and flooded land at a fishing port in Kesennuma after the 2011 tsunami.
rows.caption: Coastal damage at Kesennuma, Japan, after the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami. Run-up is the greatest height above sea level that the water reaches on land; field surveys are needed to measure it.

rows.credit: Alvesgaspar / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: A breaking wave curls and foams along the coast at Porto Covo, Portugal.
rows.caption: A wind wave shoaling and breaking at Porto Covo, Portugal, for contrast with a tsunami. Both slow and steepen in shallow water, but a tsunami shoals across the whole continental shelf and usually arrives as a fast-rising flood rather than a curling breaker.

rows.credit: NOAA Photo Library / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An aerial view of damaged buildings and washed-over land on the Bolivar Peninsula after Hurricane Ike.
rows.caption: Bolivar Peninsula, Texas, September 2008. NOAA documented coastal damage from Hurricane Ike's storm surge.

rows.credit: Mass Communication Specialist 3rd Class Dylan McCord / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of debris, damaged buildings and flooded land at a fishing port in Kesennuma after the 2011 tsunami.
rows.caption: Coastal damage at Kesennuma, Japan, after the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami. Run-up is the greatest height above sea level that the water reaches on land; field surveys are needed to measure it.

rows.credit: Alvesgaspar / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: A breaking wave curls and foams along the coast at Porto Covo, Portugal.
rows.caption: A wind wave at Porto Covo, Portugal, for contrast with a tsunami: crest to crest it spans tens of meters, while a tsunami's wavelength can exceed 100 km.

rows.credit: NASA/SDO, AIA / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A sequence of dark Venus silhouettes crosses the Sun in SDO ultraviolet observations.
rows.caption: SDO's time sequence of the 2012 transit of Venus. A transit can happen only when Venus is near a node of its orbit. Timing past transits helped measure the Earth–Sun distance, now defined precisely as the astronomical unit.

rows.credit: Astrobond / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Andromeda Galaxy, a large spiral of stars with two small companion galaxies, against a field of foreground stars.
rows.caption: The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) with its two small companion galaxies. Its light has traveled about 2.5 million years to reach us; the scattered points are much nearer stars in our own galaxy.

rows.credit: Zdeněk Bardon/ESO / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Milky Way in Centaurus with the two bright stars Alpha and Beta Centauri near the center.
rows.caption: Alpha and Beta Centauri, photographed from ESO's La Silla Observatory by Zdeněk Bardon. They look like a pair, but Alpha Centauri, the nearest star system to the Sun, is about 4.4 light-years away, while Beta Centauri is roughly 390 light-years away.

rows.credit: Astrobond / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Andromeda Galaxy, a large spiral of stars with two small companion galaxies, against a field of foreground stars.
rows.caption: The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) with its two small companion galaxies. Its light has traveled about 2.5 million years to reach us; the scattered points are much nearer stars in our own galaxy.

rows.credit: Zdeněk Bardon/ESO / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A long-exposure photograph of Orion's stars, red emission nebulae and dark dust clouds.
rows.caption: Orion photographed from ESO's La Silla Observatory by Zdeněk Bardon. Stars that appear close in the sky can lie at very different distances; long exposure reveals faint gas and dust.

rows.credit: Astrobond / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Andromeda Galaxy, a large spiral of stars with two small companion galaxies, against a field of foreground stars.
rows.caption: The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) with its two small companion galaxies. Its light has traveled about 2.5 million years to reach us; the scattered points are much nearer stars in our own galaxy.

rows.alt: The Andromeda Galaxy, a large spiral of stars with two small companion galaxies, against a field of foreground stars.
rows.caption: The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) with its two small companion galaxies. Its light has traveled about 2.5 million years to reach us; the scattered points are much nearer stars in our own galaxy.

rows.credit: National Oceanic & Atmospheric Adminstration (NOAA) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Rounded pillow lava on a fissured seafloor at the Galápagos Rift, photographed by a NOAA expedition.
rows.caption: NOAA, Galápagos Rift, 21 July 2011. Lava quenched in seawater forms pillows close to a spreading center, where new oceanic crust is built.

rows.credit: Jim D. Griggs, HVO (USGS) staff photographer[1][2] / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An arching orange lava fountain erupts from a vent on Kīlauea amid dark cooling lava.
rows.caption: Lava fountains at Kīlauea show magma reaching the surface through a vent. The conduit below cannot be seen; it is inferred from geophysical measurements and eruption behavior.

rows.credit: United States Geological Survey / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A line of lava fountains and gas rises from the Kamoamoa fissure in forest southwest of Puʻu ʻŌʻō, Hawaiʻi.
rows.caption: USGS, 5 March 2011: lava erupts along a newly opened fissure between Puʻu ʻŌʻō and Nāpau, Kīlauea. Several fountains mark the linear opening.

rows.credit: USGS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Pale pyroclastic deposits fill the Marella River valley below Mount Pinatubo.
rows.caption: USGS photograph of Pinatubo's Marella River valley, 1 July 1991. These are deposits left by pyroclastic flows, not a view of a flow in motion.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The Hawaiian volcanic islands stretch across the Pacific beneath scattered white clouds in an ISS photograph.
rows.caption: Hawaiʻi from the ISS. The volcanic chain records Pacific plate motion relative to a long-lived hotspot; the youngest main island is at the southeast end.

rows.credit: Midori / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: The broad conical slopes of Mount Fuji rise beyond Lake Kawaguchi in Japan.
rows.caption: Mount Fuji from Lake Kawaguchi, Japan. Repeated eruptions built a stratovolcano with layers of lava and fragmental deposits.

rows.credit: Jim D. Griggs, HVO (USGS) staff photographer[1][2] / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An arching orange lava fountain erupts from a vent on Kīlauea amid dark cooling lava.
rows.caption: A lava fountain about 10 meters high at Kīlauea, photographed by USGS on 25 February 1983. Magma reaches the surface here, but the mantle beneath is almost entirely solid.

rows.credit: Aravind Sivaraj / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A hand pump used to draw groundwater at Perambalur, India.
rows.caption: Groundwater hand pump at Perambalur, India. Abstraction removes water from an aquifer, and heavy pumping can lower the water table around a well.

rows.credit: Explorer2310 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Microscope photograph of leaf epidermal cells and stomatal pores under drought conditions.
rows.caption: Leaf epidermis viewed through a microscope. Stomata regulate gas exchange and water-vapor loss; transpiration is one part of evapotranspiration.

rows.credit: Sidoine MBOGNI / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
rows.caption: Forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon. Leaves intercept falling rain and absorb sunlight for photosynthesis, storing carbon in living plants.

rows.credit: Kyle Hawton / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Glen Canyon Dam holds back Lake Powell above a narrow river gorge.
rows.caption: Glen Canyon Dam and Lake Powell, Arizona. Reservoir storage and controlled releases alter the timing and size of flows downstream.

rows.credit: Sidoine MBOGNI / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
rows.caption: Tropical forest at Bodiman, Cameroon: living vegetation is a carbon store, exchanging carbon with the air and soil.

rows.credit: USFS employees / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped and resized
rows.alt: Melting snow patches and a stream near Fourth of July Lake in Idaho's Sawtooth Mountains.
rows.caption: Snowmelt near Fourth of July Lake, Idaho. Seasonal melting transfers stored snow water into streams, soils and groundwater.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: ASTER satellite image of branching tributary valleys near the Colorado River in Canyonlands, Utah.
rows.caption: ASTER false-color image, 24 September 2005: tributaries cut into sandstone in Canyonlands, Utah. Plants along the valley floors show up red. The branching network carries water toward the Colorado River (top left).

rows.credit: Gordon Hatton / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A lone ash tree growing out of a crack in a limestone pavement above Grassington.
rows.caption: An ash tree growing out of a grike in limestone pavement above Grassington, Yorkshire Dales. Roots in the crack can widen it, and acids from roots and decaying leaves help dissolve the rock.

rows.credit: Colin Smith / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: People cross pale limestone blocks separated by deep joints above Malham Cove, England.
rows.caption: Malham Cove limestone pavement. Rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide widens joints into grykes, leaving blocks called clints.

rows.credit: Colin Smith / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: People cross pale limestone blocks separated by deep joints above Malham Cove, England.
rows.caption: Malham Cove limestone pavement. Rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide widens joints into grykes, leaving blocks called clints.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rounded potholes cut into dark bedrock beside flowing water in the Presque Isle River, Michigan.
rows.caption: Presque Isle River, Michigan. Swirling, sediment-laden water has drilled potholes into the bedrock of this river in the Upper Peninsula, near Lake Superior.

rows.credit: Chris Andrews / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Angular rock blocks cover the summit of Foel Fras in Wales.
rows.caption: Blockfield on Foel Fras, Wales. Physical weathering breaks bedrock into angular fragments without changing its minerals.

rows.credit: Chris Andrews / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Angular rock blocks cover the summit of Foel Fras in Wales.
rows.caption: Blockfield on Foel Fras, Wales. Physical weathering breaks bedrock into angular fragments without changing its minerals.

rows.credit: Dexter Perkins / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
rows.alt: Rounded remnants of granite emerge from loose weathered material in an exposed rock profile.
rows.caption: Weathered granite. As its minerals break down, solid rock gradually turns into loose weathered material.

rows.credit: MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA GSFC / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Satellite image of the parallel folded ridges of the Appalachian Mountains and Chesapeake Bay.
rows.caption: NASA Terra MODIS, 15 September 2023. Appalachian ridges and valleys across Virginia, West Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania preserve the structure of an ancient mountain belt.

rows.credit: PawełS / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Younger gently dipping red sandstone overlies steep gray beds at Siccar Point, Scotland.
rows.caption: Siccar Point, Scotland: Silurian beds tilted almost vertical during the Caledonian mountain building, then eroded and covered by younger Devonian sandstone. The Caledonides formed as the Iapetus Ocean closed.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Snow-covered Himalayan peaks and valleys photographed from the International Space Station.
rows.caption: The Himalaya from the ISS: crust shortened and thickened as India collided with Eurasia.

rows.credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NOAA bathymetry map of the South Atlantic showing continental shelves and the mid-ocean ridge.
rows.caption: NOAA South Atlantic bathymetry. Color represents seafloor depth, revealing continental margins, abyssal basins and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

rows.credit: Olga Ernst / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Steep dark rock walls border the Almannagjá rift at Þingvellir, Iceland.
rows.caption: Almannagjá, Þingvellir: faults accommodate extension within Iceland's broad North American–Eurasian plate boundary zone.

rows.credit: Lysippos / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rock contact exposed along the Moine Thrust at Knockan Crag in northwest Scotland.
rows.caption: At Knockan Crag the Moine Thrust places rocks with different histories against each other. Contacts like this help reconstruct the Caledonian mountain belt and its terranes, although mapping a terrane boundary needs regional evidence, not one outcrop.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Long fault-bounded valleys and escarpments in Kenya's East African Rift, viewed from the ISS.
rows.caption: The East African Rift in Kenya: continental extension is an opening stage of a possible ocean-basin cycle. A rift does not inevitably become an ocean.

rows.credit: National Weather Service Office in Burlington, Vermont / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: US National Weather Service surface weather chart for 6 January 1998 with isobars, high and low centers and fronts.
rows.caption: US National Weather Service surface chart, 6 January 1998. Isobars join places with equal pressure; a strong high over Canada and a low near Lake Erie, with a warm front toward New England, set up a strong pressure gradient during the 1998 ice storm.

rows.credit: NASA image courtesy Jeff Schmaltz, LANCE MODIS Rapid Response. Caption by Michon Scott. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Cyclone Evan's spiral cloud bands cross the islands of Fiji in a NASA satellite image.
rows.caption: Aqua MODIS observed Cyclone Evan near Fiji on 16 December 2012. Its cloud bands spiral around the center, roughly following a logarithmic spiral.

rows.credit: Geographer / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: An orange windsock extends above a field beside the path to Green Lane Farm.
rows.caption: A windsock shows the wind direction near the ground. Friction with the land surface slows the wind and turns it across the isobars toward low pressure.

rows.credit: PHG / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 (originally GFDL) · resized
rows.alt: Wide sandy bay with the seabed exposed after the sea drew back, framed by trees and rocks, at Kata Noi Beach, Phuket.
rows.caption: Kata Noi Beach, Phuket, Thailand, 26 December 2004: the sea has drawn back before the third and strongest tsunami wave, exposing the seabed; open water is far out to the right. Many tsunamis arrive without this warning.

rows.credit: Chris / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial photograph of Spurn Point curving across the Humber estuary entrance.
rows.caption: Spurn Point, England, photographed in 2024. Longshore drift feeds this spit across the mouth of the Humber estuary.

rows.credit: Olga Ernst / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Steep dark rock walls border the Almannagjá rift at Þingvellir, Iceland.
rows.caption: Almannagjá, Þingvellir: faults accommodate extension within Iceland's broad North American–Eurasian plate boundary zone.

rows.credit: Tangopaso / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Rounded volcanic hills covered in forest above farmland, seen from a summit.
rows.caption: The Chaîne des Puys from the Puy de Dôme, France: a line of about 80 young volcanoes in the Massif Central.

rows.credit: Alvesgaspar / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: A breaking wave curls and foams along the coast at Porto Covo, Portugal.
rows.caption: A breaking wave at Porto Covo, Portugal. In shallow water a wave slows and steepens; its crest eventually breaks.

rows.credit: Jean-Marie Vugnon (2) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Moselle joins the wider Rhine beside the city of Koblenz, Germany.
rows.caption: The Rhine–Moselle confluence at Koblenz, photographed in 1988. A tributary joins the main channel here.

rows.credit: Giles Laurent / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Aletsch Glacier curves through a steep Alpine valley, with dark medial moraines running along its surface.
rows.caption: Aletsch Glacier, Switzerland. Flowing ice carries debris; its dark medial moraines record where tributary glaciers join.

rows.credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
rows.caption: Grand Canyon from Hopi Point, Arizona. Resistant beds form steps and cliffs above valleys cut by running water.

rows.credit: Terry Ott / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A turquoise glacial lake below steep gray peaks and a snow-filled gully, with spruce forest and driftwood logs.
rows.caption: Moraine Lake in Banff National Park, Alberta, in the Canadian Rockies. Glaciers carved the valley, and fine rock flour from their meltwater gives the lake its color.

rows.credit: Immelman284 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of a dark river and a muddy river flowing side by side without mixing.
rows.caption: The Meeting of the Waters near Manaus, where the dark Rio Negro joins the sediment-laden Amazon (Solimões).

rows.credit: NASA/Kjell Lindgren / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The muddy Ucayali River winds through forest in Peru, with abandoned bends beside the active channel.
rows.caption: Ucayali River, Peru, photographed from the ISS. Meander migration leaves cut-offs and abandoned channels across the floodplain.

rows.credit: Pseudopanax at English Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A broad flat river plain with autumn vegetation in the Ahuriri valley, New Zealand.
rows.caption: Ahuriri River plain near Omarama, New Zealand. River deposition builds a relatively flat valley floor between higher ground.

rows.credit: Midori / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: The broad conical slopes of Mount Fuji rise beyond Lake Kawaguchi in Japan.
rows.caption: Mount Fuji from Lake Kawaguchi, Japan. Repeated eruptions built a stratovolcano with layers of lava and fragmental deposits.

rows.credit: lwtt93 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Long, wind-eroded rock ridges rise above the desert at Dunhuang, China.
rows.caption: Yardangs at Dunhuang, China. Persistent wind erosion shapes elongated ridges in relatively soft rock or sediment.

rows.credit: none (Landsat) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: False-color Landsat image of the Lena Delta with many branching distributaries and islands.
rows.caption: Landsat's view of the Lena Delta, 2000. Distributaries spread sediment into the Arctic Ocean. The image combines infrared and red bands.

rows.credit: Ondřej Žváček / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: A sheer basalt escarpment dropping from a high grassy plateau into deep valleys in the Simien Mountains.
rows.caption: The Simien Mountains, Ethiopia. Layers of ancient lava form a high plateau that ends in cliffs more than 1,000 m high.

rows.credit: Bjørn Christian Tørrissen / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Grassland with scattered acacia trees in Serengeti National Park, Tanzania.
rows.caption: Serengeti savanna: seasonal rainfall helps explain the balance between grasses and scattered trees.

rows.credit: Rickard Törnblad / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: View from Mount Batilamu across forested volcanic ridges toward the coast of Viti Levu, Fiji.
rows.caption: View from Mount Batilamu, Viti Levu, Fiji. Forested ridges of old volcanic rock fall toward the coastal lowlands of Fiji's largest island.

rows.credit: Arild Vågen / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: White chalk cliffs running along the coast above a shingle beach.
rows.caption: The Seven Sisters chalk cliffs on the East Sussex coast, England. Waves cut the chalk back into steep white cliffs.

rows.credit: PawełS / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Younger gently dipping red sandstone overlies steep gray beds at Siccar Point, Scotland.
rows.caption: Siccar Point: Devonian sandstone overlies much older, tilted Silurian beds. The unconformity records deformation, erosion and missing time.

rows.credit: Chris Andrews / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Angular rock blocks cover the summit of Foel Fras in Wales.
rows.caption: Blockfield on Foel Fras, Wales. Physical weathering breaks bedrock into angular fragments without changing its minerals.

rows.credit: Colin Smith / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: People cross pale limestone blocks separated by deep joints above Malham Cove, England.
rows.caption: Malham Cove limestone pavement. Rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide widens joints into grykes, leaving blocks called clints.

rows.credit: Philip Pankhurst / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A long, narrow shingle beach running along the coast, with a lagoon behind it.
rows.caption: Chesil Beach seen from Portland, Dorset. The shingle barrier is about 29 km long and holds the Fleet lagoon behind it.

rows.credit: Tim Heaton / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A path crossing moorland above a long, narrow loch between hills.
rows.caption: Loch Ness in the Great Glen. The glen follows a major fault, and ice deepened it into a long trough.

rows.credit: Chris / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial photograph of Spurn Point curving across the Humber estuary entrance.
rows.caption: Spurn Point, England, photographed in 2024. Longshore drift feeds this spit across the mouth of the Humber estuary.

rows.credit: Christine Johnstone / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A low cliff of soft clay slumping onto a beach, with the sea beyond.
rows.caption: Crumbling till cliffs on the Holderness coast, one of the fastest-eroding coastlines in Europe.

rows.credit: Saffron Blaze / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A limestone arch reaching into blue sea from a curving beach below grassy cliffs.
rows.caption: Durdle Door, Dorset: an arch cut by the sea through steeply tilted limestone on the Jurassic Coast.

rows.credit: Kingsmasher678 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A karst spring in Alabama flows over rocks from a wooded limestone slope.
rows.caption: Groundwater emerges at a karst spring in Alabama. Water stored in connected pores and fractures can return to the surface as spring flow.

rows.credit: Denali National Park and Preserve / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Glacier ice occupies a steep-sided mountain basin in Denali National Park, Alaska.
rows.caption: Glacial terrain in the Muldrow Glacier area, Denali. Ice erosion enlarges mountain hollows into cirques and sharpens the ridges between them.

rows.credit: Bureau of Land Management / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Saguaro cacti and desert shrubs scattered across a gentle slope.
rows.caption: Sonoran Desert National Monument, Arizona, southwest of Phoenix.

rows.credit: Ikluft / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of the San Andreas Fault as a straight line of ridges and gullies crossing the dry Carrizo Plain.

rows.alt: Steep gullies with red, orange and white sediment walls cutting through pine woodland.
rows.caption: Providence Canyon, Georgia. These gullies formed mainly in the 1800s, when farming removed the plant cover from soft coastal-plain sediment.

rows.caption: Terra MODIS, 27 May 2003. Northeasterly trade winds favor wetter, greener windward slopes; leeward slopes are drier. The bright ocean is sunglint.

rows.credit: USFS employees / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped and resized
rows.alt: Melting snow patches and a stream near Fourth of July Lake in Idaho's Sawtooth Mountains.
rows.caption: Snowmelt near Fourth of July Lake, Idaho. Seasonal melting transfers stored snow water into streams, soils and groundwater.

rows.credit: Jocelyn Augustino / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A raised embankment separates floodwater from farmland beside the Mississippi at Hannibal, Missouri.
rows.caption: Mississippi levee at Hannibal, Missouri, 20 June 2008. This engineered embankment limits inundation; natural levees instead build up from repeated overbank deposition.

rows.credit: GlacierNPS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The sharp summit and steep ridges of Little Matterhorn in Glacier National Park, Montana.
rows.caption: Little Matterhorn, Glacier National Park, USA. Glacial erosion on several sides can leave a sharp pyramidal peak; this is not the Matterhorn in the Alps.

rows.credit:
Mike Doukas, USGS

rows.caption: USGS aerial photograph of Crater Lake, Oregon. Collapse following the eruption of Mount Mazama formed the caldera; Wizard Island is a younger volcanic cone.

rows.credit: Quintin Soloviev / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of the Delaware River curving through a gap cut across Kittatinny Ridge.
rows.caption: Delaware Water Gap, on the Pennsylvania–New Jersey border. The river cuts straight through Kittatinny Ridge in a water gap; a dry notch with no river would be a wind gap.

rows.credit: Trey Perry / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A waterfall pouring from a limestone overhang into a green pool surrounded by trees.
rows.caption: Hamilton Pool, Texas: a pool in Edwards Plateau limestone formed where the roof of an underground river collapsed.

rows.credit: Fsendek1904 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A dry, stony shore and wide pale flats in front of the shallow water of the Great Salt Lake.
rows.caption: The shore of the Great Salt Lake. With no outlet to the sea, the lake loses water only by evaporation, so it is saltier than the ocean.

rows.credit: Famartin / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: View from a forested ridge over a wide, flat farmed valley to distant hills.
rows.caption: The Shenandoah Valley, part of the Great Appalachian Valley, seen from Skyline Drive on the Blue Ridge in Virginia.

rows.credit: Buidhe / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Snow- and ice-covered Mount Rainier above conifers and autumn meadows.
rows.caption: Mount Rainier from Paradise. It is the highest volcano of the Cascade arc, above the Cascadia subduction zone.

rows.credit: Doc Searls from Santa Barbara, USA / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of elongated low hills around Horicon Marsh, Wisconsin.
rows.caption: Drumlin terrain near Horicon Marsh, Wisconsin. The streamlined hills record former glacier flow; they are landforms left after the ice retreated.

rows.credit: Mahdithewikipedian / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rocky ridges above Wadi Shahah in Ras Al Khaimah, United Arab Emirates.
rows.caption: Ras Al Khaimah, UAE. Bare, rocky mountain slopes with almost no plant cover; a road winds up to the summit ridge.

rows.credit: Alessandro Balsamo / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 igo · resized
rows.alt: Cliffs and cultivated valley floor at Bamiyan, Afghanistan.
rows.caption: Bamiyan Valley, Afghanistan. Steep sedimentary cliffs overlook the cultivated valley floor.

rows.credit: Marcin Konsek / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A pebble beach and clear water on the shore of Lake Sevan, Armenia, under a blue sky.
rows.caption: Lake Sevan, Armenia, a large freshwater lake about 1,900 m above sea level in the Lesser Caucasus.

rows.credit: jlrsousa / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rounded rock outcrops rise above woodland beside the Huambo–Dondo road in Angola.
rows.caption: Angola. Isolated rock outcrops stand above the surrounding wooded landscape.

rows.credit: Luca Galuzzi / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: The jagged white ice front of a glacier ending in a lake, with mountains behind.
rows.caption: Perito Moreno Glacier, Los Glaciares National Park, Argentina: an outlet glacier of the Southern Patagonian Ice Field.

rows.alt: The Salzach valley at Werfen, Austria, seen from Hohenwerfen Castle.
rows.caption: Werfen, Austria. Settlements and transport follow the floor of an Alpine river valley.

rows.alt: Uluru, a huge red sandstone monolith, glowing at sunset above dry grassland in central Australia.
rows.caption: Uluru, Northern Territory. This rock is a remnant of sandstone layers tilted almost on end and left standing as the land around it wore down.

rows.alt: Mountain slopes near Lahic in Azerbaijan.
rows.caption: Lahic, Azerbaijan. Steep relief in the Greater Caucasus concentrates movement and settlement in valleys.

rows.alt: A blue river winding through a green valley with villages, below rocky limestone mountains.
rows.caption: The Trebišnjica river winding through a valley near Gornji Orahovac, southern Bosnia and Herzegovina, between bare limestone mountains.

rows.alt: A misty, forested valley with a river winding below, framed by bare winter trees.
rows.caption: The Semois valley in the Belgian Ardennes, where the river has cut deep meanders into old, uplifted rock.

rows.credit: kallerna / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Snow-covered Vihren and Kutelo peaks in Bulgaria's Pirin Mountains.
rows.caption: Pirin Mountains, Bulgaria. Vihren and Kutelo stay snow-covered long after the lowlands have thawed, because temperature falls with height.

rows.alt: Pale salt margins around Laguna Honda beneath barren mountain slopes in Bolivia.
rows.caption: Laguna Honda, Bolivia. A high-altitude salt lake occupies a dry Andean basin.

rows.credit: Mussi Katz / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
rows.alt: Morning cloud in a valley among forested and cultivated slopes in Bhutan.
rows.caption: Bhutan. Valleys channel drainage through steep Himalayan relief.

rows.alt: Reeds in the shallows of a wide lake under a cloudy sky.
rows.caption: Dryviaty Lake in Braslaw Lakes National Park, Belarus, one of many lakes left among moraines by the ice sheets.

rows.credit: EdwinAlden.1995 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Green hills above Kamanyola in South Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo.
rows.caption: Kamanyola, DR Congo. Steep, partly cleared hills in South Kivu, near the western edge of the East African Rift.

rows.credit: Diego Delso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rock formations and the Tara salt flat in northern Chile's Atacama Desert.
rows.caption: Salar de Tara, Chile. An arid high basin collects salts while exposed rock frames its margins.

rows.alt: The Guáitara canyon and farmed slopes surrounding Las Lajas near Ipiales, Colombia.
rows.caption: Guáitara canyon, Colombia. A deeply incised river separates steep, cultivated slopes.

rows.credit: Rhododendrites / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The steep symmetrical cone of Arenal volcano rising above tropical forest under white clouds.
rows.caption: Arenal, a young stratovolcano in northern Costa Rica built above the subducting Cocos plate.

rows.alt: Pedoulas village and wooded slopes in the Troodos Mountains of Cyprus.
rows.caption: Troodos Mountains, Cyprus. Higher ground is cooler and generally wetter than the coastal plains.

rows.credit: Tomáš Pospíšil / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Weathered rock towers among woodland in Český ráj, Czechia.
rows.caption: Český ráj, Czechia. Resistant sandstone forms towers above the surrounding forest.

rows.caption: Møns Klint, Denmark. Chalk formed from tiny marine plankton was pushed up by glacier ice; waves and landslides keep the cliffs steep.

rows.caption: Sandstone cliffs and sand in Tassili n'Ajjer National Park, in the Algerian Sahara.

rows.caption: Cotopaxi, Ecuador, one of the highest active volcanoes in the world (5,897 m), seen across the páramo grassland of the Andes.

rows.alt: Still water and pine trees at Viru Bog in Estonia's Lahemaa National Park.
rows.caption: Viru Bog, Estonia. Waterlogged peatland stores carbon and drains slowly.

rows.alt: A strip of green reeds along the river with a tall sand dune rising right behind.

rows.alt: Snow-covered Greater Caucasus peaks above the lowland foreground in Georgia.

rows.alt: Grassy and wooded hills near Boti, Ghana.
rows.caption: Boti, Ghana. Vegetation cover varies across hills and cultivated ground.

rows.alt: A rocky granite peak rising directly behind tall public housing blocks.
rows.caption: Lion Rock above Chuk Yuen Estate, Kowloon. Hong Kong's steep granite hills rise right behind its housing.

rows.alt: The blue-green Krka River among wooded slopes in Croatia.

rows.alt: Cultivated mountain slopes at Palmes near Petit-Goâve, Haiti.

rows.alt: Bare mountain slopes and stony ground near Abyaneh, Iran.

rows.alt: Sand and rocky mountains near Wadi Rum in southern Jordan.
rows.caption: Southern Jordan. Sparse vegetation exposes desert rock and sediment to wind and occasional runoff.

rows.alt: A marsh creek in low-lying Dorchester County, Maryland.
rows.caption: Dorchester County, Maryland. Tidal channels drain a low coastal wetland landscape.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rounded potholes cut into dark bedrock beside flowing water in the Presque Isle River, Michigan.
rows.caption: Presque Isle River, Michigan. Swirling, sediment-laden water has drilled potholes into the bedrock of this river in the Upper Peninsula, near Lake Superior.

rows.credit: Chris Light / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Pink and gray granite and gneiss outcrop at the water's edge beneath spruce and birch forest.
rows.caption: Canadian Shield rock on the Minnesota shore of Rainy Lake. These gneisses and granites are 1 to 3 billion years old and were scraped bare by ice sheets.

rows.credit: Yinan Chen / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0 · cropped and resized
rows.alt: A bend of the Mississippi River viewed from Mississippi Palisades State Park in Illinois.
rows.caption: Mississippi Palisades, Illinois. A broad river flows beneath a wooded bluff.

rows.credit: USFWS Mountain-Prairie / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of many small ponds and wetlands scattered across green farmland.
rows.caption: Prairie potholes in North Dakota: shallow wetlands in hollows left by melting blocks of glacier ice.

rows.credit: Z3lvs / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
rows.alt: Rolling grass-covered hills stretching to the horizon under a pale sky.
rows.caption: The Sand Hills near Seneca, Nebraska: grass-covered dunes, the largest dune field in the Western Hemisphere.

rows.credit: EgorovaSvetlana / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A deep mountain pass between steep forested slopes, with low cloud over the ridge.
rows.caption: Franconia Notch, White Mountains, New Hampshire. Glaciers deepened this valley through the granite.

rows.credit: rheins / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Geirangerfjord between steep mountain walls, with the village of Geiranger and cruise ships on the water.
rows.caption: Geirangerfjord, Norway. A glacier deepened this valley below sea level; when the ice melted, the sea flooded the steep-sided trough to form a fjord.

rows.credit: Geologicharka / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Danube flowing through a narrow gorge between steep forested limestone walls.
rows.caption: The Kazan section of the Djerdap (Iron Gate) gorge, seen from the Serbian side. Here the Danube cuts through the Carpathian–Balkan mountains.

rows.credit: FranHogan / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A low palm-covered island in Panama's Guna Yala archipelago.
rows.caption: Guna Yala, Panama. Small low islands sit in shallow Caribbean coastal waters.
