rows.credit: Adamnewbie / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A narrow river gorge cut into dark lava rock across a flat plain, with a bridge and distant mountains.
rows.caption: The Rio Grande Gorge near Taos, cut into basalt that filled the Rio Grande rift.

rows.credit: Famartin / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Gray rocky peaks above a forested slope under a blue sky.
rows.caption: Wheeler Peak, Great Basin National Park. It is one of the Basin and Range mountains that rise between dry valleys in Nevada.

rows.credit: PointsofNoReturn / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A rounded rocky mountain rising steeply from the wide Hudson River.
rows.caption: Storm King Mountain above the Hudson River. Ice deepened this valley, and the river below is now a tidal estuary.

rows.credit: Arthur Rothstein / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Black-and-white photo of a farmer and two children walking past a shed half-buried by drifting dust.
rows.caption: Cimarron County, Oklahoma, in April 1936 (historical photograph). Drought and wind stripped plowed soil from the plains during the Dust Bowl.

rows.credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Landsat 9 image of the meandering Congaree River and its forested floodplain, with labels for meanders and a paleochannel.
rows.caption: Landsat 9, 2025: the meandering Congaree River and its forested floodplain, South Carolina. Labels mark a meander and an abandoned former channel (paleochannel).

rows.credit: Krzysztof Ziarnek, Kenraiz / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Steep eroded ridges and gullies of pale layered rock under a blue sky.
rows.caption: Badlands National Park, South Dakota. Soft sediment layers erode quickly into a maze of ridges and gullies.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rows of forested mountain ridges fading into blue haze.
rows.caption: The Great Smoky Mountains in Tennessee, part of the Blue Ridge province of the Appalachians.

rows.credit: Aiken1986 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A steep-sided mountain pass with autumn forest and cliffs, seen from high above.
rows.caption: Smugglers Notch in Vermont's Green Mountains, seen from Mount Mansfield.

rows.credit: Dietmar Rabich / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Steam and orange microbial mats around Grand Prismatic Spring in Yellowstone National Park.
rows.caption: Grand Prismatic Spring, Yellowstone National Park, Wyoming. Hot groundwater heated by a shallow magma body feeds the spring; heat-tolerant microbes color its edges.

rows.credit: Sinfinitu / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A waterfall dropping from a sheer cliff of a flat-topped sandstone mountain above rainforest.
rows.caption: Angel Falls (Kerepakupai Merú) dropping about 979 m from Auyán-tepui, Venezuela, the world's highest waterfall.

rows.credit: Richard Mortel from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Steep limestone towers reflected in water at Tràng An, northern Vietnam.
rows.caption: Tràng An, Vietnam. Limestone dissolution and valley flooding create a karst landscape of towers and waterways.

rows.credit: Claire Charters / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Palm trees and rocky shoreline beside blue coastal water in Samoa.
rows.caption: Samoa. Volcanic shores meet shallow tropical coastal waters.

rows.credit: Danie van der Merwe / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Flat-topped Table Mountain rising above Cape Town across the bay from a sandy beach.
rows.caption: Table Mountain from Bloubergstrand, South Africa. Its flat top is a layer of hard sandstone.

rows.credit: Amakuru / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: View from a mountain summit down to a small lake in a hollow between two sharp ridges.
rows.caption: Red Tarn from Helvellyn, Lake District: a corrie lake between the arêtes of Striding Edge and Swirral Edge.

rows.credit: Petersrockypics / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Snow on Gallt y Wenallt above mist in Nant Gwynant, Eryri / Snowdonia.
rows.caption: Nant Gwynant, Eryri / Snowdonia. A glacial valley lies beneath the steep Snowdon horseshoe.

rows.credit: Sophie Hurel / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Steep limestone hills rise above red soil and fields at Viñales, Cuba.
rows.caption: Viñales, Cuba. Karst erosion leaves steep mogotes above cultivated lowlands.

rows.credit: Carol M. Highsmith / Library of Congress · public domain
rows.alt: Aerial view west from above the US Capitol along the green National Mall to the Washington Monument and the Potomac River.
rows.caption: Washington, DC, looking west from above the US Capitol along the National Mall to the Washington Monument. The city sits on low ground where the Anacostia joins the tidal Potomac River (top left).

rows.credit: Johannes Philipp / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: White chalk cliffs near Dover seen from the English Channel.
rows.caption: Dover, Kent. Marine erosion exposes chalk deposited in an ancient sea.

rows.credit: NASA Johnson Space Center · STS-62 crew · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Astronaut photograph of the bird's-foot Mississippi River delta, with sediment-laden water spreading into the Gulf of Mexico.
rows.caption: The Mississippi River delta, Louisiana, photographed by Space Shuttle astronauts in March 1994. Sediment carried by the river builds the bird's-foot delta out into the Gulf of Mexico.

rows.credit: U.S. Geological Survey from Reston, VA, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A sandy inlet between rocky granite shores in Acadia National Park, Maine.
rows.caption: Acadia, Maine. Waves act on a rugged coast underlain by resistant granite.

rows.credit: Joseph Mischyshyn / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Closely packed basalt columns on the Antrim coast at Giant's Causeway, Northern Ireland.
rows.caption: Giant's Causeway, Northern Ireland. Cooling contraction formed joints in ancient basalt lava.

rows.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author or not provided / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of Bodie Island, its lighthouse, wetlands and Atlantic beach in North Carolina.
rows.caption: Bodie Island, North Carolina. A low barrier island separates Atlantic waves from sheltered wetlands.

rows.credit: N Chadwick / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rock, sandy beach and dunes on the Northumberland coast near Bamburgh.
rows.caption: Northumberland coast. Dunes store wind-blown sand above a beach backed by resistant rock.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Water falls over a sandstone ledge into a pool in Old Man's Cave Gorge, Ohio.
rows.caption: Hocking Hills, Ohio. Water erodes the Black Hand Sandstone into gorges, ledges and plunge pools.

rows.credit: Matt Feifarek / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Tilted rocky outcrops and breaking waves at Beavertail State Park, Rhode Island.
rows.caption: Beavertail, Rhode Island. Atlantic waves erode an exposed rocky headland.

rows.credit: David290 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Huangpu River curves around Lujiazui's towers in Shanghai.
rows.caption: Shanghai. Dense urban development occupies low delta ground beside the tidal Huangpu River.

rows.credit: Rodw / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Floodwater surrounds Burrowbridge in the Somerset Levels in February 2014.
rows.caption: Burrowbridge, Somerset, February 2014. Low relief slows the drainage of extensive floodwater.

rows.credit: Pere.page / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Eroded clay hills and flat-topped ridges in a dry, open landscape.
rows.caption: Bardenas Reales, Navarra: a semi-desert of eroded clay and gypsum in the dry Ebro basin.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Night-time ISS photograph of Khartoum at the meeting of the Blue and White Nile in Sudan.
rows.caption: Khartoum, Sudan, photographed at night from the International Space Station. The dark winding bands are the Blue and White Nile, which meet here; the city's lights spread along their banks.

rows.credit: Malik Ahamed from Colombo, Sri Lanka / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A broad bend of the New River in a steep forested gorge in West Virginia.
rows.caption: New River Gorge, West Virginia. River incision exposes the dissected Appalachian Plateau.

rows.credit: Bill Whittaker / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Steep, grassy Loess Hills rising behind a cornfield east of Mondamin, Iowa.
rows.caption: The Loess Hills near Mondamin, western Iowa. The hills are built of loess: wind-blown sediment made mostly of silt.

rows.credit: Matthew.kowal / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Fog covers houses and forested slopes at Section in Jamaica's Blue Mountains.
rows.caption: Blue Mountains, Jamaica. Moist air rises over high relief, supporting cloud and rainfall.

rows.credit: David Brossard / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Mississippi River and Natchez–Vidalia Bridge seen from Natchez, Mississippi.
rows.caption: Natchez, Mississippi. A broad river corridor runs below the bluffs along the state's western boundary.

rows.credit: Godot13 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view across the dry erosional basin of Makhtesh Ramon in Israel's Negev Desert.
rows.caption: Makhtesh Ramon, Israel. Differential erosion has excavated a large basin in folded sedimentary rocks; it is not an impact crater.

rows.credit: Famartin / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Sand dunes topped with grass beside a wide beach on a barrier island.
rows.caption: Dunes at Island Beach State Park, a barrier island on the New Jersey coast.

rows.credit: Fadesga / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Wooded slopes in Quebrada de los Cuervos, Uruguay.
rows.caption: Quebrada de los Cuervos, Uruguay. A wooded ravine interrupts the surrounding grassland landscape.

rows.credit: dwhartwig / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Water cascades down pale rock steps at Kent Falls State Park, Connecticut.
rows.caption: Kent Falls, Connecticut. Flowing water erodes a stepped bedrock channel within the wooded uplands.

rows.credit: Charlie fong / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Dusk panorama across the Inner Harbour to the dense buildings of the western Macau Peninsula.
rows.caption: The west side of the Macau Peninsula from across the Inner Harbour, at the mouth of the Pearl River estuary. Much of Macau's low ground is reclaimed land.

rows.credit: Jeff Schmaltz / NASA GSFC · Terra MODIS / LANCE-EOSDIS · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Terra MODIS natural-color view of Bangladesh, its delta channels and the Sundarbans beside the Bay of Bengal.
rows.caption: Bangladesh, Terra MODIS, 9 November 2011. River-borne sediment builds the broad delta and coastal plain; folded hills lie to the east.

rows.credit: Dan Sloan / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Kaieteur Falls dropping in a single plunge over a sandstone cliff into a forested gorge in Guyana.
rows.caption: Kaieteur Falls, Guyana. The Potaro River plunges about 226 m over a hard sandstone edge of the ancient Guiana Shield into a forested gorge.

rows.credit: Arian Zwegers / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Two rusting ships stranded on sand where a sea once was.
rows.caption: The ship graveyard at Moynaq, Uzbekistan, on the former bed of the Aral Sea. River water diverted for irrigation shrank the sea.

rows.credit: Taisir Mahdi / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A reed house and a boat on calm water, with water buffalo by the reeds.
rows.caption: The Mesopotamian Marshes of southern Iraq, where the Tigris and Euphrates spread across their low delta plain.

rows.credit: Andrzej Otrębski / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Grassy sand dunes rolling down toward a calm lagoon.
rows.caption: The Parnidis dune near Nida on the Curonian Spit, Lithuania, with the Curonian Lagoon beyond.

rows.credit: Art Anderson / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Beach grass on a sand dune beside a wide sandy beach and calm bay.
rows.caption: Dunes at Cape Henlopen State Park, Delaware, where Delaware Bay meets the Atlantic.

rows.credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
rows.alt: Meteosat view of Earth's day–night boundary on the December solstice, with more of the Southern Hemisphere in daylight.
rows.caption: Meteosat-9 SEVIRI, 21 December 2010. The tilted day–night boundary shows the Southern Hemisphere having longer days. Axial tilt, not a change in Earth–Sun distance, causes this seasonal pattern.

rows.credit: Photograph by Clem Rutter, Rochester, Kent. (www.clemrutter.net). / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A spherical sundial with hour markings and a movable gnomon at Green's Windmill, Nottingham.
rows.caption: A working sundial at Green's Windmill, Nottingham. A gnomon's shadow connects the Sun's apparent direction with local solar time.

rows.credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
rows.alt: Meteosat view of Earth's nearly north–south day–night boundary at the March equinox.
rows.caption: Meteosat satellite image at the March equinox: the terminator runs nearly pole to pole, as in the model when neither hemisphere tilts toward the Sun.

rows.credit: LynceanEducation / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Three time-lapse sunrises blended into one panorama, with the Sun rising further north in summer and further south in winter.
rows.caption: Composite of three time-lapse sunrises photographed from the same spot: at the summer solstice (left, furthest north), the spring equinox (center) and the winter solstice (right, furthest south). The sunrise point and the Sun's path shift through the year.

rows.credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
rows.alt: Meteosat view of Earth's nearly north–south day–night boundary at the March equinox.
rows.caption: Meteosat satellite image showing the day–night terminator. Earth's eastward rotation carries every place across this boundary at sunrise and sunset.

rows.credit: Christine Matthews / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A physical marker of the historic Greenwich Meridian at the Royal Observatory.
rows.caption: The historic Greenwich Meridian marker. Longitude is measured from here, and every 15° of longitude is about one hour of solar time.

rows.credit: Joshua Stevens / NASA Earth Observatory, Landsat data: USGS · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Big and Little Diomede islands in the Bering Strait, between snow-covered Russia and Alaska, seen by Landsat 8.
rows.caption: Landsat image of the Diomede Islands, either side of the International Date Line: a convention where the calendar date changes, not a physical line.

rows.credit: Lapos71 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: First-quarter Moon photographed from Calabria, with the right half of the visible lunar disc sunlit.
rows.caption: A first-quarter Moon: half the visible disc is lit when the Moon is about 90° from the Sun in our sky, as in the model's quarter position.

rows.credit: Luc Viatour / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Nearly full Moon photographed from Hamois, Belgium, with dark maria and bright cratered highlands.
rows.caption: A nearly full Moon, lit almost completely because it lies roughly opposite the Sun. Earth's shadow does not cause the phase.

rows.credit: Шелковников Евгений Анатольевич / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of abandoned buildings at the Kola Superdeep Borehole site in Russia in 2020.
rows.caption: The Kola Superdeep Borehole site. At 12.262 km it is the deepest hole ever drilled, yet it did not get through the continental crust.

rows.credit: C.C. Finlay, C. Kloss, N. Gillet / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Swarm-derived maps compare Earth's magnetic field intensity in 2014 and 2025, with a scale in nanotesla.
rows.caption: Maps of magnetic-field strength at Earth's surface in 2014 and 2025, modeled from Swarm satellite measurements (colors show nanotesla). The field is generated mainly by moving liquid iron in the outer core, not by a permanent bar magnet.

rows.credit: Petr Brož (Czech Academy of Science) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A pen arm resting on a white paper drum covered in fine parallel lines, one section showing a burst of wiggles.
rows.caption: A seismograph records ground motion as a wiggly line. P- and S-wave arrival times recorded around the world are the main evidence for the layers in the model.

rows.credit: Karla Panchuk, Steven Earle / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Diagram of S-wave and P-wave paths through Earth, showing the solid inner core, liquid outer core and shadow zones.
rows.caption: Diagram of seismic wave paths through Earth (not to scale). S-waves cannot cross the liquid outer core, leaving a large S-wave shadow zone; P-waves bend at the core boundary, leaving P-wave shadow zones between about 103° and 150° from the earthquake.

rows.credit: Ikluft / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of the San Andreas Fault as a straight line of ridges and gullies crossing the dry Carrizo Plain.
rows.caption: The San Andreas Fault, California: a transform boundary where the plates slide past each other horizontally.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Snow-covered Himalayan peaks and valleys photographed from the International Space Station.
rows.caption: The Himalaya from the ISS: a convergent boundary where continental crust has been shortened and thickened in a collision.

rows.credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NOAA seafloor relief map around Puerto Rico identifies the deep Puerto Rico Trench and nearby plate boundary.
rows.caption: NOAA seafloor relief of the Puerto Rico Trench, where the North American Plate meets the Caribbean Plate at an oblique convergent boundary. Colors show measured depth with vertical relief exaggerated; the labels and boundary lines are added interpretation.

rows.credit: Donnchadh H / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rounded hills and fields around the Vale of Edale, viewed from Grindslow Knoll.
rows.caption: The Vale of Edale and Lose Hill, Peak District. Compare the real valley and spur shapes with the contour patterns the model draws.

rows.credit: USGS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: USGS topographic map extract showing Yosemite Creek, a campground, contours and coordinate markings.
rows.caption: A USGS topographic sheet of Yosemite Creek. Tightly packed contours mark steep valley sides; widely spaced ones mark gentle ground.

rows.credit: Brian Deegan / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Water falls through a narrow rocky step into a dark plunge pool at Cwmorthin, Wales.
rows.caption: A waterfall and plunge pool at Cwmorthin, Wales: a steep step typical of an upper course, where the long profile is steepest.

rows.credit: Jocelyn Augustino / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A raised embankment separates floodwater from farmland beside the Mississippi at Hannibal, Missouri.
rows.caption: The Mississippi at Hannibal, Missouri: a wide lowland river on a gentle gradient, bordered by an engineered levee.

rows.credit: none (Landsat) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: False-color Landsat image of the Lena Delta with many branching distributaries and islands.
rows.caption: False-color Landsat image of the Lena Delta, Russia, where the river reaches base level and deposits its load.

rows.credit: Sidoine MBOGNI / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
rows.caption: Forest canopy in Cameroon. Leaves intercept rainfall and return water to the air by transpiration.

rows.credit: USFS employees / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped and resized
rows.alt: Melting snow patches and a stream near Fourth of July Lake in Idaho's Sawtooth Mountains.
rows.caption: Snowmelt feeding a stream in Idaho: water released from a snow store into surface flow.

rows.credit: Aravind Sivaraj / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A hand pump used to draw groundwater at Perambalur, India.
rows.caption: A groundwater hand pump in India. Abstraction removes water from the groundwater store.

rows.credit: NASA/JHUAPL / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: MESSENGER global mosaic of Mercury showing its cratered surface.
rows.caption: NASA MESSENGER mosaic of Mercury, a small rocky terrestrial planet close to the Sun.

rows.credit: NASA/JPL / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Voyager 2 image of Neptune's blue disc showing cloud bands and the Great Dark Spot.
rows.caption: Voyager 2 image of Neptune, an ice giant about 30 times farther from the Sun than Earth. Its displayed color has been processed.

rows.credit: NASA/Apollo 17 crew; taken by either Harrison Schmitt or Ron Evans / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The fully sunlit Earth showing Africa, Arabia, Antarctica and swirling clouds in the Apollo 17 photograph.
rows.caption: Earth photographed by Apollo 17: the largest of the four rocky terrestrial planets.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An SDO observation of the solar photosphere showing a large dark sunspot group.
rows.caption: NASA SDO view of the photosphere with a large sunspot group: the visible surface that supplies the sunlight in the model.

rows.credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
rows.alt: Meteosat view of Earth's day–night boundary on the December solstice, with more of the Southern Hemisphere in daylight.
rows.caption: Meteosat satellite image at the December solstice. Sunlight strikes the southern hemisphere more directly, so equal beams spread over smaller areas there.

rows.credit: Zdeněk Bardon/ESO / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A long-exposure photograph of Orion's stars, red emission nebulae and dark dust clouds.
rows.caption: Stars and nebulae in Orion. Stars that look close together in the sky can lie hundreds of light-years apart.

rows.credit: NASA/SDO, AIA / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A sequence of dark Venus silhouettes crosses the Sun in SDO ultraviolet observations.
rows.caption: SDO image sequence of Venus crossing the Sun in 2012. Timing such transits helped astronomers measure the astronomical unit.

rows.credit: Wilson44691 / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Fossilized Ogyopsis klotzi trilobite preserved in dark shale.
rows.caption: A Middle Cambrian trilobite, roughly 500 million years old, from the Mount Stephen beds, Canada. Fossils mark positions on the timeline.

rows.credit: Nationalparks / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: A rock outcrop with a dashed line drawn along a thin pale layer between darker beds below and sandstone above.
rows.caption: The K–Pg boundary at Trinidad Lake, Colorado, about 66 million years ago, when the non-bird dinosaurs disappeared.

rows.credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
rows.caption: The Grand Canyon exposes a long stack of rock layers, but unconformities mean parts of the record are missing.

rows.credit: NASA Kennedy Space Center, KSC-00PP-0096 · public domain · via Wikimedia Commons · resized
rows.alt: The Moon appears copper-red during a lunar eclipse viewed from Merritt Island, Florida.
rows.caption: A total lunar eclipse in January 2000. The Moon lies in Earth's umbra and is lit only by reddened light refracted through Earth's atmosphere.

rows.credit: NASA/SDO, AIA / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A sequence of dark Venus silhouettes crosses the Sun in SDO ultraviolet observations.
rows.caption: Venus crossing the Sun in 2012. Like an eclipse, a transit needs the bodies to line up near an orbital node.

rows.credit: Lapos71 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: First-quarter Moon photographed from Calabria, with the right half of the visible lunar disc sunlit.
rows.caption: A first-quarter Moon. With the Sun and Moon at right angles, their tidal effects partly cancel, favoring neap tides.

rows.credit: Luc Viatour / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Nearly full Moon photographed from Hamois, Belgium, with dark maria and bright cratered highlands.
rows.caption: A nearly full Moon. Near full and new Moon the Sun and Moon line up, favoring spring tides with a larger range.

rows.credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
rows.alt: Meteosat view of Earth's day–night boundary on the December solstice, with more of the Southern Hemisphere in daylight.
rows.caption: Meteosat satellite image at the December solstice. The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn, so northern noon altitudes are at their lowest.

rows.credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
rows.alt: Meteosat view of Earth's nearly north–south day–night boundary at the March equinox.
rows.caption: Meteosat satellite image at the March equinox. The Sun is overhead at the equator, and the noon altitude at any latitude is 90° minus the latitude.

rows.credit: LynceanEducation / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Three time-lapse sunrises blended into one panorama, with the Sun rising further north in summer and further south in winter.
rows.caption: Composite of three time-lapse sunrises photographed from the same spot: at the summer solstice (left, furthest north), the spring equinox (center) and the winter solstice (right, furthest south). The sunrise point and the Sun's path shift through the year.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A dark Glossopteris fossil leaf from Permian rocks in Antarctica, with a branching vein network.
rows.caption: A Glossopteris leaf fossil from Antarctica. The same plant fossils on separate southern continents suggest they were once joined in Pangaea.

rows.credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NOAA bathymetry map of the South Atlantic showing continental shelves and the mid-ocean ridge.
rows.caption: NOAA bathymetry of the South Atlantic. The continental shelves of South America and Africa fit together closely, like the model's shelf fit.

rows.credit: Dietmar Rabich / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Steam and orange microbial mats around Grand Prismatic Spring in Yellowstone National Park.
rows.caption: Grand Prismatic Spring, Yellowstone: hydrothermal activity above a continental hotspot, inside the North American Plate.

rows.credit: NOAA's National Ocean Service / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Multibeam sonar bathymetry reveals a broad undersea mountain in the Arctic Ocean.
rows.caption: NOAA multibeam survey of an Arctic seamount, shown in 3D with colors for depth; the vertical scale is probably exaggerated. Volcanoes carried away from a hotspot can cool and sink to become seamounts, although not every seamount forms this way.

rows.credit: Jim D. Griggs, HVO (USGS) staff photographer[1][2] / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An arching orange lava fountain erupts from a vent on Kīlauea amid dark cooling lava.
rows.caption: A lava fountain on Kīlauea, 1983: the active volcanic end of the Hawaiian hotspot chain.

rows.credit: NOAA NCEI / CIRES · EMAG2 v3 · public domain · resized
rows.alt: EMAG2 global magnetic-anomaly map with alternating anomalies across the ocean floor.
rows.caption: NOAA EMAG2 magnetic-anomaly map. Bands that run parallel to the mid-ocean ridges record reversals of Earth's magnetic field.

rows.credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NOAA bathymetry map of the South Atlantic showing continental shelves and the mid-ocean ridge.
rows.caption: NOAA bathymetry of the South Atlantic, showing the Mid-Atlantic Ridge running midway between the continents.

rows.credit: Olga Ernst / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Steep dark rock walls border the Almannagjá rift at Þingvellir, Iceland.
rows.caption: Þingvellir, Iceland: a place where the spreading Mid-Atlantic Ridge rises above sea level and faults open the ground.

rows.credit: Storm Prediction Center / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A skew-T chart from a weather-balloon sounding, with red temperature and green dew-point lines rising through the atmosphere.
rows.caption: A radiosonde sounding from Lake Charles, Louisiana. Weather balloons measure temperature with height, giving the profile the model uses to define the layers.

rows.credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio - Amy Moran, Lauren Dauphin, Paul Newman, Katie Jepson, Aaron E. Lepsch / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA map of low ozone concentrations over Antarctica in September 2023.
rows.caption: NASA map of the Antarctic ozone hole, September 2023. The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A green auroral band glows below the International Space Station above the southern Indian Ocean.
rows.caption: An aurora seen from the ISS, which itself orbits within the thermosphere. The green light is emitted by oxygen roughly 100–250 km above the surface.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / Scientific Visualization Studio · public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA CERES map of reflected shortwave radiation averaged over 2000–2015, with a 0–385 W m⁻² color scale.
rows.caption: NASA CERES satellite map of reflected sunlight, 2000–2015 average: shortwave energy that clouds, ice and bright surfaces send back to space.

rows.credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio - Marit Jentoft-Nilsen, Global Science and Technology, Inc./Amy Moran, Global Science and Technology, Inc./Heather Hanson / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: CERES global map of outgoing longwave radiation with a color scale in watts per square meter.
rows.caption: NASA CERES satellite map of outgoing longwave radiation: the infrared energy that Earth emits to space.

rows.credit: SAC Faye Storer / UK Ministry of Defence · Crown copyright / Open Government Licence v1.0 · cropped and resized
rows.alt: Patchy winter snow over dark exposed rock and heath on a Cairngorm mountainside.
rows.caption: Snow and dark ground in the Cairngorms: a real high- and low-albedo contrast like the model's surface choices.

rows.credit: NOAA GOES-19 / CIMSS, University of Wisconsin–Madison · public domain · 30 October 2025 · resized
rows.alt: GOES-19 satellite view of a cloud-free band beside western Lake Michigan as a land breeze pushes offshore.
rows.caption: GOES-19 satellite image: a cloud-free band beside Lake Michigan marks a land breeze, the night-time reversal of the sea breeze.

rows.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech · ECOSTRESS, PIA25423 · underlying map attribution retained in image · resized
rows.alt: ECOSTRESS thermal map shows warm urban surfaces in London late at night on 15 July 2022.
rows.caption: ECOSTRESS thermal map of London at night. Built-up areas stay warmer than green spaces: an urban heat island.

rows.credit: Colin Smith / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Sunlit shingle beach and coastal buildings at Southsea, Portsmouth.
rows.caption: Southsea beach, Portsmouth. On sunny days the land warms faster than the sea, the contrast that drives a sea breeze.

rows.credit: National Weather Service Office in Burlington, Vermont / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: US National Weather Service surface weather chart for 6 January 1998 with isobars, high and low centers and fronts.
rows.caption: A US National Weather Service surface chart. Closely spaced isobars mark a strong pressure gradient and strong winds.

rows.credit: NASA, MODIS Rapid Response System / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A broad spiral of white clouds over the Pacific northeast of Japan.
rows.caption: MODIS satellite image of a depression northeast of Japan. Clouds spiral counterclockwise around the low, as Coriolis deflection predicts in the Northern Hemisphere.

rows.credit: Jacques Descloitres, MODIS Land Rapid Response Team / NASA GSFC · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Hawaiian islands with greener windward slopes, drier leeward slopes and silvery sunglint on the Pacific.
rows.caption: MODIS satellite image of Hawaiʻi. Northeasterly trade winds, the surface branch of the Hadley cell, bring rain to windward slopes.

rows.credit: Luca Galuzzi (Lucag) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: Tall orange sand dunes under a clear sky at Sossusvlei, Namibia.
rows.caption: The Namib Desert: a subtropical desert beneath sinking air in the descending branch of the Hadley circulation, here combined with a cold offshore current.

rows.credit: National Weather Service Office in Burlington, Vermont / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: US National Weather Service surface weather chart for 6 January 1998 with isobars, high and low centers and fronts.
rows.caption: A US National Weather Service surface chart with cold, warm and occluded fronts drawn between air masses as a storm develops.

rows.credit: NASA, MODIS Rapid Response System / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A broad spiral of white clouds over the Pacific northeast of Japan.
rows.caption: MODIS satellite image of a midlatitude depression. Long cloud bands mark the fronts wrapping around the low.

rows.credit: National Weather Service Office in Burlington, Vermont / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: US National Weather Service surface weather chart for 6 January 1998 with isobars, high and low centers and fronts.
rows.caption: A US National Weather Service surface chart marking H and L pressure centers. Winds blow counterclockwise around lows in the Northern Hemisphere.

rows.credit: NASA image courtesy Jeff Schmaltz, LANCE MODIS Rapid Response. Caption by Michon Scott. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Cyclone Evan's spiral cloud bands cross the islands of Fiji in a NASA satellite image.
rows.caption: MODIS satellite image of Cyclone Evan near Fiji, in the Southern Hemisphere, where cyclones spiral clockwise.

rows.credit: Sidoine MBOGNI / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
rows.caption: Tropical rainforest in Cameroon: a landscape example of an Af (tropical wet) climate.

rows.credit: Luca Galuzzi (Lucag) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: Tall orange sand dunes under a clear sky at Sossusvlei, Namibia.
rows.caption: Namib Desert dunes: a landscape example of a hot desert (BW) climate.

rows.credit: Manfred Heyde / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Green fields and wooded valleys on Exmoor in North Devon.
rows.caption: Exmoor, North Devon: a landscape in the Cfb (temperate oceanic) climate.

rows.credit: Jean-Marie Vugnon (2) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Moselle joins the wider Rhine beside the city of Koblenz, Germany.
rows.caption: The Moselle joins the Rhine at Koblenz, Germany: a confluence, where a tributary meets the main river.

rows.credit: USFS employees / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped and resized
rows.alt: Melting snow patches and a stream near Fourth of July Lake in Idaho's Sawtooth Mountains.
rows.caption: Snowmelt streams near a source area in Idaho's Sawtooth Mountains, high in a drainage basin.

rows.credit: none (Landsat) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: False-color Landsat image of the Lena Delta with many branching distributaries and islands.
rows.caption: False-color Landsat image of the Lena Delta, Russia: the river's mouth, where water from its basin reaches the Arctic Ocean.

rows.credit: Walter Siegmund / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
rows.alt: Floodwater from the Stillaguamish River surrounds a picnic table and trees.
rows.caption: The Stillaguamish River in flood. Overbank water like this happens near the peak of a storm hydrograph.

rows.credit: Rodw / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Floodwater surrounds Burrowbridge in the Somerset Levels in February 2014.
rows.caption: Floodwater around Burrowbridge, Somerset, February 2014. Flat, saturated land produces a long, slow falling limb.

rows.credit: USFS employees / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped and resized
rows.alt: Melting snow patches and a stream near Fourth of July Lake in Idaho's Sawtooth Mountains.
rows.caption: Snowmelt in Idaho's Sawtooth Mountains. Nival regimes peak when stored snow melts in spring and early summer.

rows.credit: Kyle Hawton / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Glen Canyon Dam holds back Lake Powell above a narrow river gorge.
rows.caption: Glen Canyon Dam, Arizona. Reservoir releases smooth the natural seasonal regime of the Colorado River downstream.

rows.credit: Jerrod Wheeler (submitted to USGS by Kirk Miller, Wyoming) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A streamflow-gauging station beside Huey Creek in Antarctica's rocky McMurdo Dry Valleys.
rows.caption: A USGS stream gauge at Huey Creek, Antarctica. Fed by glacier meltwater, the stream flows only for a few weeks in the southern summer. Records of stage and discharge reveal this strongly seasonal regime.

rows.credit: Lauren Dauphin / NASA Earth Observatory · Aqua MODIS / EOSDIS · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Green phytoplankton and sediment-rich water off Mauritania's desert coast, observed by Aqua MODIS.
rows.caption: MODIS satellite image off Mauritania. The Canary Current, an eastern boundary current, is linked to upwelling of nutrient-rich water here.

rows.credit: NASA/GSFC/JPL-Caltech / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Aquarius satellite map of ocean surface salinity with warm colors in saltier subtropical waters.
rows.caption: Aquarius satellite salinity map. The saltiest surface water lies in the subtropical gyres, beneath the subtropical highs where evaporation exceeds rainfall.

rows.credit: NOAA Photo Library / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A cylindrical CTD rosette of gray water-sampling bottles hangs from a ship's crane above the sea at sunset.
rows.caption: A NOAA CTD rosette measures temperature and salinity with depth, which together set seawater density.

rows.credit: NASA/GSFC/JPL-Caltech / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Aquarius satellite map of ocean surface salinity with warm colors in saltier subtropical waters.
rows.caption: Aquarius satellite map of sea-surface salinity, one of the two controls on density in the model.

rows.credit: Unidentified NOAA photographer / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A Deep SOLO profiling float is lowered from the research vessel Kaʻimikai-O-Kanaloa in 2018.
rows.caption: A Deep SOLO float being deployed. Such floats measure temperature and salinity down to great depth, tracking deep-water masses.

rows.credit: Poyt448 Peter Woodard / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Fallen leaves and organic litter beneath white beech trees in New South Wales, Australia.
rows.caption: Leaf litter in New South Wales. Decomposers respire, returning carbon from the litter to the air: part of the fast carbon cycle.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A rock face with a dark, layered coal seam between paler beds, with dry leaves on the ledges.
rows.caption: A coal seam in Ohio. Burning this fossil fuel releases carbon stored for about 300 million years in the slow cycle.

rows.credit: Diego Delso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Still water and pine trees at Viru Bog in Estonia's Lahemaa National Park.
rows.caption: Viru Bog, Estonia. Waterlogged peat stores carbon because decomposition is very slow.

rows.credit: NASA Earth Observatory image by Lauren Dauphin, using modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2025) processed by the European Space Agency and further processed by Josh Willis, and Kevin Marlis/NASA/JPL-Caltech. Story by Emily Cassidy. / Wikimedia Commons · Attribution · resized
rows.alt: Sentinel-6 sea-surface height anomaly map shows lower-than-average levels across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific.
rows.caption: Sentinel-6 satellite map of sea-surface height in January 2025: lower sea levels in the cool central and eastern Pacific during La Niña.

rows.credit: Jesse Allen / NASA Earth Observatory · AMSR-E / Remote Sensing Systems · public domain · resized
rows.alt: AMSR-E sea-surface temperature anomalies around northern Australia in the Indo-Pacific warm pool.
rows.caption: AMSR-E map of sea-surface temperature anomalies, 19 October 2004. Blue water was cooler than average and orange warmer. The warm pool north of Australia still held some of the warmest water on Earth; it was simply less warm than usual. Alt text: 'Global AMSR-E map of sea-surface temperature anomalies, blue where cooler than average and orange where warmer.'

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Snow-covered Himalayan peaks and valleys photographed from the International Space Station.
rows.caption: The Himalaya from the ISS: mountains with very high elevation and relief.

rows.credit: Pseudopanax at English Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A broad flat river plain with autumn vegetation in the Ahuriri valley, New Zealand.
rows.caption: The Ahuriri River plain, New Zealand: low relief and gentle slopes across a broad valley floor.

rows.credit: Godot13 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view across the dry erosional basin of Makhtesh Ramon in Israel's Negev Desert.
rows.caption: Makhtesh Ramon, Israel: an erosional basin enclosed by higher ground.

rows.credit: Brian Deegan / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Water falls through a narrow rocky step into a dark plunge pool at Cwmorthin, Wales.
rows.caption: Cwmorthin, Wales: a waterfall over a nick point with a plunge pool eroded below it.

rows.credit: Karthoo / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Wutach flows through a narrow, wooded gorge below exposed rock walls in the Black Forest.
rows.caption: Wutach Gorge, Germany: a narrow gorge cut by rapid downcutting.

rows.credit: Malik Ahamed from Colombo, Sri Lanka / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A broad bend of the New River in a steep forested gorge in West Virginia.
rows.caption: New River Gorge, West Virginia: steep slopes falling to the river form a V-shaped valley.

rows.credit: NASA/Kjell Lindgren / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The muddy Ucayali River winds through forest in Peru, with abandoned bends beside the active channel.
rows.caption: The Ucayali River, Peru, from the ISS. Meanders build slip-off slopes on inner bends while cut banks erode the outer bends.

rows.credit: Jocelyn Augustino / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A raised embankment separates floodwater from farmland beside the Mississippi at Hannibal, Missouri.
rows.caption: An engineered levee on the Mississippi. Natural levées form where floodwater drops sediment beside the channel; this one is built.

rows.credit: Operational Land Imager / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Landsat view of the Thames estuary, coastal shallows and offshore wind farms.
rows.caption: Landsat image of the Thames estuary. Pale water carries suspended sediment that settles where the flow slows.

rows.credit: Ustill / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 de · resized
rows.alt: A broad, grassy former river valley near Blumberg, now drained by the much smaller Aitrach.
rows.caption: The Aitrach valley, Germany: a beheaded stream now far too small for the valley left after the Wutach captured its headwaters.

rows.credit: DanHobley / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: View up a dry valley in Ladakh toward a notch in the mountain ridge on the skyline, with a village in the foreground.
rows.caption: A wind gap above the Karu valley, Ladakh. Glacial erosion on the far side of the ridge beheaded this valley, leaving the outline of its U-shaped head as a dry notch on the skyline, with no river flowing through it.

rows.credit: Dave Fergusson / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A small stream meandering across the wide, flat floor of a Highland glen between rounded hills.
rows.caption: Gleann nan Eun, east of Loch Ness, Scotland. The small stream winding across the floor is far too small to have carved such a wide valley: a misfit stream in a glen shaped by ice and meltwater.

rows.credit: Jakub Hałun / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The isolated rock stack Hvítserkur rises from shallow coastal water in northwestern Iceland.
rows.caption: Hvítserkur, Iceland: a sea stack with arches eroded through its base.

rows.credit: Lewis Clarke / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: White chalk cliffs, offshore remnants and a wave-cut base near the Pinnacles in Purbeck.
rows.caption: Chalk cliffs and offshore remnants in Purbeck, Dorset: stacks and stumps left as the cliff retreats.

rows.credit: Iraphne R. Childs / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A groyne extends across the beach at Tallebudgera Creek on Australia's Gold Coast.
rows.caption: A groyne at Tallebudgera Creek, Australia, interrupting longshore drift.

rows.credit: Diliff / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Yosemite Valley's forested floor between steep granite walls, viewed from Tunnel View.
rows.caption: Yosemite Valley: a U-shaped trough, with Bridalveil Fall dropping from a hanging valley on the right.

rows.credit: GlacierNPS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The sharp summit and steep ridges of Little Matterhorn in Glacier National Park, Montana.
rows.caption: Little Matterhorn, Montana: a pyramidal horn left by glacial erosion on several sides.

rows.credit: Doc Searls from Santa Barbara, USA / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of elongated low hills around Horicon Marsh, Wisconsin.
rows.caption: Aerial view of drumlins near Horicon Marsh, Wisconsin, streamlined by former ice flow.

rows.credit: Daredeep33 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Turquoise water fills the steep-sided Bimmah sinkhole in Oman.
rows.caption: Bimmah sinkhole, Oman: a doline formed by dissolution and collapse.

rows.credit: Immanuel Giel / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Thin straw stalactites hanging from the brown limestone roof of White Scar Cave.
rows.caption: Straw stalactites in White Scar Cave, Yorkshire Dales. Each thin tube grows as dripping water loses carbon dioxide and leaves a ring of calcite at its tip.

rows.credit: NPS Photo / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Visitors and a park ranger stand in the broad limestone Broadway passage of Mammoth Cave, Kentucky.
rows.caption: Broadway passage, Mammoth Cave, Kentucky: a large passage enlarged by groundwater dissolving limestone.

rows.credit: Lysippos / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rock contact exposed along the Moine Thrust at Knockan Crag in northwest Scotland.
rows.caption: The Moine Thrust at Knockan Crag, Scotland: a low-angle reverse fault (a thrust). The hanging wall above the fault plane carries older rocks over the younger footwall rocks below, recording compression.

rows.credit: Robert E. Wallace / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of Wallace Creek, whose channel bends sharply where it crosses the San Andreas Fault.
rows.caption: Wallace Creek, California: the stream channel is offset sideways where it crosses the San Andreas, a strike-slip fault.

rows.credit: Olga Ernst / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Steep dark rock walls border the Almannagjá rift at Þingvellir, Iceland.
rows.caption: Þingvellir, Iceland: normal faults bound the rift where the crust is being stretched.

rows.credit: lwtt93 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Long, wind-eroded rock ridges rise above the desert at Dunhuang, China.
rows.caption: Yardangs at Dunhuang, China: streamlined ridges carved by wind abrasion.

rows.credit: Chris M Morris / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A mesquite shrub grows on a mound of trapped sand in the Mojave Desert.
rows.caption: A nabkha in the Mojave Desert: sand trapped around a mesquite shrub.

rows.credit: Arthur Rothstein / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A car on a Texas Panhandle road beneath a wall of airborne dust during the Dust Bowl.
rows.caption: A 1930s Dust Bowl storm in Texas: deflation lifting fine soil into suspension.

rows.credit: National Oceanic & Atmospheric Adminstration (NOAA) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Rounded pillow lava on a fissured seafloor at the Galápagos Rift, photographed by a NOAA expedition.
rows.caption: Pillow lava at the Galápagos Rift: igneous rock formed as lava cools in seawater.

rows.credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
rows.caption: The Grand Canyon's layered cliffs: sedimentary rocks formed by deposition and lithification.

rows.credit: Dexter Perkins / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
rows.alt: Rounded remnants of granite emerge from loose weathered material in an exposed rock profile.
rows.caption: Weathered granite breaking down into loose material: the first step toward new sediment.

rows.credit: The original uploader was Michaila vnuk at Ukrainian Wikipedia. / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A soil profile on the Karelian Isthmus with a dark surface, pale leached layer and browner subsoil.
rows.caption: A podzolic soil in Karelia. A thin pale gray E horizon lies just below the dark topsoil, above a rusty-brown B horizon. The paler sand near the bottom is the parent material.

rows.credit: Samuel Rios / USDA NRCS · public domain · via Wikimedia Commons · resized
rows.alt: A deep reddish Nipe-series soil profile with a measuring tape in Puerto Rico.
rows.caption: A deep red Oxisol in Puerto Rico, formed by long, intense tropical weathering.

rows.credit: https://www.flickr.com/photos/soilscience/5140644166/ / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A Puerto Rican soil profile has a dark surface above pale carbonate-rich subsoil, with a depth scale.
rows.caption: A Mollisol near Ponce, Puerto Rico, with a dark organic-rich A horizon over pale carbonate-rich subsoil.

rows.credit: Marie-Lan Taÿ Pamart / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A pale specimen of kaolinite from Ixtassou, France.
rows.caption: Kaolinite, a clay mineral. Clay as a texture class means particles smaller than 0.002 mm, whatever the mineral.

rows.credit: Bill Whittaker / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Steep, grassy Loess Hills rising behind a cornfield east of Mondamin, Iowa.
rows.caption: Iowa's Loess Hills are made of silt-rich wind-blown sediment, which would plot near the silt corner of the texture triangle.

rows.credit: Chris Andrews / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Angular rock blocks cover the summit of Foel Fras in Wales.
rows.caption: Angular blocks on Foel Fras, Wales: mechanical weathering, such as frost shattering, breaks rock without changing its minerals.

rows.credit: Gordon Hatton / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A lone ash tree growing out of a crack in a limestone pavement above Grassington.
rows.caption: An ash tree growing out of a grike in limestone pavement above Grassington, Yorkshire Dales. Roots in the crack can widen it, and acids from roots and decaying leaves help dissolve the rock.

rows.credit: Colin Smith / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: People cross pale limestone blocks separated by deep joints above Malham Cove, England.
rows.caption: Limestone pavement at Malham: carbonation, a type of chemical weathering, has dissolved the joints into grykes.

rows.credit: US Navy / USDA NRCS Photo Gallery, NRCSIA99138 · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Close-up photograph of a raindrop splashing on soil and throwing droplets and particles outward.
rows.caption: A raindrop hitting bare soil (USDA NRCS): rain splash detaches particles before runoff moves them.

rows.credit: Till Niermann (User:Till.niermann) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Dry, deeply dissected loess slopes near Hunyuan in Shanxi, China.
rows.caption: Loess hills in Shanxi, China, deeply cut by gullies where concentrated runoff erodes soft silt.

rows.credit: Arthur Rothstein / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A car on a Texas Panhandle road beneath a wall of airborne dust during the Dust Bowl.
rows.caption: A Dust Bowl dust storm in Texas: wind erosion of bare, dry soil.

rows.credit: USGS · public domain · 14 August 2021 ShakeMap · resized
rows.alt: USGS ShakeMap of the 14 August 2021 Haiti earthquake with colored zones of shaking intensity.
rows.caption: USGS ShakeMap of the 2021 Haiti earthquake. The star marks the epicenter and the colored rings show intensity falling with distance.

rows.credit: Petr Brož (Czech Academy of Science) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A pen arm resting on a white paper drum covered in fine parallel lines, one section showing a burst of wiggles.
rows.caption: A seismograph drum records the shaking as a line on paper. The arrival times of P-, S- and surface waves are used to locate the focus.

rows.credit: Midori / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: The broad conical slopes of Mount Fuji rise beyond Lake Kawaguchi in Japan.
rows.caption: Mount Fuji, Japan: a steep-sided stratovolcano built from layers of lava and fragmental deposits.

rows.credit: USGS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Pale pyroclastic deposits fill the Marella River valley below Mount Pinatubo.
rows.caption: Pyroclastic-flow deposits filling a valley below Pinatubo after its 1991 eruption.

rows.credit: United States Geological Survey / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A line of lava fountains and gas rises from the Kamoamoa fissure in forest southwest of Puʻu ʻŌʻō, Hawaiʻi.
rows.caption: A fissure eruption on Kīlauea, 2011: runny basaltic lava erupting along a linear crack.

rows.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Wanmei Liang, using data provided by the ARIA team at NASA/JPL-Caltech. The displacement map is based on Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey and ALOS-2 data from the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Story by Adam Voiland. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA ARIA map showing measured ground displacement along the Kamchatka Peninsula after the 2025 earthquake.
rows.caption: NASA ARIA satellite map of ground displacement after the 2025 Kamchatka megathrust earthquake. This kind of sudden seabed movement can trigger a tsunami.

rows.credit: メルビル / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A pillar inside Sendai Airport's terminal with a blue band and a marker labeled 3.02 m near the ceiling.
rows.caption: A pillar in Sendai Airport's terminal marks how high the 2011 tsunami water rose there: 3.02 m above the floor. Survey teams measure marks like this to map inundation and run-up.

rows.credit: EOSDIS Worldview / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Satellite view of Typhoon Mangkhut with a compact eye and spiraling cloud bands in September 2018.
rows.caption: Satellite image of Typhoon Mangkhut, 2018, with a compact eye and spiral rainbands.

rows.credit: NASA image courtesy Jeff Schmaltz, LANCE MODIS Rapid Response. Caption by Michon Scott. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Cyclone Evan's spiral cloud bands cross the islands of Fiji in a NASA satellite image.
rows.caption: MODIS satellite image of Cyclone Evan near Fiji: a Southern Hemisphere tropical cyclone spiraling clockwise.

rows.credit: NOAA Corps aerial survey: Mark Moran, Phil Eastman and Dave Demers · public domain · 2005 · resized
rows.alt: Flooded streets and houses in New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina in 2005.
rows.caption: New Orleans flooded after Hurricane Katrina, 2005: storm surge and failed defenses caused much of the damage.

rows.credit: Strebe / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: NASA Blue Marble satellite imagery displayed in a Mollweide projection with a graticule.
rows.caption: A Mollweide world map with the graticule drawn: meridians converge at the poles, while parallels never meet.

rows.credit: Joshua Stevens / NASA Earth Observatory, Landsat data: USGS · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Big and Little Diomede islands in the Bering Strait, between snow-covered Russia and Alaska, seen by Landsat 8.
rows.caption: The Diomede Islands, either side of the International Date Line, which roughly follows the 180° meridian.

rows.credit: Reto Stöckli / NASA Earth Observatory · public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA Blue Marble satellite composite of Earth in an equirectangular global map.
rows.caption: NASA Blue Marble on an equirectangular latitude–longitude grid. No lines are drawn here, but on this projection every meridian and parallel would plot as an evenly spaced straight line.

rows.credit: Mdf / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA Blue Marble imagery in Mercator projection, with strongly enlarged high-latitude regions.
rows.caption: The Mercator projection keeps local angles but greatly enlarges high latitudes.

rows.credit: Strebe / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: NASA Blue Marble satellite imagery displayed in a Mollweide projection with a graticule.
rows.caption: The Mollweide projection keeps relative areas correct but distorts shapes near its edges.

rows.credit: Hondius, Jodocus; Rossi, Giuseppe Di. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Digitized historical sheets of narrow, tapered terrestrial map strips intended to cover a 19-centimeter globe.
rows.caption: Globe gores from 1615: tapering strips that could be pasted on to a sphere with little distortion.

rows.credit: U.S. Geological Survey, US Topo 7.5-minute map for Covington, LA (2018) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped
rows.alt: Northwest corner of a USGS US Topo map of Covington, Louisiana, with a 1 km UTM grid labeled 776000 m E and 3377000 m N, and principal digits 77 to 83 along the top edge.
rows.caption: A USGS US Topo map with its 1 km UTM grid. Read the principal digits along the edges: eastings along the top and bottom first, then northings up the sides.

rows.credit: USGS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: USGS topographic map extract showing Yosemite Creek, a campground, contours and coordinate markings.
rows.caption: An older USGS topographic sheet of Yosemite Creek. Its red numbered squares are Public Land Survey System sections (township and range), not UTM grid squares: always check which grid a map uses.

rows.credit: Contains Ordnance Survey data © Crown copyright and database right · OS OpenData / Open Government Licence v3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Ordnance Survey 1:250,000 map sheet NO of northeast Scotland with the British National Grid.
rows.caption: An Ordnance Survey sheet of northeast Scotland. The British National Grid works the same way as the US National Grid, but a two-letter code (here NO) names each 100 km square.

rows.credit: Christine Matthews / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A physical marker of the historic Greenwich Meridian at the Royal Observatory.
rows.caption: The Greenwich Meridian marker. WGS84 GPS longitude differs from this historic line by about 102 meters, a reminder that coordinate systems differ.

rows.credit: David Martin / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Uneven displaced ground and scarps above the coast at Redcliff Point, Dorset.
rows.caption: Rotational slumping above Redcliff Point, Dorset: blocks slide and tilt on a curved shear surface.

rows.credit: Voice of America (Tang Huiyun) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · cropped and resized
rows.alt: Houses on top of a steep coastal slope at Redhill Peninsula, Hong Kong, with a bare brown landslide scar running down the vegetated slope to the sea.
rows.caption: Redhill Peninsula, Hong Kong, after the record rainstorm of September 2023. The bare brown strip below the houses is the landslide scar, where saturated soil and rock slid down the steep slope toward the sea.

rows.credit: Rémih / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A bank of cloud spills over a mountain ridge above Cilaos on Réunion.
rows.caption: A föhn cloud wall over a ridge on Réunion: moist air rises and cools on the windward side, then sinks and warms on the lee side.

rows.credit: Matthew.kowal / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Fog covers houses and forested slopes at Section in Jamaica's Blue Mountains.
rows.caption: Fog and cloud on the Blue Mountains of Jamaica, where moist air forced up over high ground produces orographic cloud and rain.

rows.credit: Michael Rivera / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A USGS groundwater observation station in Stephen C. Foster State Park, Georgia.
rows.caption: A USGS observation well in Georgia that records changes in the water table.

rows.credit: Aravind Sivaraj / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A hand pump used to draw groundwater at Perambalur, India.
rows.caption: A hand pump in India. Pumping abstracts groundwater and can create a cone of depression around the well.

rows.credit: Peter Pearson / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Gray London Clay exposed below yellow-brown Red Crag in the sea cliffs at Walton-on-the-Naze, Essex.
rows.caption: London Clay at Walton-on-the-Naze, Essex: a low-permeability layer that can act as an aquitard.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Snow-covered Himalayan peaks and valleys photographed from the International Space Station.
rows.caption: The Himalaya from the ISS. High mountains are supported by a deep root of thickened crust, as in the model.

rows.credit: Giles Laurent / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Aletsch Glacier curves through a steep Alpine valley, with dark medial moraines running along its surface.
rows.caption: The Aletsch Glacier, Switzerland. Ice sheets far thicker than this pressed the crust down, and it rebounds when the ice melts.

rows.credit: Lysippos / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Rock contact exposed along the Moine Thrust at Knockan Crag in northwest Scotland.
rows.caption: The Moine Thrust at Knockan Crag, Scotland: a record of Caledonian collision when the Iapetus Ocean closed.

rows.credit: MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA GSFC / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Satellite image of the parallel folded ridges of the Appalachian Mountains and Chesapeake Bay.
rows.caption: MODIS satellite image of the Appalachian ridges, folded during continental collisions that assembled Pangaea.

rows.credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NOAA bathymetry map of the South Atlantic showing continental shelves and the mid-ocean ridge.
rows.caption: NOAA bathymetry of the South Atlantic: passive margins on both sides of an ocean that opened as Africa and South America rifted apart.

rows.credit: Plorpy2 / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
rows.alt: Photographs of clay samples comparing gray reduced material and oxidized reddish material.
rows.caption: Gley clay compared with oxidized clay. Waterlogged soils at the foot of a slope often become gray gleys.

rows.credit: CWALTER / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A thin, dark soil lies directly over jointed granite on Île de Berder, Brittany.
rows.caption: A thin ranker soil over granite in Brittany, typical of steep upper slopes where soil stays shallow.

rows.credit: https://www.flickr.com/photos/soilscience/5140644166/ / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: A Puerto Rican soil profile has a dark surface above pale carbonate-rich subsoil, with a depth scale.
rows.caption: A Puerto Rico soil whose parent material includes colluvium, sediment moved downslope and deposited.

rows.credit: Chris Andrews / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Angular rock blocks cover the summit of Foel Fras in Wales.
rows.caption: A blockfield on Foel Fras, Wales, broken up by frost shattering in past periglacial conditions.

rows.credit: Andreas Schwarzkopf / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Patches of late-lying snow on the grassy slopes of a hollow below the Feldberg summit, with spruce forest.
rows.caption: Late-lying snow in the Zastler Loch on the Feldberg, Black Forest, in June. Where snow patches linger in hollows, freeze–thaw and meltwater (nivation) slowly loosen and remove material, deepening the hollow.

rows.credit: NOAA Corps aerial survey: Mark Moran, Phil Eastman and Dave Demers · public domain · 2005 · resized
rows.alt: Flooded streets and houses in New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina in 2005.
rows.caption: New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina, 2005: low-lying neighborhoods flooded after the surge and the failure of flood defenses.

rows.credit: Eirian Evans / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: The Thames Barrier's silver piers beside the tidal river in London.
rows.caption: The Thames Barrier, London. Its gates close to keep tidal surges out of the upper estuary.

rows.credit: Jesse Allen / NASA Earth Observatory · Landsat · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Landsat view of the northern Gulf of Mexico coast, with barrier islands off Mississippi and Alabama and the faint Chandeleur arc off Louisiana.
rows.caption: Landsat image of the northern Gulf coast (colors enhanced). The faint, broken arc at lower left is Louisiana's Chandeleur Islands, which storm surges and waves repeatedly overwash and break up. The brighter islands across the top lie off Mississippi and Alabama.

rows.credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
rows.alt: Meteosat view of Earth's nearly north–south day–night boundary at the March equinox.
rows.caption: Meteosat-9 satellite image at the March equinox, 2011. The terminator runs almost from pole to pole, so London and Lerwick both get about 12 hours of daylight. Compare it with December's tilted boundary.

rows.credit: Photograph by Clem Rutter, Rochester, Kent. (www.clemrutter.net). / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A spherical sundial with hour markings and a movable gnomon at Green's Windmill, Nottingham.
rows.caption: A spherical sundial at Green's Windmill, Nottingham. It shows local solar time. In December the midday Sun is low over Britain, and lower still at Lerwick, so days are short and shadows are long.

rows.credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · contains modified EUMETSAT Meteosat data (2011 publication) · resized
rows.alt: Meteosat view of Earth's day–night boundary on the December solstice, with more of the Southern Hemisphere in daylight.
rows.caption: Meteosat-9 satellite image, 21 December 2010. At the solstice the Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun, so high northern latitudes receive weak, low-angle sunlight while places nearer the tropics still receive a much higher noon Sun.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / Scientific Visualization Studio · public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA CERES map of net radiation averaged over 2000–2015, with a −200 to +200 W m⁻² color scale.
rows.caption: NASA CERES satellite map of net radiation (2000–2015 average). Southern Florida sits in the low-latitude band that gains energy over a year; Minnesota sits farther north, where the yearly balance is close to a loss.

rows.credit: David Medcalf / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: An exposed bank of poorly sorted glacial sediment containing stones of several sizes.
rows.caption: A bank of glacial till elsewhere in Britain, not at Holderness. It illustrates the poorly sorted mixture of clay and stones that makes the Holderness cliffs easy for waves to erode.

rows.credit: Iraphne R. Childs / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A groyne extends across the beach at Tallebudgera Creek on Australia's Gold Coast.
rows.caption: A groyne at Tallebudgera Creek, Gold Coast, Australia. It is not Holderness, but it shows how groynes trap sediment on one side, the process that affects coasts south of Mappleton.

rows.credit: David Martin / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Uneven displaced ground and scarps above the coast at Redcliff Point, Dorset.
rows.caption: Slumping above Redcliff Point, near Weymouth, Dorset, on the Jurassic Coast. Weak clays let blocks rotate down curved slip surfaces as the cliff retreats.

rows.credit: Jakub Hałun / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: The isolated rock stack Hvítserkur rises from shallow coastal water in northwestern Iceland.
rows.caption: Hvítserkur, Iceland (not the Jurassic Coast). This sea stack, with arches cut through its base, illustrates the cave–arch–stack stages seen at Durdle Door and Old Harry Rocks.

rows.credit: Antiquary / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Sourmilk Gill falling as a white stream down a steep wooded slope toward Buttermere.
rows.caption: Sourmilk Gill, Buttermere, Lake District. The stream falls steeply from the hanging corrie of Bleaberry Tarn down to the floor of the main glacial trough.

rows.credit: Chris Andrews / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Angular rock blocks cover the summit of Foel Fras in Wales.
rows.caption: Angular frost-shattered blocks cover the summit of Foel Fras in the Carneddau, within Eryri. Freeze–thaw on the high ground continued after the glaciers left.

rows.credit: Denali National Park and Preserve / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Glacier ice occupies a steep-sided mountain basin in Denali National Park, Alaska.
rows.caption: Glacier-filled cirques and sharp ridges in Denali National Park, Alaska. They show active ice carving the cirques and arêtes that are now ice-free around Yr Wyddfa.

rows.credit: Kingsmasher678 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A karst spring in Alabama flows over rocks from a wooded limestone slope.
rows.caption: A karst spring in Alabama, USA. Water that sinks into limestone can re-emerge at a spring like this one, as streams do at resurgences in the Dales.

rows.credit: Immanuel Giel / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Thin straw stalactites hanging from the brown limestone roof of White Scar Cave.
rows.caption: Straw stalactites in White Scar Cave, near Ingleton in the Yorkshire Dales: calcite redeposited as dripping water loses carbon dioxide.

rows.credit: Fractal Caleidoscope / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Frost-covered reeds and grass beside frozen drainage channels on flat land in the Netherlands.
rows.caption: Flat, frosty winter ground in the Netherlands, crossed by ice-covered drainage channels. This is not Somerset, but it shows a similar problem: in very low-lying land, water levels must be managed with channels and pumping.

rows.credit: Jocelyn Augustino / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A raised embankment separates floodwater from farmland beside the Mississippi at Hannibal, Missouri.
rows.caption: A levee on the Mississippi at Hannibal, Missouri, holding back floodwater in 2008. It illustrates how embankments, like those along Somerset rivers, change where floodwater can go.

rows.credit: Operational Land Imager / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Landsat view of the Thames estuary, coastal shallows and offshore wind farms.
rows.caption: Landsat image of the Thames estuary. The tidal river widens toward the North Sea; pale water carries suspended sediment.

rows.credit: Peter Pearson / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Gray London Clay exposed below yellow-brown Red Crag in the sea cliffs at Walton-on-the-Naze, Essex.
rows.caption: London Clay in the cliffs at Walton-on-the-Naze, Essex. This low-permeability clay underlies much of the lower Thames basin and limits how groundwater moves.

rows.credit: Olga Ernst / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Steep dark rock walls border the Almannagjá rift at Þingvellir, Iceland.
rows.caption: Þingvellir, Iceland: open fissures and a rift valley where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart. Gentle basaltic fissure eruptions come from cracks like these.

rows.credit: USGS · public domain · 14 August 2021 ShakeMap · resized
rows.alt: USGS ShakeMap of the 14 August 2021 Haiti earthquake with colored zones of shaking intensity.
rows.caption: USGS ShakeMap for the 2021 Haiti earthquake, not California. The same method maps how shaking intensity spreads out from the epicenter after Californian earthquakes.

rows.credit: Petr Brož (Czech Academy of Science) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A pen arm resting on a white paper drum covered in fine parallel lines, one section showing a burst of wiggles.
rows.caption: A seismograph records the shaking from an earthquake as a line on paper. Networks of instruments record earthquakes on faults such as the San Andreas.

rows.credit:
Mike Doukas, USGS

derivative work: User:Maps and stuff (cropped to 3:2 ratio; increased brightness in dark areas; color balanced; saved as a high quality JPG) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Deep blue Crater Lake fills a broad volcanic depression, with Wizard Island near its western shore.
rows.caption: Crater Lake, Oregon, fills the caldera of Mount Mazama, a Cascade arc volcano fed by magma generated above the Cascadia subduction zone.

rows.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Wanmei Liang, using data provided by the ARIA team at NASA/JPL-Caltech. The displacement map is based on Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey and ALOS-2 data from the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Story by Adam Voiland. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA ARIA map showing measured ground displacement along the Kamchatka Peninsula after the 2025 earthquake.
rows.caption: NASA ARIA displacement map after the 2025 Kamchatka megathrust earthquake, Russia. It shows the type of subduction-zone event that Cascadia can also produce.

rows.credit: Mass Communication Specialist 3rd Class Dylan McCord / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Aerial view of debris, damaged buildings and flooded land at a fishing port in Kesennuma after the 2011 tsunami.
rows.caption: Kesennuma, Japan, after the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami. A subduction-zone earthquake generated the tsunami, a hazard the Cascadia coast also faces.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The Hawaiian volcanic islands stretch across the Pacific beneath scattered white clouds in an ISS photograph.
rows.caption: The Hawaiian islands from the ISS: an oceanic hotspot chain to compare with Yellowstone's track of older volcanic centers across the Snake River Plain.

rows.credit:
Mike Doukas, USGS

derivative work: User:Maps and stuff (cropped to 3:2 ratio; increased brightness in dark areas; color balanced; saved as a high quality JPG) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Deep blue Crater Lake fills a broad volcanic depression, with Wizard Island near its western shore.
rows.caption: Crater Lake, Oregon, a caldera formed by collapse after a large eruption. It illustrates caldera formation; Yellowstone's much larger calderas are harder to see from the ground.

rows.credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The Hawaiian volcanic islands stretch across the Pacific beneath scattered white clouds in an ISS photograph.
rows.caption: The main Hawaiian islands from the ISS. The youngest, largest island is at the southeastern end; the islands become older and more eroded toward the northwest.

rows.credit: United States Geological Survey / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A line of lava fountains and gas rises from the Kamoamoa fissure in forest southwest of Puʻu ʻŌʻō, Hawaiʻi.
rows.caption: Lava fountains along the Kamoamoa fissure on Kīlauea, March 2011. Repeated basaltic eruptions like this build broad shield volcanoes.

rows.credit: Jacques Descloitres, MODIS Land Rapid Response Team / NASA GSFC · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Hawaiian islands with greener windward slopes, drier leeward slopes and silvery sunglint on the Pacific.
rows.caption: Terra MODIS satellite image of the Hawaiian islands, 2003. The older islands to the northwest are smaller than the young Island of Hawaiʻi, having subsided and eroded since their volcanoes became inactive.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: ASTER satellite image of branching tributary valleys near the Colorado River in Canyonlands, Utah.
rows.caption: ASTER satellite image of Canyonlands, Utah, upstream on the Colorado River system. It shows the same process of incision into the uplifted Colorado Plateau, not the Grand Canyon itself.

rows.credit: PawełS / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Younger gently dipping red sandstone overlies steep gray beds at Siccar Point, Scotland.
rows.caption: Siccar Point, Scotland, not Arizona. This angular unconformity illustrates the kind of missing time also recorded by the Great Unconformity in the Grand Canyon.

rows.credit: Jocelyn Augustino / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A raised embankment separates floodwater from farmland beside the Mississippi at Hannibal, Missouri.
