rows.caption: An engineered levee beside the Mississippi at Hannibal, Missouri, in June 2008. This reach is upstream of the lower river, but it shows how embankments confine floodwater.

rows.credit: Jesse Allen / NASA Earth Observatory · Landsat · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Landsat view of the northern Gulf of Mexico coast, with barrier islands off Mississippi and Alabama and the faint Chandeleur arc off Louisiana.
rows.caption: Landsat image of the northern Gulf coast (colors enhanced). The faint curved arc at lower left is the Chandeleur Islands, remnants of an abandoned Mississippi delta lobe, now eroding because the river's sediment goes elsewhere. Delta marshes lie to their left; the coast across the top is Mississippi and Alabama.

rows.credit: NASA Johnson Space Center · STS-62 crew · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Astronaut photograph of the bird's-foot Mississippi River delta, with sediment-laden water spreading into the Gulf of Mexico.
rows.caption: The Mississippi River delta, Louisiana, photographed by Space Shuttle astronauts in March 1994. Sediment carried by the river builds the bird's-foot delta out into the Gulf of Mexico.

rows.credit: USGS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: USGS topographic map extract showing Yosemite Creek, a campground, contours and coordinate markings.
rows.caption: USGS topographic sheet of Yosemite Creek, in the uplands north of Yosemite Valley. Closely spaced contours mark the steep sides of the creek's valley; Yosemite Valley itself is off this extract.

rows.credit: Gryffindor / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Lower Manhattan and the Battery seen from above beside New York Harbor.
rows.caption: Lower Manhattan and the Battery beside New York Harbor. Sandy's 2012 storm surge flooded low ground at this tip of the island.

rows.credit: User:Kgwo1972 / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: Rolling Kansas grassland with two traditional farm windmills.
rows.caption: Grassland in Kansas, part of the Great Plains affected in the 1930s. Undisturbed grass cover holds the soil that plowing exposed to the wind.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: ASTER satellite image of branching tributary valleys near the Colorado River in Canyonlands, Utah.
rows.caption: ASTER satellite image of tributaries draining to the Colorado River in Canyonlands, Utah, upstream of Lake Powell.

rows.credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
rows.caption: The Grand Canyon, Arizona, between Lake Powell and Lake Mead. Water released from Glen Canyon Dam flows through it on its way to Lake Mead.

rows.credit: Strebe / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: NASA Blue Marble satellite imagery displayed in a Mollweide projection with a graticule.
rows.caption: A world map with its graticule. The central meridian of this Mollweide map is the prime meridian through Greenwich, from which longitude is measured east and west.

rows.credit: Photograph by Clem Rutter, Rochester, Kent. (www.clemrutter.net). / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: A spherical sundial with hour markings and a movable gnomon at Green's Windmill, Nottingham.
rows.caption: A sundial at Green's Windmill, Nottingham, about 1.2° west of Greenwich. It shows local solar time, which here runs about four and a half minutes behind solar time at Greenwich.

rows.credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: GOES-19 full-disc view of the Americas on 21 December 2024, with daylight reaching eastern South America while North America is dark.
rows.caption: GOES-19 GeoColor view, 21 December 2024 at 09:30 UTC. Dawn is reaching eastern South America while North America is still in darkness; the night side is shown with infrared cloud imagery. Different longitudes reach sunrise at different times.

rows.credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
rows.alt: Green crystalline mantle peridotite enclosed by darker volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona.
rows.caption: A mantle xenolith from Peridot Mesa, Arizona, not Kola. Rock from the mantle reaches the surface only when magma carries it up; drilling has never reached the mantle.

rows.credit: Petr Brož (Czech Academy of Science) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A pen arm resting on a white paper drum covered in fine parallel lines, one section showing a burst of wiggles.
rows.caption: A seismograph records seismic waves. Waves recorded around the world reveal layers far deeper than the Kola borehole's 12 km.

rows.credit: Petersrockypics / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Snow on Gallt y Wenallt above mist in Nant Gwynant, Eryri / Snowdonia.
rows.caption: Nant Gwynant in Eryri. Steep valley sides like these raise the local horizon, so the Moon appears later than it would over flat ground.

rows.credit: Lapos71 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: First-quarter Moon photographed from Calabria, with the right half of the visible lunar disc sunlit.
rows.caption: First-quarter Moon photographed from Calabria, Italy. The phase depends on Sun–Earth–Moon geometry, so observers in Eryri see the same half-lit disc at the same time.

rows.credit: Diliff / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Yosemite Valley's forested floor between steep granite walls, viewed from Tunnel View.
rows.caption: Yosemite Valley from Tunnel View. The high granite walls hide the horizon, delaying when a rising full Moon becomes visible from the valley floor.

rows.credit: NASA Kennedy Space Center, KSC-00PP-0096 · public domain · via Wikimedia Commons · resized
rows.alt: The Moon appears copper-red during a lunar eclipse viewed from Merritt Island, Florida.
rows.caption: Lunar eclipse of 20 January 2000, photographed from Florida. An eclipse happens only when a full Moon lies near a node of its inclined orbit; most full Moons miss Earth's shadow.

rows.credit: NOAA Photo Library / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: An aerial view of damaged buildings and washed-over land on the Bolivar Peninsula after Hurricane Ike.
rows.caption: Bolivar Peninsula, Texas, after Hurricane Ike (2008). Overwash spread sand across the low barrier and destroyed buildings, a process the Outer Banks also experience.

rows.credit: Kingsmasher678 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: A karst spring in Alabama flows over rocks from a wooded limestone slope.
rows.caption: A karst spring in Alabama. It shows how water moving through limestone passages re-emerges at the surface, as underground rivers do near Mammoth Cave.

rows.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech · ECOSTRESS, PIA25423 · underlying map attribution retained in image · resized
rows.alt: ECOSTRESS thermal map shows warm urban surfaces in London late at night on 15 July 2022.
rows.caption: ECOSTRESS thermal map of London at night, July 2022. It is not Phoenix, but it shows how measured surface temperatures reveal an urban heat island that an ordinary photograph cannot.

rows.credit: Robert Simmon / NASA Earth Observatory · Aqua MODIS / EOSDIS · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Afternoon cumulus clouds over Sri Lanka, observed by Aqua MODIS on 9 April 2013.
rows.caption: Aqua MODIS image of Sri Lanka, April 2013, illustrating the process: cumulus forms over the sun-warmed island as sea-breeze air moves inland, while the cooler sea stays clear.

rows.credit: NOAA GOES-19 / CIMSS, University of Wisconsin–Madison · public domain · 30 October 2025 · resized
rows.alt: GOES-19 satellite view of a cloud-free band beside western Lake Michigan as a land breeze pushes offshore.
rows.caption: GOES-19 satellite image of Lake Michigan, October 2025. A cloud-free band along the shore marks a land breeze, the night-time reverse of a sea breeze.

rows.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / Scientific Visualization Studio · public domain · resized
rows.alt: NASA CERES map of reflected shortwave radiation averaged over 2000–2015, with a 0–385 W m⁻² color scale.
rows.caption: NASA CERES satellite map of reflected sunlight. Snow- and ice-covered regions and cloudy areas reflect strongly; this is reflected energy in W m⁻², not albedo itself.

rows.credit: NASA / Expedition 66 crew · ISS066-E-86970 · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Orange and blue atmospheric layers above Earth's curved horizon, with a crescent Moon in the black sky.
rows.caption: Earth's atmosphere seen edge-on from the ISS. The weather layer is far thicker than Denver's 1.6 km elevation, so the city lies well inside the troposphere.

rows.credit: Storm Prediction Center / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: A skew-T chart from a weather-balloon sounding, with red temperature and green dew-point lines rising through the atmosphere.
rows.caption: A radiosonde sounding chart. Weather balloons launched twice daily from upper-air stations, including one at Denver, measure how temperature and moisture change with height.

rows.credit: Syced / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
rows.alt: Dense urban development around Hong Kong's harbor, seen from the hills in 2005.
rows.caption: Hong Kong in 2005. Dense development climbs steep hillsides above the harbor, which is why slope stability matters so much here.

rows.credit: Dexter Perkins / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
rows.alt: Rounded remnants of granite emerge from loose weathered material in an exposed rock profile.
rows.caption: Deeply weathered granite with rounded unweathered cores (location outside Hong Kong). It illustrates saprolite, the weak weathered material that forms many Hong Kong slopes.

rows.credit: Syced / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
rows.alt: Dense urban development around Hong Kong's harbor, seen from the hills in 2005.
rows.caption: Hong Kong's harbor and high-rise waterfront, which Mangkhut's winds and storm surge struck in September 2018.

rows.credit: Charlie fong / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
rows.alt: Dusk panorama across the Inner Harbour to the dense buildings of the western Macau Peninsula.
rows.caption: The west side of the Macau Peninsula from across the Inner Harbour, at the mouth of the Pearl River estuary. Much of Macau's low ground is reclaimed land.

rows.credit: NASA astronaut Ed Lu / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
rows.alt: The clear eye and tall spiral cloud walls of Hurricane Isabel, photographed from the ISS.
rows.caption: Hurricane Isabel photographed from the ISS in 2003. An Atlantic hurricane and a Pacific typhoon such as Mangkhut are the same kind of storm, with an eye and an eyewall.

rows.credit: Bill Whittaker / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
rows.alt: Steep, grassy Loess Hills rising behind a cornfield east of Mondamin, Iowa.
rows.caption: Loess Hills, western Iowa, USA. They show the same process as the Loess Plateau: wind-deposited silt that erodes easily once exposed, here farmed along the contours.

rows.credit: US Navy / USDA NRCS Photo Gallery, NRCSIA99138 · public domain · resized
rows.alt: Close-up photograph of a raindrop splashing on soil and throwing droplets and particles outward.
rows.caption: A raindrop striking bare soil (USDA NRCS). Splash detaches particles, the first step in the water erosion that cut the plateau's gullies.
